category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Contrast the course of the bile duct with the portal vein and hepatic artery within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
back:
* Bile duct: Anterior and to the right.
* Hepatic artery: Anterior and to the left.
* Portal vein: Posterior to both structures.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A barium swallow shows narrowing at the level of the T4/T5 vertebrae. Identify the two specific anatomical structures causing this physiological constriction.
back: * Arch of the aorta. * Left principal (main) bronchus. * This represents the middle site of esophageal narrowing.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the tongue tip with that of the posterior one-third.
back:
* Tip: Drains to submental nodes (often bilateral).
* Posterior 1/3: Drains directly to the deep cervical nodes (Jugulodigastric nodes).

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is typically projected on the anterior abdominal wall at the intersection of the right [___] and the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle.
back:
• 9th costal cartilage.
• Corresponds to the point where the linea semilunaris crosses the costal margin.
• Marks the location of the gallbladder fundus.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Describe the anatomical role of paraumbilical veins in establishing portal-systemic circulation during pathology.
back:
*   Paraumbilical veins are portal tributaries located within the falciform ligament
*   They connect the portal vein to superficial systemic abdominal veins
*   In portal hypertension, retrograde flow creates distended "Caput Medusae"

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Superficial venous drainage from the lower anterolateral abdominal wall primarily enters the femoral vein via the [___] vein.
back:
*   Superficial epigastric vein
*   Drains into the femoral vein via the great saphenous vein
*   Enlarges during caval obstruction to form thoracoepigastric shunts
*   Drains the lower anterolateral abdominal wall skin

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A posterior duodenal ulcer that penetrates the wall is most likely to erode the [___] artery, leading to life-threatening hemorrhage.
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery.
* This vessel runs posterior to the first part of the duodenum.
* Erosion typically presents with severe hematemesis or melena.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Contrast the physiological purpose of the tonsillar crypts with the lymphoid follicles within Waldeyer's ring.
back: Crypts increase the surface area for antigen entrapment and exposure to the environment. Follicles are the sites of lymphocyte proliferation and antibody production. Together, they facilitate an active immune loop against inhaled or ingested pathogens.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Distinguish between the primary nodal stations of the stomach's antrum versus the fundus.
back:
* Antrum: Drains to pyloric and right gastric nodes.
* Fundus: Drains to splenic nodes via short gastric vessels.
* Both contribute to the celiac nodal pool.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Distinguish between the hepatic artery proper and the gastroduodenal artery in terms of their courses after arising from the common hepatic artery.
back: * Hepatic Artery Proper: Ascends within the lesser omentum to the liver * Gastroduodenal Artery: Descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum * Gastroduodenal gives rise to the right gastroepiploic artery

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Specify the two anatomical and physiological mechanisms targeted during surgical intervention for chronic peptic ulcers to reduce acid production.
back:
1. Vagus nerves: Interruption of nervous control (Vagotomy).
2. Pyloric antrum: Removal of the hormonal (Gastrin) source (Partial gastrectomy).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A patient is diagnosed with acute mesenteric ischemia due to Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) embolism. Identify the specific segments of the small intestine that will likely undergo necrosis.
back:
*   Distal half of the second part of the duodenum
*   Entirety of the jejunum and ileum
*   Vascular Basis: These segments are supplied by intestinal branches of the SMA

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: Distinguish the location and drainage of the major duodenal papilla from the minor duodenal papilla.
back:
* Major Papilla: Located halfway down the second part of the duodenum; receives main pancreatic and bile ducts.
* Minor Papilla: Located 0.75 inches above the major papilla; receives the accessory pancreatic duct.

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: Classify the underlying origin of indirect inguinal hernias compared to the origin of direct inguinal hernias.
back:
• Indirect: Congenital (preformed sac from processus vaginalis)
• Direct: Acquired (weakness of abdominal wall muscles in old age)

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Distinguish between the ileum and the jejunum regarding their internal mucosal features and lymphoid tissue.
back: * Jejunum: Large, closely set plicae circulares; no Peyer's patches. * Ileum: Low, sparse plicae circulares; contains aggregated lymphoid nodules (Peyer's patches) on the antimesenteric border.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The internal mucosa of the stomach is characterized by longitudinal folds called [___], which serve to increase surface area and flatten during distension.
back:
Rugae.
- Most prominent in the body of the stomach.
- Assist in accommodating large food volumes.
- Form the 'Magenstrasse' (gastric canal) along the lesser curvature.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Lymphoid Anatomy of the Small Intestine
front: Distinguish between the location and appearance of Peyer’s patches in the small intestine.
back:
● Location: Ileum (specifically the antimesenteric border).
● Appearance: Aggregations of lymphoid tissue appearing as oval, elevated patches on the mucosa.
● Function: Localized immune surveillance.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Contrast the physical examination findings of 'Biliary Colic' with 'Acute Cholecystitis' regarding systemic signs and pain duration.
back:
• Biliary Colic: Transient pain (<6 hours), no fever, no inflammatory markers.
• Acute Cholecystitis: Persistent pain (>6 hours), fever, leukocytosis, and positive Murphy’s sign due to gallbladder wall inflammation.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Explain the role of the cremaster muscle and its developmental origin within the spermatic cord.
back:
* Originates from the internal oblique muscle.
* Regulates testicular temperature and provides protection by raising the testis.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: List the three structures that form the boundaries of the superficial inguinal ring's triangular opening.
back: * Base: Pubic crest. * Medial crus: Attachment to pubic symphysis. * Lateral crus: Attachment to pubic tubercle. * Fibers of external oblique aponeurosis.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Which specific part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and lies horizontally across the L3 vertebra, making it susceptible to compression in crush injuries?
back:
Third (Horizontal) Part.
- Crosses the IVC and Aorta.
- Lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
- Vulnerable to being crushed against the vertebral column.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: During a cholecystectomy, a surgeon identifies a ductal junction to avoid injuring the main biliary drainage. Which two ducts meet to form the Common Bile Duct?
back:
* Cystic duct.
* Common hepatic duct.
* This junction typically occurs within the right free margin of the lesser omentum.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the specific lobes of the liver drained by the right and left hepatic ducts.
back:
• Right hepatic duct: Drains the large right lobe
  • Left hepatic duct: Drains the left lobe, caudate lobe, and quadrate lobe
  • Functional significance: Divides the liver into functional halves

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Specify the terminal group of lymph nodes that receive drainage from the appendix after passing through the mesoappendicular nodes.
back:
• Superior mesenteric lymph nodes
• Located around the origin of the superior mesenteric artery
• Follows the midgut lymphatic pathway.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Describe how the autonomic fibers within the spermatic cord contribute to testicular function.
back:
• Sympathetic fibers: Derived from T10-T11 segments via the renal and aortic plexuses
• Function: Regulate vasomotor tone and assist in ductal contraction.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Advanced gastric malignancy may manifest as a periumbilical nodule via spread along paraumbilical lymphatics, clinically known as the [___] nodule.
back:
• Sister Mary Joseph nodule
• Spreads via paraumbilical veins/lymphatics
• Indicates advanced intra-abdominal adenocarcinoma

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Name the triangular peritoneal fold that contains the appendicular artery and determines the degree of mobility of the appendix.
back:
Mesoappendix.
- Derived from the posterior layer of the ileal mesentery.
- Transmits the appendicular artery (branch of ileocolic).
- Short mesoappendix may limit the appendix to a fixed position.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Explain the role of the pampiniform plexus in maintaining testicular physiology within the spermatic cord.
back:
• Countercurrent heat exchange
• Cools arterial blood in the testicular artery by transferring heat to the venous blood
• Maintains temperature ~3°C below core body temp for spermatogenesis.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A patient with a chronic posterior gastric ulcer presents with sudden, life-threatening hematemesis. Erosion has most likely occurred into the [___] artery.
back:
Splenic artery.
- Runs along the upper border of the pancreas.
- Forms part of the stomach bed behind the lesser sac.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Explain the role of the mesenteric arterial arcades in maintaining small bowel perfusion during active gut motility and peristalsis.
back: * Provide a series of redundant anastomotic loops * Ensure continuous blood flow despite local compression of vasa recta * Prevent focal ischemia during vigorous smooth muscle contraction

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Contrast the hepatic portal vein and the hepatic veins regarding their site of termination and connection to the heart.
back:
• Portal Vein: Terminates at the porta hepatis; does not join the IVC
• Hepatic Veins: Emerge from the posterior liver surface; drain directly into the IVC

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A patient with known gallstones develops acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated serum amylase. Explain the anatomical basis for this specific complication.
back:
• Gallstone impaction in the Ampulla of Vater
• Common channel blockage leads to bile reflux into the pancreatic duct, triggering pancreatitis.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Specify the total length of the esophagus and its terminal vertebral level.
back: • Length: ~25 cm (10 inches). • Terminal Level: T11 vertebra. • Ends at the cardiac orifice of the stomach.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: The [___] muscle originates from the posterior nasal spine and palatine aponeurosis, functioning to shorten and elevate the uvula.
back:
• Musculus uvulae
  • Innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X)
  • Helps provide bulk to the soft palate to ensure a tight seal against the pharyngeal wall

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Explain the role and regulation of the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (Sphincter of Oddi).
back:
* Circular smooth muscle surrounding the terminal ducts and ampulla.
* Remains closed between meals to divert bile to the gallbladder.
* Relaxes in response to Cholecystokinin (CCK) to allow bile entry into the duodenum.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A 60-year-old patient is diagnosed with diverticulosis. Identify the specific anatomical 'weak points' where these mucosal herniations typically occur.
back:
• Location: Between the teniae coli longitudinal bands
• Anatomy: Where nutrient arteries (vasa recta) pierce the circular muscle layer
• Most common site: The sigmoid colon is the most frequent region involved.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: The [___] nerve is a constituent of the spermatic cord and provides motor innervation to the cremasteric fascia.
back:
* Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
* Supplies the cremaster muscle.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Identify the appendiceal position that most frequently results in early vomiting and diarrhea due to its direct proximity and irritation of the terminal ileum.
back:
Pre-ileal or Post-ileal (Retro-ileal).
- Tip lies anterior or posterior to the terminal ileum.
- Irritation causes hyperperistalsis of the small bowel.
- Can mimic gastroenteritis symptoms.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct with one impacted in the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater).
back:
• Cystic Duct: Biliary colic or cholecystitis; no jaundice.
• Ampulla: Obstructive jaundice; possible acute pancreatitis due to bile reflux into the pancreatic duct.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: In surgical anatomy, the [___] incision is performed approximately 2.5 cm (1 inch) lateral to the midline, involving the incision of the anterior rectus sheath and lateral retraction of the rectus abdominis muscle with its nerve supply intact.
back:
* Paramedian incision.
* Used for upper or lower abdominal exposure.
* Maintains the integrity of the rectus muscle and its nerves.
* Creates a strong repair as the muscle acts as a shutter over the incision.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: During an inguinal hernia repair, the surgeon identifies a thin layer of connective tissue lining the deep surface of the transversus abdominis muscle known as the [___].
back:
• Transversalis fascia.
• It forms the deep inguinal ring.
• It continues over the spermatic cord as the internal spermatic fascia.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
front: Explain the role of the inguinal ligament in defining the boundaries of the inguinal canal.
back: - Forms the floor (inferior wall) of the canal - Created by the 'rolled-under' edge of the external oblique aponeurosis - Provides structural support for the spermatic cord or round ligament

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: The superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall is divided into an outer fatty layer called Camper's fascia and a deeper membranous layer known as [___].
back:
• Scarpa's fascia.
• It is thin, membranous, and lacks fat.
• It continues into the perineum as Colles' fascia.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a protrusion medial to the inferior epigastric artery that appears during coughing. Weakness in which specific muscle-derived structure most likely allows this herniation?
back: Conjoint tendon. - Forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in the Hesselbach's triangle. - Medial position to the vessels confirms a direct inguinal hernia rather than indirect.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The first major unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta arising at the level of the T12 vertebra to supply the foregut is the [___].
back:
• Celiac Trunk (Celiac Artery)
• Supplies the esophagus to the second part of the duodenum
• Divides into left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Within the hepatoduodenal ligament, the portal vein is located in which specific position relative to the bile duct?
back: * Posterior. * The bile duct lies anterior and to the right. * The hepatic artery lies anterior and to the left.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: A patient with a firm parotid mass presents with total facial muscle paralysis. Distinguish this from a mass where facial function is preserved.
back:
- Facial palsy: Indicates parotid malignancy (e.g., mucoepidermoid carcinoma).
- Preserved function: Suggests benign pathology (e.g., Pleomorphic Adenoma).
- Mechanism: Malignant cells infiltrate the facial nerve (CN VII) during tissue invasion.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish the sensory innervation of the hard palate from that of the soft palate.
back:
* Hard Palate: Greater palatine and Nasopalatine nerves (V2)
* Soft Palate: Lesser palatine (V2) and Glossopharyngeal (CN IX)
* V2 provides primary supply via pterygopalatine ganglion

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient with cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. Explain the anatomical basis of the bleeding source found at the distal esophagus.
back:
• Portosystemic anastomosis between left gastric and azygos veins.
• Increased portal pressure causes these thin-walled veins to dilate (varices).
• Rupture leads to massive, life-threatening upper GI bleeding.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Medial Ligamentous Extensions of the Groin
front: Contrast the medial attachments of the inguinal ligament with those of the lacunar ligament during a surgical dissection of the groin.
back: - Inguinal ligament: Directly attaches to the pubic tubercle - Lacunar ligament: Extends posteriorly from the medial inguinal ligament to the pectineal line - Forms the medial femoral ring border

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: State the cutaneous nerve segment (dermatome) that provides sensory innervation to the umbilicus, used as a landmark for abdominal mapping.
back: * T10 dermatome. * Derived from the 10th intercostal nerve. * Marks the watershed area for lymphatic drainage. * Critical surface landmark for subcostal and transverse incisions.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the anatomical route the greater palatine artery takes to reach the oral surface of the hard palate.
back:
• Originates from the Maxillary artery in the pterygopalatine fossa.
• Descends through the greater palatine canal.
• Emerges via the greater palatine foramen.
• Runs anteriorly in a groove near the alveolar border.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the primary lymphatic node of the gallbladder and the subsequent nodal stations it drains into before reaching the celiac nodes.
back:
• Cystic node (of Lund) at the neck
• Hepatic nodes (along hepatic artery)
• Terminal drainage into Celiac nodes.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Gallbladder Fundus
front: The [___] of the gallbladder is the rounded distal portion that projects beyond the inferior border of the liver, typically contacting the anterior abdominal wall at the intersection of the right semilunar line and the 9th costal cartilage.
back:
• Fundus
• Covered completely by peritoneum
• Positioned on the transpyloric plane (L1 level)
• Often full of bile in a fasting state.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Specify the vertical peritoneal reflections that facilitate the spread of infected fluid from the gallbladder region to the pelvis.
back:
* Right paracolic gutter
* Provides a continuous vertical channel lateral to the ascending colon
* Allows fluid to gravitate toward the recto-vesical/recto-uterine pouch.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Distinguish between the anatomical locations of the subphrenic spaces and the paracolic gutters within the peritoneal cavity.
back:
Comparison:
- Subphrenic spaces: Located between the diaphragm and the liver (anterior and posterior).
- Paracolic gutters: Grooves found lateral and medial to the ascending and descending colons.
- Both serve as conduits for infected fluid.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Explain the anatomical mechanism by which irritation of the hepatic 'bare area' or diaphragmatic peritoneum results in referred pain to the right shoulder.
back: Phrenic nerve mediation. • Irritation affects the diaphragmatic peritoneum (C3-C5). • Pain is referred to C3-C4 dermatomes via supraclavicular nerves. • Both nerves share the same spinal cord segments.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Name the four most common anatomical positions of the appendix tip as described in standard medical texts.
back:
Common Appendiceal Positions
1.  Retrocecal (behind cecum)
2.  Pelvic (against right pelvic wall)
3.  Subcaecal/Paracecal (lateral to cecum)
4.  Pre-/Post-ileal (related to terminal ileum)

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The common hepatic duct and the [___] unite to form the bile duct, which then descends behind the first part of the duodenum.
back:
* Cystic duct.
* The resulting bile duct (common bile duct) is approximately 3 inches (8 cm) long.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: List the sequence of biliary ducts bile must traverse from the liver to the duodenum in a patient who has undergone a cholecystectomy.
back:
• Right and Left Hepatic Ducts.
• Common Hepatic Duct.
• Bile Duct (Common Bile Duct).
• Major Duodenal Papilla.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Anatomical Dimensions of the Biliary Tree
front: Distinguish between the common hepatic duct and the bile duct (Common Bile Duct) regarding their average anatomical lengths.
back: The common hepatic duct is approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm) long. The bile duct is twice as long, measuring approximately 3 inches (8 cm) in total.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Distinguish the originating cranial nerves and ganglia for the secretomotor pathways of the parotid versus the submandibular gland.
back:
- Parotid: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the Otic ganglion.
- Submandibular: Facial nerve (CN VII) via the Submandibular ganglion.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: The communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs is the epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow), which is bounded anteriorly by the [___].
back:
* Free margin of the lesser omentum.
* Contains the portal triad: portal vein, hepatic artery proper, and bile duct.
* Serves as the entrance to the omental bursa.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Describe how the final destination of all gastric lymph relates to the major vessels of the posterior abdominal wall.
back:
1. Gastric lymph reaches celiac nodes.
2. Celiac nodes surround the celiac trunk origin.
3. Located anterior to the abdominal aorta at T12/L1 level.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Distinguish between the jejunum and ileum regarding their wall thickness and internal mucosal folds.
back:
*   Jejunum: Thicker, redder walls with large, closely set plicae circulares
*   Ileum: Thinner, paler walls with smaller, widely separated or absent plicae circulares
*   Clinical: Useful for differentiating proximal from distal small bowel

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: Distinguish between the Iliohypogastric and Ilioinguinal nerves regarding their final exit points through the external oblique muscle.
back:
- Iliohypogastric: Pierces the external oblique aponeurosis superior to the superficial inguinal ring.
- Ilioinguinal: Passes through the inguinal canal and emerges specifically via the superficial inguinal ring.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: A patient with suspected portal vein blockage presents with a 'caput medusae.' Why is this specific clinical sign absent in cases of pre-hepatic portal vein thrombosis occurring distal to the paraumbilical origin?
back: The paraumbilical veins arise from the left branch of the portal vein. If the blockage is distal to this point, portal pressure is not transmitted to the umbilical anastomosis.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the anatomical origin of the 'Common Bile Duct' with its physiological termination point.
back:
• Origin: Union of the cystic duct and common hepatic duct
• Termination: Joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
• Drainage: Empties into the 2nd part of the duodenum

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
coreConcept: Protective Function of the Greater Omentum
front: Explain the functional mechanism by which the greater omentum prevents generalized peritonitis during acute appendicitis.
back:
Peritoneal Adhesion Mechanism

*   Inflammatory exudate makes the omentum sticky
*   It adheres to and wraps around the infected organ
*   Physical barrier prevents spread of toxins to the greater sac

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A 65-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. An ultrasound suggests a mass in the head of the pancreas. Identify the biliary structure most likely obstructed in its third part.
back: The bile duct (Common Bile Duct). It lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head; compression here results in proximal biliary dilation and obstructive jaundice.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Explain the anatomical formation of the portal vein, including its primary tributaries and anatomical location.
back:
• Formation: Union of the Superior Mesenteric Vein and the Splenic Vein.
• Location: Posterior to the neck of the pancreas.
• Termination: Enters the porta hepatis and divides into right and left branches.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: The deep inguinal ring is formed as an oval opening within the [___] fascia.
back: * Transversalis fascia. * Located 1.25 cm above the inguinal ligament. * Positioned at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the ASIS and symphysis pubis.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the motor innervation of the Tensor Veli Palatini with the other four muscles of the soft palate.
back:
• Tensor Veli Palatini: Mandibular division of Trigeminal Nerve (CN V3).
• Others (Levator Veli Palatini, Palatoglossus, Palatopharyngeus, Musculus Uvulae): Pharyngeal plexus (Cranial Accessory/Vagus).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A surgeon performing an esophagogastric resection notes nerves on the esophageal surface. Identify these trunks and their origins.
back: • Anterior Vagal Trunk: Derived primarily from the left vagus nerve. • Posterior Vagal Trunk: Derived primarily from the right vagus nerve. • Enter abdomen through the T10 hiatus.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: A 22-year-old male presents with low abdominal pain and urinary frequency. Physical exam reveals minimal anterior abdominal tenderness, but digital rectal examination elicits significant pain on the right side. Identify the likely appendiceal position.
back:
Pelvic position.
- Tips hangs down into the true pelvis.
- Irritates the obturator internus muscle (Positive Obturator sign).
- May contact the bladder or rectum, causing pelvic symptoms.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Describe the anatomical boundaries and clinical significance of the "bare area" of the liver.
back:
• Posterior surface area devoid of peritoneum.
• Bounded by the layers of the coronary ligament.
• Clinically significant for direct lymphatic spread of infection to the thorax.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Contrast the localization and character of pain arising from the parietal peritoneum with that of the visceral peritoneum.
back:
*   Parietal: Sharp, severe, and precisely localized (somatic).
*   Visceral: Dull, vague, and poorly localized (referred to midline).
*   Somatic nerves supply the former, while autonomic afferents supply the latter.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Contrast the surface markings of the parotid duct with the location of the accessory parotid gland.
back:
• Duct: Middle third of a line from tragus to mid-upper lip.
• Accessory Gland: Small detached part often found superior to the duct.
• Both lie superficial to the masseter muscle.

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: A patient with suspected cholecystitis experiences tenderness in the Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ). To find the fundus of the gallbladder, you should palpate where the right [___] meets the costal margin.
back:
* Linea semilunaris (at the tip of the 9th costal cartilage)
* Quadrant: Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ)

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: The [___] fascia of the spermatic cord is the innermost layer and is directly continuous with the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring.
back:
* Internal spermatic fascia.
* Derived from the transversalis fascia.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A 60-year-old male with a history of chronic posterior gastric wall ulceration presents with sudden massive hematemesis and signs of shock. The eroded vessel likely responsible for this hemorrhage is the [___].
back:
• Splenic artery
• Located on the superior border of the pancreas
• Forms the immediate posterior relation of the stomach

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Describe the reciprocal autonomic control of the pyloric sphincter regarding its motor and inhibitory nerve fibers.
back:
Pyloric Autonomic Control:
- Sympathetic: Fibers from the celiac plexus are motor (cause contraction) to the sphincter.
- Parasympathetic: Vagal fibers are inhibitory (cause relaxation).
- This mechanism regulates the emptying of chyme into the small intestine.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: Name the two distinct layers of the superficial fascia found in the lower part of the anterolateral abdominal wall.
back:
• Camper’s Fascia: Outer fatty superficial layer
• Scarpa’s Fascia: Inner membranous deep layer
• Scarpa's is continuous with Colles' fascia in the perineum
• Scarpa's fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: Contrast the peritoneal reflections of the pancreatic head with those of the pancreatic tail.
back:
* Head: Strictly retroperitoneal; fixed to the posterior abdominal wall behind the parietal peritoneum.
* Tail: Intraperitoneal; passes forward within the splenorenal ligament to reach the hilum of the spleen.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The smooth muscle complex that regulates the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum at the major papilla is the [___].
back:
• Sphincter of Oddi (Sphincter of hepatopancreatic ampulla)
• Function: Remains closed during non-digestive periods to allow gallbladder storage
• Reflex: Relaxes in response to cholecystokinin (CCK)

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Contrast the venous drainage patterns seen in Caput Medusae versus the 'Caval-Caval' shunt observed in superior vena cava obstruction.
back:
• Caput Medusae: Portal-Systemic (Paraumbilical to Superficial Epigastric); blood radiates from umbilicus
• Caval-Caval: Systemic-Systemic (Lateral Thoracic to Superficial Epigastric); blood flows upward/downward bypasses vena cava

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Detail how the mesoappendix influences the mobility and blood supply of the appendix across its varying anatomical positions.
back:
* Triangular peritoneal fold derived from the mesentery.
* Carries the appendicular artery (branch of ileocolic).
* Short mesoappendix limits mobility, keeping the appendix fixed.
* Positions like subcecal depend on mesoappendiceal length.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with shifting dullness and a distended abdomen. Explain the anatomical basis for where fluid first accumulates in the supine position.
back: • Hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch). • Right subphrenic space. • Most dependent part of upper peritoneal cavity when supine. • Communicates with right paracolic gutter.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Explain the role of Cholecystokinin (CCK) upon its release into the duodenum during the digestion of fatty foods.
back:
* Triggers gallbladder contraction.
* Induces relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.
* Facilitates bile entry into the second part of the duodenum via the major papilla.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Lymph from the gallbladder first drains into the [___] lymph node located near its neck before passing to hepatic and celiac nodes.
back: The cystic lymph node. It is situated near the neck of the gallbladder and cystic duct; efferent vessels pass to the hepatic nodes and ultimately to the celiac lymph nodes.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient presents with a wrinkled, atrophied right side of the tongue that deviates toward the right when protruded. Describe the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
*   Lesion of the right Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
*   Paralysis of the ipsilateral genioglossus muscle.
*   The healthy contralateral muscle pushes the tongue toward the weak side.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Contrast the anatomical mechanism of intussusception with that of volvulus.
back:
* Intussusception: Telescoping of a proximal bowel segment into a distal segment (e.g., ileocolic).
* Volvulus: Twisting of a mobile bowel loop around its mesentery (e.g., sigmoid).
* Both result in intestinal obstruction and vascular compromise.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Explain the significance of 'streaming' within the portal vein regarding the anatomical distribution of metastatic disease to the liver.
back:
• Right Lobe: Receives SMV blood (midgut)
• Left/Caudate/Quadrate: Receives Splenic and IMV blood (hindgut/spleen)
• Laminar flow: Prevents complete mixing before entry
• Result: Metastases localize based on primary organ drainage

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Medial Bony Extent of the Inguinal Ligament
front: Identify the specific bony landmark that serves as the medial-most extent of the inguinal ligament.
back: - The pubic tubercle - Acts as the medial anchor for the inguinal ligament - Serves as a reference for the superficial inguinal ring and femoral canal

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: During a diagnostic peritoneal lavage or paracentesis, the needle is often inserted through the [___] to ensure it passes through a relatively bloodless, fibrous plane.
back: * Linea alba. * Formed by the decussation of aponeuroses. * Located in the midline. * Provides safe access to the parietal peritoneum while avoiding the rectus muscles.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Explain the microanatomic mechanism by which the dual blood supply of the liver reaches the central vein of a lobule.
back:
• Arterial (hepatic artery) and venous (portal vein) blood mix within liver sinusoids.
• Blood percolates past hepatocytes for metabolic exchange.
• Converges into the central vein for drainage into hepatic veins.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: The central part of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum receives its sensory innervation via the [___] nerves.
back:
• Phrenic nerves
• Nerve roots C3, C4, and C5
• Irritation often refers pain to the shoulder tip (C4 dermatome)

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Distinguish between the drainage endpoints of the Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV) and the Inferior Mesenteric Vein (IMV) within the portal system.
back:
• SMV: Joins splenic vein to form the portal vein trunk
• IMV: Typically drains into the splenic vein behind the body of the pancreas

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The bile duct terminates by joining the main pancreatic duct to form the [___], which enters the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.
back: Hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater). It serves as the common dilated channel for both bile and pancreatic exocrine secretions.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Identify the two primary ducts that unite to form the 'Common Bile Duct' (CBD).
back:
• Cystic duct (from the gallbladder)
• Common hepatic duct (from the liver)
• Location: Usually occurs at the level of the transpyloric plane (L1)

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The small pit located at the apex of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis, representing the embryological origin of the thyroid gland, is the [___].
back:
* Foramen cecum.
* Remnant of the thyroglossal duct.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: Surgical incisions should ideally follow the natural lines of cleavage in the skin, known as [___], to minimize tension and wide scarring.
back: * Langer's lines. * Parallel rows of collagen fibers in the dermis. * Horizontal/oblique orientation on the trunk. * Healing results in narrow, cosmetically superior scars.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A patient with suspected appendicitis exhibits pain during right hip extension (Psoas sign). Describe the anatomical relationship explaining this finding.
back:
* Retrocecal appendix position
* Appendix lies directly on the right psoas major muscle
* Inflammation irritates the psoas fascia
* Stretching the muscle during extension causes localized somatic pain

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Describe the anatomical basis for why a posterior gastric ulcer often presents as referred pain in the back.
back:
* The stomach’s posterior wall forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac.
* Penetrating ulcers can involve the pancreas or splenic artery.
* Irritation of these retroperitoneal structures refers pain to the back.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches in terms of their muscular contents and relative positions.
back:
• Palatoglossal Arch: Anterior; contains the palatoglossus muscle.
• Palatopharyngeal Arch: Posterior; contains the palatopharyngeus muscle.
• Palatine tonsil lies in the tonsillar fossa between these arches.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: Distinguish between the histological acini types of the submandibular and sublingual glands.
back:
* Submandibular: Mixed gland, predominantly serous acini
* Sublingual: Mixed gland, predominantly mucous acini
* Submandibular secretions are more serous compared to the highly viscous sublingual mucus

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the external vascular and mesenteric fat distribution of the jejunum with that of the ileum.
back:
● Jejunum: 1-2 large arterial arcades; long vasa recta; translucent 'windows' (less fat near gut).
● Ileum: 3-4+ small arcades; short vasa recta; opaque mesentery (fat reaches gut wall).

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: A 65-year-old male with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, severe periumbilical pain. Blockage of the vessel supplying the gut from the distal duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon is suspected. Identify this vessel.
back:
• Vessel: Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA).
• Origin: Abdominal aorta at L1 level.
• Course: Passes behind the neck of the pancreas and in front of the third part of the duodenum.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Explain the functional mechanism by which the entry of fatty chyme into the duodenum leads to the delivery of bile into the small intestine.
back:
* Fat triggers Cholecystokinin (CCK) release from duodenal mucosa.
* CCK causes gallbladder contraction.
* Simultaneously relaxes the Sphincter of Oddi at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
coreConcept: Autonomic Supply of the Small Bowel
front: Describe the source and pathway of sympathetic innervation to the small intestine distal to the duodenum.
back:
* Derived from T9-T11 spinal segments.
* Fibers pass through the Lesser and Greater splanchnic nerves.
* Synapse in the Superior Mesenteric Plexus/Ganglion.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: A patient with late-stage appendicitis exhibits localized guarding and rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Apply your knowledge of nerve supply to explain which layer is now involved.
back:
- Parietal peritoneum.
- Somatic sensory nerves (Lower thoracic/L1) are irritated by the underlying inflammation.
- Reflex spasm of overlying muscles occurs via the same segmental nerve supply.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 22-year-old male presents with acute pain in the right iliac fossa. To locate the base of the appendix on the cadaveric cecum, the surgeon should follow the [___] to their point of convergence.
back:
### Teniae Coli convergence
* All three bands meet at the posteromedial surface of the cecum.
* This point marks the anatomical base of the appendix.
* Used to differentiate the appendix from small bowel loops.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: During a cholecystectomy, the surgeon identifies the cystic artery within the cystohepatic triangle. What is the typical origin of this vessel?
back: * Right hepatic artery. * Branch of the hepatic artery proper. * Located in Calot's triangle.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: In preparation for an appendectomy, a muscle-splitting McBurney's incision is typically centered at a point [___] inches above and medial to the anterior superior iliac spine.
back:
2 inches (5 cm).
- Located in the right iliac region.
- Splits the external/internal obliques and transversus in line with their fibers.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Explain the characteristic vascular arrangement of the jejunum that distinguishes it from the ileum during surgical inspection.
back: * Possesses few large arterial arcades * Contains long, infrequent vasa recta (straight arteries) * Mesentery typically contains less fat, allowing easier visualization of these vessels

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Contrast the typical clinical complications of a perforated ulcer on the anterior wall versus the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.
back:
• Anterior: Perforation into the greater sac, causing diffuse peritonitis
• Posterior: Erosion of the gastroduodenal artery, causing severe hemorrhage
• Anterior fluids may track to the right iliac fossa.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of a retrocecal appendix with a pelvic appendix regarding findings on physical examination.
back:
Retrocecal vs. Pelvic Positions
*   Retrocecal: Often ‘silent’ on abdominal palpation; positive psoas sign
*   Pelvic: Suprapubic tenderness; tenderness on the right side during rectal or vaginal examination

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: The free margin of the falciform ligament contains a fibrous cord called the [___], which represents the obliterated remains of the fetal left umbilical vein.
back:
• Ligamentum teres (Round ligament of the liver).
• Extends from the umbilicus to the notch on the liver's lower border.
• Joins the left branch of the portal vein.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the role of the ileocecal valve in gastrointestinal transit and the hormonal factor that induces its relaxation.
back:
Ileocecal Valve Function
- Controls flow from the ileum to the cecum.
- Prevents fecal reflux into the small intestine.
- Relaxation is induced by the hormone Gastrin.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is surface projected at the intersection of the right [___] and the 9th costal cartilage.
back:
• Linea semilunaris (lateral edge of rectus abdominis)
• Corresponds to the tip of the ninth costal cartilage
• Clinically significant for localizing the gallbladder during palpation.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers reach the parotid gland via the [___] nerve.
back:
- Auriculotemporal nerve.
- Branch of the Mandibular nerve (V3).
- Conveys fibers originating from the Otic ganglion.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the three anatomical sites of esophageal constriction and their approximate distances from the upper incisor teeth.
back: * Pharyngoesophageal junction (C6): 15 cm. * Aortic arch and Left bronchus (T4/T5): 25 cm. * Diaphragmatic hiatus (T10): 40 cm.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: The peritoneal pouch located behind the cecum where the appendix is most commonly found is the [___] recess.
back:
• Retrocecal recess.
• One of three common recesses in the cecal region.
• Clinically important site for localized retrocecal appendicitis and potential internal herniation.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: A 22-year-old patient undergoes an emergency appendectomy where the surgeon splits the external and internal oblique muscles in the direction of their fibers at McBurney's point. Identify the specific surgical incision and its primary anatomical advantage.
back: - McBurney’s (Gridiron) incision - Muscle-splitting technique - Fibers are separated, not transected - Minimizes nerve damage and preserves wall integrity

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Anatomical Formation of the Portal Vein
front: The hepatic portal vein is formed by the union of the splenic vein and the [___] vein at the L2 vertebral level.
back: * Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV). * Occurs posterior to the neck of the pancreas. * Collects blood from the midgut and splenic territories.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: List the anatomical layers traversed by a needle during a midline abdominal paracentesis.
back: ● 1. Skin and Superficial fascia. ● 2. Linea alba (fibrous tissue). ● 3. Transversalis fascia. ● 4. Extraperitoneal fat. ● 5. Parietal peritoneum.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: Explain the anatomical advantage of the McBurney’s 'muscle-splitting' incision used during a routine appendectomy.
back: * Muscles are split in the direction of their fibers rather than cut. * External oblique, internal oblique, and transversus are separated. * Spares segmental nerves. * Fibers fall back together upon closure, maintaining wall strength.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Name the specific peritoneal reflection that contains the ligamentum teres hepatis and connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
* Falciform ligament.
* A two-layered vertical reflection.
* Extends from the umbilicus to the anterior and superior surfaces of the liver.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the typical arterial origin of the cystic artery and the anatomical space in which it is usually found during cholecystectomy.
back:
• Origin: Right hepatic artery
• Space: Cystohepatic Triangle (Calot's Triangle)
• Surgeons must ligate this carefully to avoid injuring the common hepatic duct.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the arterial supply of the transverse colon's proximal two-thirds with its distal one-third on an anatomical model.
back:
• Proximal 2/3: Middle colic artery (branch of SMA)
• Distal 1/3: Left colic artery (branch of IMA)
• Clinical: Marks the midgut-hindgut embryological transition

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The three longitudinal muscle bands of the large intestine, known as the teniae coli, converge at the base of the [___] on the posteromedial surface of the cecum.
back: * Vermiform appendix. * This convergence serves as a critical surgical landmark for locating the appendix. * The longitudinal muscle becomes a continuous layer at this point.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
coreConcept: Surgical Safety in Submandibular Gland Excision
front: During submandibular gland excision, the [___] branch of the facial nerve must be protected by placing the skin incision at least 2 cm below the lower border of the mandible.
back:
* Marginal mandibular branch
* Injury causes paralysis of the muscles of the lower lip
* It usually loops below the mandible before crossing it

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: A patient presents with a perforated posterior gastric ulcer. Fluids are found accumulating in the omental bursa. Identify the anatomical pathway that connects this bursa to the greater sac.
back: * Epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow). * Located behind the free border of the lesser omentum. * Bound by the inferior vena cava posteriorly and the portal triad anteriorly.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Chronic gastric ulcers typically occur within the alkaline-producing mucosa of the stomach, most frequently located on or near the [___].
back:
The lesser curvature.
- Usually located close to the incisura angularis.
- Occurs where acid-secreting and alkaline-secreting mucosa meet.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: List the primary structures that constitute the 'Stomach Bed'.
back:
• Left crus of diaphragm
  • Left suprarenal gland and upper left kidney
  • Splenic artery and Pancreas
  • Transverse mesocolon

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Describe how the liver receives its dual blood supply in terms of vessel contribution and nutrient content.
back: * Portal Vein (70%): Brings venous blood rich in products of digestion. * Hepatic Artery (30%): Supplies oxygenated blood. * Both drain into liver sinusoids then to central veins.

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: The horizontal abdominal plane passing through the level of the L1 vertebra, which intersects the hila of both kidneys and the pylorus, is the [___] plane.
back: The Transpyloric plane. This high-yield landmark is situated at the L1 vertebral level. It bisects the pylorus of the stomach, the neck of the pancreas, the duodenojejunal flexure, and the hila of both kidneys.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: The rectus sheath extends from the xiphoid process to the pubic crest; however, the level at which the posterior wall ends and the rectus abdominis muscle begins to lie directly upon the transversalis fascia is the [___].
back: • Arcuate line (of Douglas). • Formation: Above this line, Internal Oblique aponeurosis splits to enclose the muscle. Below it, all three lateral muscle aponeuroses move anteriorly. • Provides a transition point for inferior epigastric vessel entry.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Explain the clinical significance of McBurney’s point in a physical examination for suspected appendicitis.
back:
* Surface landmark for the base of the appendix
* Point between lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of spinoumbilical line
* Identifies site of maximal tenderness in acute cases

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
coreConcept: Muscular Boundaries of the Inguinal Canal
front: A 28-year-old male presents with an inguinal hernia. During surgical repair, the surgeon identifies a muscle whose lower free border arches over the spermatic cord to form the 'roof' of the inguinal canal. This muscle is the [___].
back:
Internal Oblique.
- Fibers run superomedially (upwards and medially).
- Lower fibers give rise to the cremasteric muscle.
- Contributes to the conjoint tendon (with transversus abdominis).
- Forms part of the anterior and posterior walls of the canal.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
coreConcept: Nerve supply of Tensor Veli Palatini
front: The only muscle of the soft palate not innervated by the pharyngeal plexus is the [___].
back: Tensor veli palatini. It is innervated by the mandibular nerve (V3) via the nerve to the medial pterygoid. This muscle is unique as it is the only palatal muscle derived from the first branchial arch.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Distinguish between the mesentery of the small intestine and the lesser omentum based on their visceral connections.
back:
• Mesentery: Connects jejunum/ileum to the posterior abdominal wall
• Lesser Omentum: Connects liver to lesser curvature of stomach and duodenum
• Both serve as conduits for neurovascular structures.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals dilated veins in the lower esophagus. These varices result from an anastomosis involving which portal tributary?
back:
• Left Gastric Vein
• Anastomoses with esophageal branches of the azygos system
• Key portal-systemic communication site

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: During cholecystectomy, the surgeon identifies the cystohepatic triangle (of Calot), which is bounded medially by the common hepatic duct and inferiorly by the [___].
back:
• Cystic duct.
• Superior boundary is the liver's visceral surface.
• Contains the cystic artery, a vital landmark for ligation.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A 40-year-old female with a history of three C-sections presents with vomiting and abdominal distension. Imaging shows dilated small bowel loops. What is the most likely anatomical cause of her obstruction?
back: • Peritoneal adhesions. • Result from previous surgical trauma. • Fibrin replaced by fibrous tissue. • Forms abnormal bands that kink or compress the gut.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Distinguish between the localized manifestations of an anterior duodenal ulcer versus a posterior duodenal ulcer.
back:
- Anterior: Peritonitis (free air in greater sac).
- Posterior: Hemorrhage (gastroduodenal artery erosion) or pancreatic involvement.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Outline the anatomical step-by-step pathway of lymphatic drainage from the palatine tonsil.
back: Lymph leaves the tonsil and pierces the superior constrictor muscle. It enters the loose areolar tissue and then drains into the jugulodigastric node. This node is situated in the upper deep cervical chain behind the angle of the mandible.

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: Contrast the terminal sensory distribution of the T7-T11 nerves with that of the Iliohypogastric and Ilioinguinal nerves.
back:
- T7-T11: Supply the epigastric and umbilical regions; pass through the rectus sheath.
- Iliohypogastric/Ilioinguinal (L1): Supply the skin above the inguinal ligament and pubis; do not enter the rectus sheath.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Identify the specific hepatic and gastric landmarks that serve as the vertical attachment sites for the two layers of the lesser omentum.
back:
* Liver: Fissure for ligamentum venosum and margins of the porta hepatis.
* Stomach: Lesser curvature.
* Duodenum: First 2 cm (approx. 1 inch) of the superior part.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Distinguish the drainage territories of the right and left hepatic ducts within the liver.
back:
* Right Hepatic Duct: Drains the right lobe of the liver.
* Left Hepatic Duct: Drains the left lobe, caudate lobe, and quadrate lobe.
* They unite to form the common hepatic duct at the porta hepatis.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Identify the primary lymphatic group that receives drainage from the lower half of the greater curvature.
back: Right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) nodes. • Located between the layers of the greater omentum. • Efferents pass to the subpyloric nodes. • Final destination is the celiac group.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The most common anatomical variation of the vermiform appendix, occurring in approximately 64% of the population, is the [___] position.
back:
Retrocecal (or retrocolic).
- Tip lies behind the cecum or ascending colon.
- Often situated in the retrocecal recess.
- Associated with a positive Psoas sign.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: List the anatomical and clinical features associated with the 'Rule of 2s' for an ileal diverticulum.
back:
* Found in 2% of the population.
* Located 2 feet from the ileocecal valve.
* Approximately 2 inches in length.
* May contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric/pancreatic).

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: List the boundaries of the Cystohepatic Triangle (of Calot), which is essential for identifying biliary structures during surgery.
back:
* Superior: Visceral surface of liver
* Lateral: Cystic duct
* Medial: Common Hepatic Duct
* Contains the cystic artery

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the primary group of lymph nodes that receive drainage from the tissues of the hard palate.
back:
• Upper deep cervical lymph nodes.
• Specifically the jugulodigastric nodes.
• Some drainage also passes to the submandibular lymph nodes.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Describe the anatomical pathway of lymphatic drainage from the stomach to the thoracic duct.
back:
Lymph follows arteries to regional nodes (Gastric, Gastroepiploic).
- All drain into Celiac Lymph Nodes.
- Passes to Intestinal Lymph Trunk.
- Enters Cisterna Chyli and then Thoracic Duct.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Contrast the clinical significance of the right subphrenic space versus the right paracolic gutter regarding infected fluid movement.
back:
• Subphrenic space: Common site for abscess collection due to dependency in supine patients.
• Paracolic gutter: Provides a pathway for fluid to travel from the upper abdomen to the pelvis.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Specify the vertebral levels where the esophagus passes through the diaphragm and where it terminates at the stomach.
back:
• Diaphragmatic Hiatus: T10 level
• Termination (Cardiac Orifice): T11 level
• Course: Approximately 1.25 cm of abdominal length.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: A patient presents with a sore throat and an enlarged, tender lymph node behind the angle of the mandible. Apply anatomical knowledge to identify the most likely primary site of infection.
back: The palatine tonsil. This organ drains primarily to the jugulodigastric node of the deep cervical chain. Inflammation of the tonsil (tonsillitis) frequently causes this specific node to become enlarged, tender, and palpable clinically.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Describe the mechanism by which venous blood from the upper anal canal reaches the liver versus the systemic circulation in a portal hypertension model.
back: * Upper canal: Superior rectal vein drains into the portal system. * Lower canal: Middle/inferior rectal veins drain into systemic iliac veins. * Anastomosis at the pectinate line causes hemorrhoids.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Why is the midline approach through the linea alba considered anatomically safer for paracentesis than a lateral approach through the rectus sheath?
back:
• The linea alba is a relatively avascular fibrous plane.
• Lateral approaches risk lacerating the inferior epigastric artery.
• Lateral approaches require traversing multiple vascularized muscle layers (obliques/transversus).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A 45-year-old male presents with severe hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Identify the artery most likely eroded.
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery
* Located posterior to the 1st part of the duodenum
* Erosion leads to massive, life-threatening hemorrhage into the lesser sac
* It is a branch of the hepatic artery.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Contrast the diagnostic findings of a barium swallow in a patient with Achalasia versus a patient with advanced GERD leading to a peptic stricture.
back:
• Achalasia: Smooth, symmetrical 'bird-beak' narrowing with proximal dilatation
• GERD Stricture: Fixed, irregular narrowing in the lower third
• Strictures result from chronic inflammation and fibrosis

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Identify the venous tributaries that unite within the parotid gland to form the retromandibular vein.
back:
• Superficial temporal vein.
• Maxillary vein.
• The retromandibular vein eventually divides into anterior and posterior divisions.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Identify the cranial nerves whose injury would cause deviation of the tongue and the uvula respectively.
back:
• Tongue: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); deviates toward lesion side
• Uvula: Vagus nerve (CN X); deviates away from lesion side
• Key clinical distinction for brainstem lesions.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: Identify the two specific muscle aponeuroses that fuse to form the conjoint tendon and state its medial insertion point.
back: * Internal oblique and transversus abdominis. * Inserts into the pubic crest and pectineal line. * Forms the medial part of the inguinal canal's posterior wall.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: Contrast the anatomical location of the neck of the sac in direct versus indirect inguinal hernias relative to the inferior epigastric artery.
back: Indirect: Lateral to the artery (through deep ring). • Direct: Medial to the artery (through Hesselbach's triangle). • Direct hernias are typically acquired due to weak musculature.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: Describe how the relationship between the conjoint tendon and the superficial inguinal ring compensates for the 'weak spot' in the external oblique aponeurosis.
back: * Conjoint tendon lies immediately posterior to the superficial ring. * Provides a strong muscular barrier where the anterior wall is weakest. * Prevents direct protrusion through the external oblique defect.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A 70-year-old male presents with acute intestinal obstruction. Radiology shows a 'coffee bean' sign in the sigmoid colon. Explain the anatomical basis of this rotation.
back:
* Sigmoid volvulus
* Rotation around its long, mobile mesentery (sigmoid mesocolon)
* Leads to vascular occlusion and gangrene
* Common in areas with high redundancy

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Clinical dermatome mapping for the anterior abdominal wall indicates that the umbilicus is supplied by the [___] spinal nerve.
back: T10 (Tenth thoracic nerve). - T7 supplies the xiphoid process region. - L1 (iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal) supplies the skin just above the inguinal ligament and pubis.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Identify the precise anatomical site where the common bile duct typically enters the duodenum.
back:
* Major duodenal papilla.
* Located on the medial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum.
* Situated approximately halfway down the length of the segment.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Esophageal varices represent an anatomical portal-systemic anastomosis at the lower esophagus between the [___] vein (portal) and the azygos veins (systemic).
back:
- Left gastric vein (Coronary vein)
- Dilates during portal hypertension
- High risk of life-threatening hematemesis

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Contrast the structures found within the parotid gland by listing them in order from the most superficial to the deepest layer.
back:
• Facial Nerve (CN VII): Most superficial, branches into five terminal groups.
• Retromandibular Vein: Formed by maxillary and superficial temporal veins.
• External Carotid Artery: Deepest structure, divides into terminal branches.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Explain the anatomical mechanism by which bile and pancreatic secretions enter the intestinal lumen.
back:
• Bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite
• Form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
• Opens into the second (descending) part of the duodenum
• Exits via the major duodenal papilla

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Contrast the anatomical division of the liver with its functional (physiological) division regarding the Quadrate and Caudate lobes.
back:
• Anatomical: Belong to the Right Lobe (based on ligamentous attachments).
• Functional: Belong to the Left Lobe.
• Based on the primary division of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and biliary drainage.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: While the visceral peritoneum is sensitive only to stretch and tearing, the parietal peritoneum is uniquely sensitive to pain, temperature, touch, and [___].
back:
*   Pressure.
*   Parietal peritoneum is somatically innervated.
*   Visceral peritoneum lacks receptors for localized thermal or tactile stimuli.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: The hepatic portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins behind the [___] of the pancreas.
back:
• Neck
• Typically occurs at the level of the L2 vertebra

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the upper third, middle third, and lower third of the esophagus.
back:
• Upper Third: Deep cervical nodes.
• Middle Third: Superior and posterior mediastinal nodes.
• Lower Third: Left gastric and celiac nodes.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Organs such as the pancreas, kidneys, and the ascending colon that lie against the posterior abdominal wall and are only partially covered by peritoneum are termed [___].
back:
Retroperitoneal organs.
- They lack a supporting mesentery.
- They are relatively fixed in position.
- Includes suprarenal glands, ureters, and most of the duodenum.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: A patient is diagnosed with gastric carcinoma. To ensure complete oncological clearance, which ultimate nodal group must the surgeon target as the final site of gastric lymphatic drainage?
back:
• Celiac lymph nodes
  • Located around the root of the celiac artery
  • Final common pathway for all gastric lymph vessels

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Compare the clinical signs of a retrocecal appendix with those of a pelvic appendix.
back:
* Retrocecal: May lack anterior tenderness; causes psoas irritation (hip flexion relieves pain)
* Pelvic: Tenderness above symphysis pubis; extreme tenderness on rectal or vaginal examination of the right pelvic peritoneum.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The primary arterial supply to the midgut, which provides branches from the second part of the duodenum down to the distal third of the transverse colon, is the [___] artery.
back: Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA). * Arises from the abdominal aorta at the L1 level. * Supplies the jejunum, ileum, cecum, and ascending colon. * Key branches include ileocolic and right/middle colic arteries.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A 45-year-old female presents with epigastric pain radiating to the right infrascapular region following a fatty meal. Identify the nerve fibers and spinal segments mediating this visceral sensation.
back:
• Afferent sympathetic fibers
• Passing through the celiac plexus
