• Entering spinal cord segments T7 to T9.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Describe the physiological mechanism triggered by fatty food entry into the duodenum that leads to gallbladder emptying.
back:
* Fat stimulates duodenal mucosa to release Cholecystokinin (CCK)
* CCK travels via the bloodstream to the gallbladder
* Causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the Sphincter of Oddi
* Resulting in concentrated bile ejection into the duodenum

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: The specialized lymphoid structure in the nasopharynx that, when hypertrophied, is referred to as adenoids is the [___] tonsil.
back: ● Pharyngeal tonsil ● Situated in the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx ● Lacks true crypts, featuring longitudinal folds instead ● Reaches maximum size in childhood and usually atrophies after puberty.

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: A 70-year-old male with chronic cough presents with a wide-based bulge in the groin. Why is this type of hernia less likely to undergo strangulation than an indirect hernia?
back:
• Wide neck of the hernial sac
• Does not pass through narrow inguinal rings
• Results from generalized muscle weakness rather than a narrow congenital tube

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is situated at the level of the tip of the [___] costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.
back:
* Ninth costal cartilage.
* This location marks the intersection with the linea semilunaris.
* It is the primary site for eliciting Murphy's sign during physical examination.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The angular notch, or [___], is a permanent indentation on the lesser curvature of the stomach that serves as a landmark for the junction between the body and the pyloric antrum.
back:
Incisura angularis.
- Located at the lower end of the lesser curvature.
- Marks the transition point to the pyloric part.
- Visible on both anatomical models and radiographs.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: A surgeon performs a mid-inguinal incision and accidentally transects a superficial artery in the subcutaneous tissue. Which branch of the femoral artery is most likely involved?
back:
*   Superficial epigastric artery
*   A branch of the femoral artery in the inguinal region
*   Runs toward the umbilicus within the superficial fascia
*   Supplies skin and superficial fascia of the lower abdomen

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the motor innervation of the Tensor Veli Palatini with that of all other muscles of the soft palate.
back:
* Tensor Veli Palatini: Nerve to medial pterygoid (Mandibular V3)
* Others: Pharyngeal plexus (Vagus nerve fibers)
* Reflects origin from 1st vs 4th/6th branchial arches

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Identify the peritoneal folds that bound the 'bare area' of the liver and name the major vascular structure in direct contact with this area.
back:
• Bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament.
• Apex formed by the right triangular ligament.
• Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) lies in direct contact.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Analyze the differences in nerve supply and pain localization between the parietal and visceral layers of the peritoneum.
back:
- Parietal: Somatic nerves (T7-L1); sharp, precise, well-localized pain.
- Visceral: Visceral afferents with sympathetic nerves; dull, vague, midline pain.
- Parietal responds to chemical/mechanical irritation; Visceral responds primarily to distension.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Describe the anatomical basis for the development of internal hemorrhoids in a patient with chronic liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
back:
• Portal-systemic anastomosis at the anorectal junction.
• Superior rectal vein (portal) communicates with middle/inferior rectal veins (systemic).
• Increased portal pressure causes these thin-walled veins to dilate and varicosed.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Contrast the composition of the posterior wall of the rectus sheath at the level of the umbilicus versus the level 2 cm above the pubic symphysis.
back: - Umbilicus (above arcuate line): Formed by the posterior lamella of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeurosis. - Above Pubis (below arcuate line): Absent; rectus muscle lies directly on transversalis fascia.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Distinguish between the origins of the Left Gastric and Right Gastric arteries.
back:
• Left Gastric: Arises directly from the celiac trunk.
• Right Gastric: Arises from the hepatic artery (specifically hepatic artery proper).
• Anastomosis: Join along the lesser curvature.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by the [___] nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
back:
* Lingual nerve
* Branch of Mandibular nerve (V3)
* Carries general somatic afferents (pain, touch, temperature)

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Explain the anatomical route taken by lymph from the lesser curvature of the stomach toward the thoracic duct.
back:
* Enters left and right gastric nodes.
* Passes to celiac nodes.
* Enters the intestinal lymph trunk.
* Drains into the cisterna chyli.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the anatomical attachments and mobility of the transverse colon with the descending colon as seen on a cadaver.
back: * Transverse Colon: Intraperitoneal and highly mobile; suspended by the transverse mesocolon. * Descending Colon: Retroperitoneal and fixed; covered by peritoneum only on its anterior and lateral surfaces.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Pathological accumulation of excess serous fluid within the peritoneal cavity is termed [___], commonly occurring in portal hypertension or malignancy.
back: ● Ascites. ● Often requires over 1500mL to be clinically detectable in obese patients. ● Primary cause is liver cirrhosis (portal venous congestion).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A 15-year-old presents with vague periumbilical pain that later shifts to sharp, localized pain in the right iliac fossa. Explain the anatomical basis for this shift.
back:
• Initial: Visceral afferents (T10) from appendiceal distension
• Shift: Irritation of the somatic parietal peritoneum
• Nerve supply: Segmental spinal nerves (T12–L1) provide the localized, sharp sensation.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Name the intermediary lymph node group located at the hilum of the spleen that acts as a relay for gastric lymph.
back:
Splenic (pancreaticosplenic) nodes.
- Receives lymph from the fundus and upper greater curvature.
- Sends efferents along the splenic artery to celiac nodes.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: The thick-walled, muscular component of the spermatic cord that is palpable as a cord-like structure is the [___].
back:
• Vas deferens (Ductus deferens)
• Located in the posterior part of the cord
• Transports sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: A child with a cleft palate frequently suffers from middle ear effusions. Which specific muscle dysfunction is primarily responsible for the failure to aerate the middle ear cavity?
back: Tensor veli palatini. In cleft palate, the muscle's malinsertion prevents it from dilating the auditory tube during swallowing. This leads to negative middle ear pressure and the accumulation of fluid.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: A surgeon palpates the abdomen of two patients; one has localized rebound tenderness, the other has vague, midline aching. Contrast the innervation pathways involved in these two findings.
back:
• Localized pain: Somatic sensory nerves (parietal peritoneum); sensitive to touch/pressure.
• Vague pain: Visceral afferents (visceral peritoneum); sensitive only to stretch.
• Parietal pain is precisely localized via segmental thoracic/lumbar nerves.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the anatomical nature of the cardiac orifice with the pyloric orifice regarding sphincter structure.
back:
* Cardiac Orifice: A physiologic sphincter only (no muscular thickening).
* Pyloric Orifice: A true anatomic sphincter (thickened circular smooth muscle).
* Cardiac is at T11; Pylorus is at L1.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: A patient in the ICU with systemic hypotension develops sudden abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Identify the 'watershed' area most likely affected and the vessels involved.
back: * Splenic flexure (Griffith's point) * The junction between SMA (middle colic) and IMA (left colic) territories * Highly vulnerable to ischemia during low-flow states

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the only tongue muscle not innervated by the hypoglossal nerve and state its specific innervation source.
back:
* Muscle: Palatoglossus.
* Innervation: Vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Describe the anatomical basis for the development of internal hemorrhoids in a patient with portal hypertension.
back:
• Site: Anorectal canal anastomosis.
• Portal: Superior rectal vein (tributary of inferior mesenteric).
• Systemic: Middle and inferior rectal veins (tributaries of internal iliac).
• Result: Retrograde pressure causes varicosity of the internal rectal venous plexus.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Contrast the portal vein and hepatic artery in terms of their relative contributions to the liver's total blood volume and oxygen requirements.
back: Blood Supply Dualism. • Portal Vein: 70% of volume; nutrient-rich but deoxygenated. • Hepatic Artery: 30% of volume; oxygen-rich. • Both enter the liver at the porta hepatis to supply sinusoids.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Describe the hemodynamic route blood follows from the portal vein to the superior vena cava when the esophageal site is utilized.
back:
• Portal vein → Left gastric vein
• Left gastric vein → Esophageal systemic tributaries
• Esophageal veins → Azygos vein
• Azygos vein → Superior Vena Cava (SVC)

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Describe the anatomical origin and clinical significance of the Marginal Artery (of Drummond).
back:
• Origin: Anastomosis of colic branches from the SMA (right and middle colic) and IMA (left colic).
• Distribution: Runs along the mesenteric border of the colon.
• Significance: Provides critical collateral circulation if a major mesenteric vessel is occluded.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Explain the mechanism by which portal hypertension leads to the development of internal hemorrhoids at the anorectal junction.
back:
*   Back-pressure in the superior rectal vein (portal)
*   Blood shunts into middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic)
*   Causes dilation of the submucosal venous plexus in the anal canal

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Stomach Bed Relations and Clinical Anatomy
front: A 55-year-old patient with a chronic gastric ulcer on the posterior wall presents with referred pain to the back. Which organ is the most significant component of the stomach bed in this region?
back:
• Pancreas
  • The ulcer may erode into the splenic artery or pancreatic substance
  • Triggers severe referred back pain

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Anatomical Landmarks of the Large Intestine
front: The longitudinal muscle layer of the large intestine is not continuous but is concentrated into three distinct flat bands called [___], which converge at the base of the vermiform appendix.
back:
### Teniae coli
* Help in locating the appendix during surgery.
* Their contraction creates the sacculated appearance of the colon.
* Absent in the small intestine.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient undergoes surgery on the roof of the mouth. Contrast the territory of the Greater Palatine nerve with that of the Lesser Palatine nerve.
back:
* Greater Palatine: Hard palate mucosa and inner gingiva up to the canine.
* Lesser Palatine: Soft palate and palatine tonsils.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Referred Pain Mechanism of the Stomach
front: A patient experiences dull, poorly localized pain in the epigastric region. If this pain is originating from the stomach, which spinal cord segments are involved in this referred sensation?
back:
T5 to T9 segments:
- Afferent pain fibers accompany sympathetic nerves through the celiac plexus.
- Fibers travel via the greater splanchnic nerves.
- Pain is referred to the epigastrium due to shared dermatomal segments.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is situated at the level of the tip of the [___] right costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.
back: * 9th costal cartilage. * Landmark for Murphy's sign. * Palpated during deep inspiration.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The posterior one-third of the hard palate's skeletal framework is specifically formed by the [___] of the palatine bones.
back:
• Horizontal plates.
• Form the posterior third of the hard palate.
• Articulate with the maxilla at the transverse palatine suture.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the role of the right crus of the diaphragm in preventing gastroesophageal reflux.
back: 1. Acts as an external physiological sphincter. 2. Compresses the lower esophagus during inspiration. 3. Maintains the intra-abdominal pressure gradient.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
coreConcept: Parotid Malignancy and Facial Nerve Palsy
front: A 45-year-old female presents with a hard, fixed mass in the pre-auricular region. Examination reveals inability to close the eye and a drooping mouth on the same side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Malignant parotid tumor.
• Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy suggests nerve infiltration within the gland.
• Benign tumors typically do not cause paralysis.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the visual characteristics of the vasa recta and arterial arcades in the jejunum versus the ileum as seen on a mesenteric cadaveric specimen.
back:
• Jejunum: Long vasa recta with fewer, simpler arterial arcades.
• Ileum: Short vasa recta with numerous, complex (3-4+) arcade tiers.
• Jejunum typically has less mesenteric fat, making vessels more visible.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Following a tonsillectomy, a patient has severe hemorrhage from the tonsillar bed. Which vein, located lateral to the tonsillar capsule, is the most likely source?
back: ● External Palatine Vein ● Resides in the loose connective tissue of the paratonsillar space ● Located between the capsule and superior constrictor ● Most frequent source of primary postoperative bleeding.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Describe the physiological 'loop' of blood returning from the descending colon to the heart via the portal system.
back: * IMV drains to Splenic vein. * Splenic vein joins SMV to form Portal vein. * Portal vein enters liver sinusoids → Hepatic veins → IVC → Right atrium.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic gastric ulcers presents with sudden hematemesis. Imaging reveals a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach. Which major vessel is most likely eroded?
back:
Splenic artery:
- Runs along the superior border of the pancreas.
- Forms a critical part of the posterior stomach bed.
- Erosion leads to massive hemorrhage into the lesser sac (omental bursa).

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: A patient complains of a 'lump' in the back of the throat. Visual inspection reveals irregular lymphoid masses on the posterior third of the tongue. Identify this structure.
back:
Lingual tonsil. 
- Forms the inferior part of Waldeyer's ring. 
- Lies posterior to the sulcus terminalis.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with sudden epigastric pain. Imaging suggests a perforated ulcer in the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. The artery most susceptible to erosion and hemorrhage here is the [___].
back:
*   Gastroduodenal artery
*   Anatomical Relation: Descends immediately posterior to the first part of the duodenum
*   Clinical: Erosion leads to life-threatening hematemesis or melena

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Describe the embryological origin of the appendix as it relates to the development of the midgut loop.
back:
• Derived from the distal end of the cecal diverticulum
• Forms during the 8th week as a narrow, rudimentary part of the cecum
• Retains its origin even as the cecum descends into the right iliac fossa.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: An epigastric hernia typically protrudes through a defect in the [___] between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus.
back: Linea alba. • Often contains extraperitoneal fat. • Starts as a small protrusion that may eventually pull a peritoneal sac with it.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with severe hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Which major artery is most likely eroded?
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery.
* Descends directly behind the first part of the duodenum.
* Erosion leads to massive, life-threatening hemorrhage.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Identify the specific segmental nerves that provide sensory innervation to the parietal peritoneum lining the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
- Lower six thoracic nerves (T7-T12).
- First lumbar nerve (L1).
- These segments also provide the innervation for the overlying muscles and skin.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Contrast the vertical attachment of the root of the mesentery with the horizontal reflection of the transverse mesocolon.
back:
* Root of Mesentery: Extends obliquely from L2 to the right sacroiliac joint
* Transverse Mesocolon: Attaches horizontally across the head and body of the pancreas
* Both provide pathways for major mesenteric neurovasculature.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
coreConcept: Vascular Relations of the Pancreatic Neck
front: Identify the vascular structures that form the immediate posterior boundary of the pancreatic neck.
back:
* Formation of the portal vein (union of splenic and superior mesenteric veins).
* Origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the abdominal aorta.
* These structures are shielded anteriorly by the pancreatic neck.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Identify the cervical fascia layer that forms the parotid capsule and the nerve that provides its sensory innervation.
back:
- Fascia: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
- Nerve: Great Auricular nerve (C2, C3) and Auriculotemporal nerve (V3).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The [___] ligament, also known as the suspensory muscle of the duodenum, anchors the duodenojejunal flexure to the right crus of the diaphragm.
back:
* Ligament of Treitz.
* Formed by a peritoneal fold.
* Stabilizes the junction between the fourth part of the duodenum and the jejunum.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the physiological role of the soft palate during the involuntary phase of deglutition.
back:
• Levator veli palatini raises the palate.
• Tensor veli palatini tightens the aponeurosis.
• Seals the pharyngeal isthmus against the posterior pharyngeal wall.
• Prevents nasal regurgitation of food bolus.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: The parotid gland is enclosed by a capsule derived from the [___] layer of the deep cervical fascia.
back:
• Investing layer.
• It splits to enclose the gland.
• The superficial lamina is thick and attached to the zygomatic arch.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the origin and primary action of the hyoglossus muscle.
back:
*   Origin: Body and greater cornu of hyoid bone.
*   Action: Depresses the tongue.
*   Innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Pancreatic Head Carcinoma and Biliary Obstruction
front: A 60-year-old male presents with painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder. A tumor is most likely compressing the [___] part of the bile duct.
back:
* Third (pancreatic) part
* Located posterior to the head of the pancreas
* Compression leads to obstructive jaundice and proximal biliary dilatation

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: A 60-year-old male with a history of stroke presents with tongue deviation to the right. However, no atrophy or fasciculations are noted, and the tongue deviates away from the brain lesion. Contrast this with a peripheral nerve injury.
back:
• Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) Lesion: Contralateral deviation; no wasting/atrophy
• Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Lesion: Ipsilateral deviation; significant wasting and fasciculations
• Brainstem vs. peripheral nerve involvement.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
coreConcept: Terminal Lymphatic Drainage of the Stomach
front: In the anatomical organization of the stomach's lymphatic system, all terminal vessels from the organ's various zones eventually converge on the [___] nodes located at the origin of the celiac trunk.
back:
Celiac lymph nodes.
- Located on the posterior abdominal wall.
- Final common pathway for all gastric lymph.
- Efferents form the intestinal lymph trunk.
- Drains into the cisterna chyli.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Specify the three components that constitute the 'Pyloric part' of the stomach on a prosected cadaveric specimen.
back:
1. Pyloric Antrum
2. Pyloric Canal
3. Pyloric Sphincter (Orifice)

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: During cholecystectomy, the surgeon must ligate the [___] artery, which typically arises from the right hepatic artery to supply the gallbladder.
back:
• Cystic artery.
• Usually located within the cystohepatic triangle.
• Subject to significant anatomical variations requiring careful identification.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Distinguish between the clinical consequences of a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct versus the common bile duct (CBD).
back:
• Cystic Duct: Biliary colic or cholecystitis; no jaundice.
• Common Bile Duct (Choledocholithiasis): Obstructive jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools due to blockage of biliary drainage.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A 15-year-old boy presents with periumbilical pain that has shifted to the right iliac fossa. Identify the specific surface landmark for the base of the potentially inflamed organ.
back:
* McBurney's point.
* Location: Junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line from the ASIS to the umbilicus.
* Corresponds to the base of the appendix.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: In the cervical region, the esophagus is related anteriorly to the trachea, with the [___] nerves ascending in the groove between these two structures.
back: * Recurrent laryngeal nerves. * Provides motor supply to most laryngeal muscles. * Essential for voice and swallowing coordination.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: An [___] hernia involves the protrusion of extraperitoneal fat and a peritoneal sac through the widest part of the linea alba, typically between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus.
back: Epigastric hernia. * Occurs through the midline fibrous band. * Most common in middle-aged manual laborers. * Sac often contains a small piece of greater omentum.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Surgical identification of the appendix base is traditionally performed by tracing the [___] until they converge at the cecum.
back:
* Teniae coli
* These longitudinal muscle bands converge at the appendicular base
* Provides a reliable surgical guide regardless of tip position

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The second part of the duodenum features the [___], a small internal elevation where the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) opens into the lumen.
back:
* Major duodenal papilla.
* Site for the combined entrance of the bile and main pancreatic ducts.
* Marks the transition from foregut to midgut derivatives.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: List the three concentric layers of fascia that cover the spermatic cord from superficial to deep.
back:
* 1. External spermatic fascia
* 2. Cremasteric fascia
* 3. Internal spermatic fascia

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: The central portion of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum receives its somatic sensory innervation from the [___] nerve.
back:
- Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5).
- Irritation here typically results in referred pain to the shoulder.
- Contrast with peripheral diaphragmatic peritoneum, supplied by intercostal nerves.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Pain during biliary colic is typically referred to the skin of the [___] dermatomes on the lower chest and upper abdominal walls.
back:
• T7 to T9 dermatomes.
• Sensory fibers travel with sympathetic nerves to the celiac plexus.
• Often presents as vague pain in the epigastric region.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is typically located at the intersection of the right [___] and the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.
back:
* Linea semilunaris (the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle).
* This corresponds to the site where gallbladder tenderness is clinically elicited.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Lateral Bony Anchor of the Inguinal Ligament
front: Identify the landmark representing the lateral extent of the inguinal ligament and its role in defining the inguinal region.
back: - Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) - Serves as the lateral anchor for the ligament - Marks the starting point for tracing the ligament toward the pubic tubercle

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish between the venous drainage of the thoracic esophagus and the abdominal esophagus.
back:
• Thoracic: Drains into Azygos and Hemiazygos veins
• Abdominal: Drains into the Left Gastric vein
• Key distinction: Systemic vs. Portal drainage.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the anatomical basis for the 'shaggy' and thick-walled appearance of the jejunal mucosa compared to the smoother distal ileum on a cadaveric specimen.
back:
● Plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes).
● Jejunum: Large, permanent, and closely set circular folds.
● Ileum: Folds are smaller, widely separated, or entirely absent in the distal portion.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: During a physical exam, a multiparous patient's recti muscles separate when she is asked to lift her head while supine. This condition arises due to stretching of the [___].
back: Linea alba. - Condition: Divarication of the recti (Diastasis recti). - Results from weakened aponeuroses after multiple pregnancies or excessive intra-abdominal pressure.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Identify the three major structures entering/leaving the porta hepatis and their typical orientation from anterior to posterior.
back:
• Bile Ducts (Anterior).
• Hepatic Artery (Middle).
• Portal Vein (Posterior).
• Memory Aid: D-A-V (Duct-Artery-Vein).

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: A patient with a subphrenic abscess experiences referred pain to the right shoulder. What is the neuroanatomical basis for this presentation?
back:
Phrenic Nerve Irritation

*   Abscess irritates central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum
*   Sensory supply: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5)
*   Referred to C3-C4 dermatomes via supraclavicular nerves

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the three primary branches of the celiac trunk observed upon reflecting the lesser omentum.
back:
• Left Gastric Artery (runs along lesser curvature)
• Splenic Artery (tortuous course along pancreas)
• Common Hepatic Artery (passes toward the liver)

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: The only muscle of the soft palate not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus is the [___], which receives its motor innervation from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
back:
• Tensor veli palatini
  • Innervated by the nerve to the medial pterygoid (V3)
  • Functions to tense the soft palate and open the auditory tube during swallowing

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: Which specific anatomical landmark is used for a midline paracentesis to avoid major vascular injury and ensure a bloodless entry?
back:
The Linea Alba.
- Vertical line between umbilicus and symphysis pubis.
- Bloodless due to lack of major muscle fibers and vessels.
- Traverses transversalis fascia and peritoneum.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
coreConcept: Referred Pain Pathways of the Stomach
front: Explain the anatomical basis for visceral referred pain felt in the epigastrium during the early stages of gastric pathology.
back:
- Afferent pain fibers travel with sympathetic nerves.
- Pass through celiac plexus to greater splanchnic nerves.
- Enter spinal cord at T5–T9 segments.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Explain the embryological basis of an ileal (Meckel’s) diverticulum and its typical location on the intestinal wall.
back:
* Persistence of the proximal portion of the vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct.
* Found on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
* Usually located approximately 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal junction.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Explain the pathway of lymph flow from the upper right portion of the stomach (proximal lesser curvature) to the celiac axis.
back:
- Drained by the left gastric lymph nodes.
- Follows the course of the left gastric artery.
- Nodes are located within the lesser omentum.
- Vessels terminate directly into the celiac nodes.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A 15-year-old female presents with persistent post-prandial vomiting and weight loss. Imaging reveals the third part of the duodenum is compressed by the Superior Mesenteric Artery. Name the posterior structure forming the other half of this 'nutcracker' effect.
back:
• Abdominal Aorta
• Condition: Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome
• Compression occurs at the L3 level
• Often associated with rapid loss of mesenteric fat

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: The [___] is a constant notch located on the lower part of the lesser curvature of the stomach, marking the transition to the pyloric antrum.
back:
• Incisura angularis (Angular notch)
  • Serves as a key landmark during gastroscopy and radiology

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the clinical sign where deep inspiration causes sharp pain during palpation of the right subcostal region, indicating gallbladder inflammation.
back:
* Murphy’s sign.
* Occurs as the descending liver pushes the inflamed gallbladder against the examiner's hand.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
coreConcept: Origin and Level of the Celiac Trunk
front: The celiac trunk, providing the primary arterial supply to the foregut, arises from the abdominal aorta at the vertebral level of [___].
back:
• Vertebral Level: T12.
• Territory: Abdominal esophagus to the middle of the second part of the duodenum.
• Main Branches: Left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Contrast the primary anatomical site of perforation and the typical associated arterial risk between a gastric ulcer and a duodenal ulcer.
back:
• Gastric: Lesser curvature; erodes splenic artery posteriorly
• Duodenal: First part; erodes gastroduodenal artery posteriorly
• Perforated anterior duodenal ulcers lead to air under diaphragm

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Identify the critical anastomotic channel that runs along the inner border of the large intestine, connecting the branches of the SMA and IMA.
back: * Marginal artery (of Drummond) * Formed by anastomoses of ileocolic, right, middle, and left colic arteries * Serves as a vital collateral pathway during arterial occlusion

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: A 5-year-old child presents with nasal regurgitation of fluids during swallowing. Which specific muscular failure prevents the closure of the pharyngeal isthmus?
back:
• Levator veli palatini (primarily)
  • Failure to elevate the soft palate against the posterior pharyngeal wall
  • Allows communication between the oropharynx and nasopharynx during deglutition

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Explain the physiological response of the pyloric sphincter to vagal stimulation versus sympathetic activation.
back:
• Vagus (Parasympathetic): Inhibitory, leading to sphincter relaxation.
• Sympathetic: Motor, causing sphincter contraction.
• Regulation: Controls the rate of chyme delivery to the duodenum.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Distinguish between the common hepatic duct and the bile duct (common bile duct) regarding their formation.
back:
• Common Hepatic: Formed by the union of right and left hepatic ducts.
• Bile Duct: Formed by the union of the common hepatic and cystic ducts.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the general sensory and special taste innervation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
back:
• General sensation: Lingual nerve (Mandibular V3)
• Taste: Chorda tympani (Branch of Facial VII)
• These fibers travel together before the chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: During an assessment of a patient with Mumps, the patient complains of severe pain specifically when opening the mouth or chewing. Which anatomical relationship explains this symptom?
back:
• Glenoid process extension.
• Part of the gland lies behind the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).
• Jaw movement compresses the inflamed, swollen gland against the joint.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Specify the anatomical location of the stomach's cardiac orifice in relation to the xiphisternal junction and the vertebral column.
back:
Location: 3 fingerbreadths below and to the left of the xiphisternal junction.
- Vertebral level: T10 vertebra.
- Function: Junction with the abdominal esophagus.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: The fan-shaped fold of peritoneum that attaches the coils of the jejunum and ileum to the posterior abdominal wall is known as the [___].
back:
• Mesentery of the small intestine.
• Contains superior mesenteric vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
• Its root extends from the left side of L2 to the right sacroiliac joint.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: An elderly patient presents with intestinal obstruction. Radiology reveals a large gallstone at the ileocecal valve. Based on posterior relations, identify the likely source of this fistula.
back:
• Cholecystoenteric fistula involving the duodenum (1st or 2nd part).
• Gallstone ulcerates through the gallbladder wall directly into the duodenal lumen.
• Results in "gallstone ileus."

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Vague, poorly localized pain in early appendicitis is referred to the [___] dermatome because afferent fibers enter the spinal cord at this specific level.
back:
T10 (Umbilicus)
*   Visceral pain fibers accompany sympathetic nerves
*   Travel via the superior mesenteric plexus
*   Localization shifts only when the parietal peritoneum is irritated

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: List four primary anatomical sites of portosystemic anastomosis in the abdomen.
back:
*   Lower end of esophagus
*   Umbilicus (Paraumbilical site)
*   Anal canal (Anorectal junction)
*   Retroperitoneal surfaces (Ascending/Descending colon and Pancreas)

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The duodenojejunal flexure is maintained in its position by a peritoneal fold known as the [___] (Ligament of Treitz), which attaches to the right crus of the diaphragm.
back:
* Suspensory ligament of the duodenum.
* Stabilizes the duodenojejunal junction.
* Serves as an anatomical landmark for the transition from upper to lower GI tract.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Distinguish between the right (hepatic) and left (splenic) colic flexures regarding their vertebral levels and superior relations.
back:
Colic Flexures Contrast
- Right: Lower level (L3); lies inferior to the liver.
- Left: Higher level; lies inferior to the spleen.
- Left is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: An autopsy reveals a fold of peritoneum extending from the bladder apex to the umbilicus. Identify this fold and its embryological origin.
back:
• Median umbilical fold.
• Contains the urachus, which is the fibrous remnant of the fetal allantois.
• Lies in the midline, distinct from the medial and lateral umbilical folds.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Contrast the distribution of mesenteric fat and the presence of Peyer patches between the jejunum and the ileum.
back:
* Fat: Scanty near the wall in jejunum; deposited throughout the mesentery in ileum.
* Peyer patches: Abundant in the distal ileum; absent in the jejunum.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: At the umbilicus, the [___] veins connect the left branch of the portal vein to the superficial systemic veins of the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
*   Paraumbilical veins
*   Run within the falciform ligament
*   Anastomose with superficial epigastric and thoracoepigastric veins

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Peritoneal Relations of the Large Intestine
front: Contrast the peritoneal status and mobility of the ascending colon versus the transverse colon as seen on a cadaver.
back:
### Peritoneal Coverage
* **Ascending Colon:** Retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior wall.
* **Transverse Colon:** Intraperitoneal and mobile, suspended by the **transverse mesocolon**.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Third Part of Duodenum
front: Describe the anatomical relationship between the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum and the superior mesenteric vessels.
back:
* The third part runs horizontally to the left.
* It passes posterior to the superior mesenteric artery and vein.
* It is crossed anteriorly by the root of the mesentery.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Define the contents and functional role of the mesenteries in the abdominal cavity.
back:
Mesenteries consist of:
- Two-layered peritoneal folds connecting intestines to the posterior wall.
- Provide a conduit for blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
- Anchor mobile viscera while allowing necessary motility.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Greater Curvature
front: Identify the specific arteries supplying the greater curvature and their respective parent vessels.
back:
• Left gastroepiploic artery: Branch of the splenic artery.
• Right gastroepiploic artery: Branch of the gastroduodenal artery.
• Distribution: Run between the layers of the greater omentum.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Lymphatic drainage from the gallbladder passes through the cystic node and follows the hepatic artery to reach the [___] lymph nodes.
back: * Celiac lymph nodes. * Located around the celiac trunk. * Part of the preaortic nodal chain.

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
coreConcept: Abdominal Quadrants and Appendix Surface Projections
front: A 19-year-old student presents with periumbilical pain that has shifted to the Right Lower Quadrant. The specific anatomical landmark in this quadrant representing the base of the appendix is [___].
back: McBurney’s point. It is located in the Right Lower Quadrant at the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the spinoumbilical line. This specific site corresponds to the base of the vermiform appendix.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: In surgical oncology, a total gastrectomy for carcinoma must include the removal of the [___] omentum and the [___] gland tail to ensure clearance of the lymphatic field.
back:
1. Greater omentum.
2. Pancreas (tail/body).
- Includes removal of gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Explain the anatomical basis for why diverticula of the colon typically protrude through the circular muscle layer between the teniae coli.
back:
* Protrusion occurs at weak points where blood vessels (vasa recta) pierce the circular muscle
* Mucosa herniates through these vascular gaps
* Commonly affects the sigmoid colon due to higher intraluminal pressure.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the anatomical relationships of the bile duct in its supraduodenal versus retroduodenal parts.
back:
* Supraduodenal: Located in the free margin of the lesser omentum, anterior to the portal vein and right of the hepatic artery.
* Retroduodenal: Passes behind the first part of the duodenum, situated to the right of the gastroduodenal artery.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Internal Boundary of the Inguinal Canal
front: A surgeon is performing an open repair for an indirect inguinal hernia. Upon entering the inguinal canal, the hernia sac is found emerging from an opening lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Identify this opening.
back: * Deep inguinal ring. * This opening exists in the transversalis fascia. * It marks the internal entry to the inguinal canal, situated midway between the ASIS and symphysis pubis.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The most common anatomical variation in the location of the vermiform appendix, found in approximately two-thirds of individuals, is the [___] position.
back:
* Retrocecal position
* Found in the majority of UHS clinical cases
* Tip may extend toward the right kidney or liver

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: A patient with an infected subphrenic abscess complains of sharp pain in the right shoulder. Explain the neuroanatomical basis for this referred pain.
back:
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum (innervated by Phrenic nerve, C3-C5).
• Supraclavicular nerves share C3-C4 spinal segments.
• Sensory cortex misinterprets the origin of pain as the shoulder dermatome.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
front: The deep inguinal ring is an oval opening in the [___] fascia, located approximately 1.25 cm superior to the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the symphysis pubis.
back: * Transversalis fascia. * Positioned lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. * It represents the internal entry to the inguinal canal.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A 52-year-old male with cirrhosis presents with caput medusae. This manifestation results from retrograde flow into the [___] veins, which form an anastomosis between the portal vein and the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall.
back: - Paraumbilical veins. - Travel in the falciform ligament with the ligamentum teres. - Connect the left branch of the portal vein to systemic epigastric veins.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: A surgeon requires access to the lesser sac to inspect the pancreas. Contrast the two primary peritoneal routes (omenta) that can be incised or traversed to reach this space.
back: * Lesser omentum: Access via the hepatogastric or hepatoduodenal ligaments. * Greater omentum: Access by incising the gastrocolic ligament along the greater curvature. * Transverse mesocolon: Posterior surgical approach.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: All lymphatic drainage from the stomach eventually reaches the [___] lymph nodes situated around the root of the eponymous artery on the posterior abdominal wall.
back:
* Celiac nodes.
* Located at the origin of the celiac trunk.
* Final common pathway for all gastric anatomical zones.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A patient is found to have a tumor compressing the neck of the pancreas. Analyze the primary anatomical consequence regarding the formation of the portal vein.
back: * Compression of the SMV and Splenic vein junction. * Potential portal hypertension due to obstructed venous return. * Formation site is L2 level, immediately anterior to the IVC.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the primary autonomic source for sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation of the gallbladder.
back: * Celiac plexus. * Sympathetic: Greater splanchnic nerves. * Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve (contracts gallbladder).

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The [___] artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery, is the primary vessel providing blood to the gallbladder.
back:
• Cystic artery.
• Usually arises within the cystohepatic triangle (Calot's triangle).
• Venous drainage is typically via the cystic vein into the portal vein.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Summarize the hierarchical frequency of the two most common anatomical positions of the appendix found in clinical practice.
back:
* 1. Retrocecal (~64%): Most common; found behind the cecum.
* 2. Pelvic (~32%): Second most common; found in the pelvis.
* Other variants (subcecal, ileal) comprise the remaining <5%.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the peritoneal attachments and arterial supply found along the Lesser Curvature with those along the Greater Curvature of the stomach.
back:
* Lesser: Lesser omentum; Right/Left gastric arteries.
* Greater: Greater omentum; Right/Left gastro-omental and short gastric arteries.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Explain why the gallbladder is anatomically more resistant to gangrene and ischemic necrosis than the vermiform appendix.
back:
Anatomical Basis:

*   Appendix: Supplied by a single, non-anastomosing appendicular artery (functional end artery).
*   Gallbladder: Dual supply via the cystic artery and small vessels from the liver's visceral surface.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A patient reports a sudden onset of severe, localized pain in the right iliac fossa following vague periumbilical discomfort. Describe the neuroanatomical basis for this shift.
back:
* Initial pain: Visceral afferents (T10) carry stretch/spasm sensations from the appendix.
* Shifted pain: Inflammation irritates the somatic parietal peritoneum.
* Provides precise localization due to somatic nerve supply.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
coreConcept: Protective Function of the Greater Omentum
front: Describe the 'policeman of the abdomen' mechanism by which the greater omentum limits the spread of localized infection.
back:
• Highly mobile fold moves via intestinal peristalsis
• Adheres to inflamed areas (e.g., appendicitis)
• Wraps around infection to form adhesions and localize peritonitis.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Distinguish the typical clinical manifestation of a dilated gastroesophageal anastomosis from that of a dilated anorectal anastomosis in a cirrhotic patient.
back:
Gastroesophageal: Hematemesis (vomiting blood).
Anorectal: Internal hemorrhoids (painless rectal bleeding).
* Both signify severe portal hypertension.
* Gastroesophageal is more clinically urgent.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of Gastric Lymphatic Spread
front: A 60-year-old male with a history of chronic gastric ulcers presents with a hard, painless swelling in the left supraclavicular fossa. Identify the specific clinical name for this node and the vessel that facilitates metastasis to this site.
back:
Virchow's Node (Troisier Sign).
- Indicates advanced gastric malignancy.
- Metastasis occurs via the thoracic duct.
- Located at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Specify the primary lymphatic drainage route for a malignant lesion located at the tip of the tongue.
back:
* Submental lymph nodes (Level Ia)
* Secondary drainage to submandibular and deep cervical nodes
* Often involves bilateral drainage

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A patient describes vague, midline periumbilical discomfort that suddenly shifts to sharp, intense, and localized pain in the right iliac fossa. Contrast the anatomical structures involved in these two stages of pain.
back:
• Early (Visceral): Stretching of visceral peritoneum/mesentery; mediated by autonomic afferents (T10 level).
• Late (Somatic): Inflammation involves the parietal peritoneum; mediated by somatic intercostal nerves.
• Somatic pain is sharper and precisely localized.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The small pit at the apex of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis, representing the embryologic remnant of the thyroglossal duct, is known as the [___].
back:
*   Foramen cecum.
*   Marks the site of origin for the thyroid gland.
*   Located between the oral and pharyngeal parts of the tongue.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The esophagus commences at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, corresponding to the [___] vertebral level.
back: • C6 vertebra level. • It is continuous with the laryngopharynx superiorly. • Marks the site of the first anatomical constriction (cricoesophageal).

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
front: Name the bony landmark used as the primary reference point to locate the superficial inguinal ring.
back: * Pubic tubercle. * This small bony protuberance on the superior ramus of the pubis is the reference for the superficial ring. * The ring lies immediately above and medial to it.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A patient presents with a perforated posterior gastric ulcer. Based on the 'Stomach Bed' relations, which tortuous artery is most at risk of erosion and massive hemorrhage?
back: Splenic Artery (runs along the upper border of the pancreas, posterior to the stomach).

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Biliary Dynamics and Sphincter of Oddi
front: Explain the role of the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (Sphincter of Oddi) in the regulation of biliary flow during the interdigestive period.
back: The sphincter remains tonically contracted, closing the duodenal exit. This causes bile to back up through the cystic duct for storage and concentration within the gallbladder.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: A 68-year-old patient with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings. Imaging confirms an embolism in the artery supplying the gut from the distal duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon. Identify the vessel.
back:
Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA). 
- Arises at the L1 vertebral level. 
- Supplies midgut derivatives including the jejunum, ileum, and ascending colon.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the mechanism ensuring that general sensation and taste are carried by different cranial nerves in the oral part of the tongue.
back:
*   General sensation: Lingual nerve (V3).
*   Taste: Chorda tympani (VII).
*   Occurs because the anterior 2/3 develops from the first pharyngeal arch.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Superficial Inguinal Ring
front: Describe the surface landmarking used to locate the superficial inguinal ring during a physical examination.
back: * Identify the pubic tubercle as the primary bony landmark. * The ring is a triangular gap in the aponeurosis of the external oblique. * It is situated immediately superior and medial to this tubercle.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Abdominal Wall
front: A surgeon performs a McBurney's incision for an appendectomy. List the muscular and fascial layers encountered in order from superficial to deep to reach the transversalis fascia.
back:
• Skin and superficial fascia (Camper’s and Scarpa’s)
• External oblique aponeurosis/muscle
• Internal oblique muscle
• Transversus abdominis muscle
• Transversalis fascia

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Analyze how an anterior wall perforation of the first part of the duodenum differs in outcome from a posterior wall perforation.
back:
* Anterior: Causes generalized peritonitis due to escape of contents into the greater sac
* Posterior: Leads to massive hemorrhage (gastroduodenal artery) or content escape into the lesser sac.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of referred pain from a subphrenic abscess involving the central versus the peripheral diaphragmatic peritoneum.
back:
• Central: Referred to the shoulder (C3–C5) via the phrenic nerve.
• Peripheral: Localized to the lower chest and upper abdominal wall.
• Mechanism: Peripheral irritation travels via lower intercostal nerves (T7–T11).

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the role of the genioglossus muscle in tongue dynamics.
back:
*   Primary protrusor of the tongue.
*   Bilateral contraction pulls the root forward.
*   Originates from the superior genial tubercle of the mandible.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: Contrast the surgical risk of a midline incision through the linea alba versus a transrectus incision regarding the muscle's nerve supply.
back:
• Midline: Bloodless and avoids nerve damage (fibrous fusion)
• Transrectus: Risks sectioning terminal branches of T7-T12 nerves
• Result: Leads to postoperative muscle weakness or atrophy

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: A surgeon is performing an lymphadenectomy for a tumor on the right side of the lesser curvature. Which specific nodal group is being targeted, and where do its efferents lead?
back: Right gastric lymph nodes. • Located along the right gastric artery. • Efferents drain toward the hepatic nodes. • Eventually join the celiac nodal group for terminal abdominal drainage.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Detail the anatomical mechanism by which a gallstone impacted in the hepatopancreatic ampulla leads to acute pancreatitis.
back:
• Stone obstructs the common exit of bile and pancreatic ducts.
• Reflux of infected bile into the pancreatic duct occurs.
• Causes premature enzyme activation and pancreatic autodigestion.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: Contrast the composition of the posterior wall of the rectus sheath at the level of the umbilicus with its structure below the arcuate line.
back:
• Above Arcuate Line: Formed by the internal oblique (posterior lamina) and transversus abdominis aponeuroses
• Below Arcuate Line: Posterior wall is absent
• Rectus muscle lies directly on the transversalis fascia below the line

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Contrast the anatomical relationships of the three major structures passing through the parotid gland from the most superficial to the deepest plane.
back:
* Superficial: Facial nerve and its five terminal branches
* Intermediate: Retromandibular vein (formed by maxillary and superficial temporal veins)
* Deepest: External carotid artery (dividing into terminal branches)

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: In the lower part of the rectus sheath, the long strap-like rectus abdominis muscle may occasionally contain the small, triangular [___] muscle anteriorly.
back:
• Pyramidalis muscle
• It functions to keep the linea alba taut during contraction.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
coreConcept: Clinical signs of CN X lesion
front: A patient presents with nasal regurgitation of fluids and a uvula that deviates to the right during phonation. Name the dysfunctional muscle responsible for elevating the left side of the soft palate.
back: Levator veli palatini. Left-sided CN X paralysis prevents elevation of the soft palate on the affected side. The uvula is pulled toward the functional right side by the intact muscles during phonation.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: Detail the 'shutter mechanism' involving the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles during increased intra-abdominal pressure.
back:
• Muscles contract during coughing or straining
• Arched lower fibers flatten the roof of the inguinal canal
• Effectively closes the canal against the floor (inguinal ligament)
• Prevents herniation of abdominal contents

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: A surgeon performing a radical gastrectomy for a tumor in the antrum removes nodes located inferior to the pylorus near the gastroduodenal artery. Identify these nodes and their primary drainage territory.
back:
Subpyloric Lymph Nodes.
- Located near the head of the pancreas.
- Drain the pyloric antrum and right greater curvature.
- Efferents pass to the celiac nodes.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: Identify the fascial layer that represents the adult remnant of the processus vaginalis' acquisition of a covering from the transversalis fascia.
back:
• Internal spermatic fascia.
• Attached to the margins of the deep inguinal ring.
• Forms a tubular sheath around the spermatic cord.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Explain the role of the Vagus nerve in the motor function of the abdominal portion of the esophagus.
back:
- Anterior and posterior vagal trunks provide parasympathetic innervation.
- Controls coordinated relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing.
- Stimulates peristaltic activity in the esophageal smooth muscle.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Identify the primary group of lymph nodes to which malignant cells from any part of the stomach eventually migrate.
back:
Celiac lymph nodes.
- Located around the root of the celiac artery.
- Final pathway for gastric lymphatic drainage.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the anatomical and physiological factors at the cardiac orifice that prevent gastroesophageal reflux despite the absence of a distinct anatomical sphincter.
back:
* Pinch-cock effect of Right crus of diaphragm
* Acute Angle of His (cardiac notch)
* Intra-abdominal esophagus pressure
* Valvelike mucosal folds

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Contrast the vascular architecture and mesenteric fat distribution between the jejunum and the ileum.
back:
* Jejunum: Long vasa recta, simple arterial arcades (1-2), less fat (transparent windows in mesentery).
* Ileum: Short vasa recta, complex/multiple arcades (3-4), fat deposited throughout mesentery (no windows).

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
coreConcept: Main Arterial Origins of the GIT
front: The primary arterial supply to the foregut derivatives arises from the [___] artery, which originates from the abdominal aorta at the level of the T12 vertebra.
back:
Celiac artery (or Celiac trunk). 
- Arises just below the diaphragm. 
- Supplies the gut from the distal esophagus to the mid-second part of the duodenum.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Explain why an inflamed appendix is highly susceptible to gangrene and perforation compared to other GIT segments.
back:
* Supplied by the appendicular artery (an end artery)
* Inflammatory edema compresses this vessel
* Lack of collateral circulation leads to rapid necrosis
* Appendicular artery is a branch of the posterior cecal artery

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: During a cholecystectomy, a surgeon identifies the cystic duct. Specify the anatomical structure formed by the union of this duct with the common hepatic duct.
back:
* The Bile Duct (Common Bile Duct)
* Descends in the free margin of the lesser omentum
* Passes posterior to the first part of the duodenum
* Joins the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Explain the hormonal mechanism triggered by the entry of fatty chyme into the duodenum that results in the delivery of concentrated bile.
back:
• Duodenal mucosa releases Cholecystokinin (CCK)
• CCK causes gallbladder muscular contraction
• CCK relaxes the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (Oddi)
• Bile is squirted into the second part of the duodenum.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the functional mechanism that differentiates the intrinsic tongue muscles from the extrinsic muscles.
back:
* Intrinsic: Originate/insert within the tongue; alter the shape (curling, flattening).
* Extrinsic: Originate from bone (mandible/hyoid/styloid); alter the position (protrusion/retraction).

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Explain the hormonal mechanism that coordinates gallbladder emptying and the simultaneous entry of bile into the duodenum.
back:
* Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by the duodenum in response to fat.
* It triggers gallbladder contraction.
* Simultaneously relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter (Sphincter of Oddi).

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: A 5-year-old child presents with chronic mouth breathing, nocturnal snoring, and a 'nasal' quality to their voice. Pathophysiological hypertrophy of which Waldeyer’s ring component is likely?
back:
Pharyngeal tonsil (Adenoids). 
- Located in the roof of the nasopharynx. 
- Hypertrophy obstructs the posterior nares and pharyngeal isthmus.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Locate the 'Incisura Angularis' (Angular Notch) on a stomach model and state its significance in dividing stomach parts.
back:
* Location: Lower part of Lesser Curvature.
* Significance: Marks the functional boundary between the gastric body and the pyloric antrum.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
coreConcept: Protective Function of the Greater Omentum
front: Explain the biological mechanism that allows the greater omentum to function as the 'abdominal policeman' during local infection.
back:
Mechanisms include:
- High mobility due to intestinal peristalsis.
- Ability to migrate to sites of inflammation.
- Adheres to and wraps around infected viscera (e.g., appendix).
- Seals off the focus to prevent generalized peritonitis.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: Following a blunt blow to the epigastrium in a sports injury, a patient develops signs of chemical peritonitis. Analyze the anatomical vulnerability of the pancreas in this scenario.
back:
* Pancreas is fixed retroperitoneally against the rigid L1-L2 vertebral column.
* Blunt force compresses the gland against the vertebrae, causing tearing or rupture.
* Release of activated pancreatic enzymes causes auto-digestion of surrounding tissues.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Describe the clinical significance of the right lateral paracolic gutter in the spread of inflammatory exudate from the upper abdomen.
back: * Serves as a pathway for fluid to travel to the right iliac fossa. * Can cause a perforated duodenal ulcer to mimic acute appendicitis. * Continuous superiorly with the right subphrenic space.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: The [___] artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, descends behind the first part of the duodenum and provides critical supply to both the pancreas and the stomach curvatures.
back:
• Artery: Gastroduodenal Artery.
• Branches: Right gastro-omental and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
• Clinical: Vulnerable to erosion and life-threatening hemorrhage from posterior duodenal ulcers.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: A patient with a history of neck trauma presents with a tongue that is wasted on the right side and deviates to the right when stuck out. Explain the anatomical basis for these findings.
back:
- Right-sided hypoglossal nerve injury.
- Muscle wasting (atrophy) occurs on the ipsilateral side.
- Deviation occurs because the left genioglossus is unopposed.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A patient experiences vague, dull pain localized to the periumbilical region. If this pain originates from a midgut structure like the jejunum, identify the spinal segments involved in this visceral referral.
back:
* T10 spinal segment.
* Visceral afferents travel via sympathetic nerves through the superior mesenteric plexus.
* Pain is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: While the superficial inguinal ring is a defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, the deep inguinal ring is formed as an oval opening in the [___].
back: • **Transversalis fascia** • Located 0.5 inches superior to the midinguinal point. • Gives attachment to the internal spermatic fascia of the cord.

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: A patient with basal pleurisy reports sharp pain in the upper abdominal wall. Provide the anatomical basis for this 'referred pain'.
back:
- The lower intercostal nerves (T7-T11) innervate the costal parietal pleura and the abdominal skin.
- Irritation of the pleura is perceived by the brain as coming from the corresponding abdominal dermatome.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Distinguish the visceral pain associated with biliary colic from the somatic pain associated with progressed acute cholecystitis.
back:
• Biliary Colic: Dull, midline, poorly localized; due to ductal distension.
• Acute Cholecystitis: Sharp, well-localized to RUQ; due to irritation of the parietal peritoneum.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: Explain the role of the processus vaginalis in the development of an indirect inguinal hernia.
back: Failure of the processus to obliterate. • Creates a preformed peritoneal sac. • Allows abdominal viscera to enter the inguinal canal during increased pressure.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: A 24-year-old male presents with right lower quadrant pain. Digital rectal examination reveals exquisite tenderness on the right side of the pelvic peritoneum. Identify the likely anatomical position of the appendix.
back:
* Pelvic position.
* Tip hangs over the pelvic brim into the true pelvis.
* Irritates the parietal peritoneum of the pelvic wall.
* Second most common position (~32%).
