category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Explain the neuro-anatomical defect within the esophageal wall that leads to the failure of lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation in achalasia.
back:
Degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus.
* Location: Between circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
* Effect: Loss of inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide/VIP).
* Result: Sustained LES contraction and aperistalsis in the distal esophagus.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the functional state of the hepatopancreatic sphincter (Sphincter of Oddi) during the interdigestive state versus the postprandial state.
back: • Interdigestive (Fasting): Sphincter contracts to divert bile into the gallbladder for storage • Postprandial: Sphincter relaxes to allow concentrated bile flow into the duodenum

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Contrast the drainage pathway of the Inferior Mesenteric Vein (IMV) with that of the Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV).
back: * IMV: Usually joins the splenic vein behind the body of the pancreas. * SMV: Directly joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. * Both contribute blood to the liver.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: A 22-year-old male presents with a "bag of worms" sensation in the scrotum that disappears when supine. Dilation of which spermatic cord structure is responsible?
back:
• Pampiniform plexus of veins
• Occurs due to impaired venous return; more common on the left side into the renal vein.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Contrast the diagnostic clinical findings between biliary colic and acute cholecystitis regarding inflammatory markers and pain duration.
back:
• Biliary Colic: Temporary pain (<6 hours), no fever, and normal WBC count.
• Acute Cholecystitis: Persistent pain (>6 hours), fever, leukocytosis, and positive Murphy’s sign.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The arterial supply to the gallbladder is primarily provided by the [___], which most commonly originates as a branch of the right hepatic artery.
back:
• Cystic artery
• Found within the Calot's triangle
• Variations are clinically significant during cholecystectomy.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Distinguish between the common hepatic duct and the common bile duct based on their formation and approximate length.
back:
• Common Hepatic: Formed by Right/Left hepatic ducts; ~4 cm long
• Common Bile: Formed by CHD and cystic duct; ~8 cm long.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: A patient sustains a deep laceration to the cheek. Saliva is seen leaking from the wound, and the patient cannot whistle or blow. Which structures are likely damaged?
back:
• Parotid duct (Stensen's duct)
• Buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
• Results in salivary leakage and buccinator muscle paralysis

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: General sensory innervation to the mucous membrane of the soft palate is primarily mediated by the [___] nerve.
back:
• Lesser palatine nerve.
• Branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2).
• Includes some contributions from the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The gallbladder is less susceptible to gangrene than the appendix because it receives additional collateral blood supply from small vessels on the [___] surface of the liver.
back:
* Visceral surface.
* These vessels pass directly between the liver and gallbladder body.
* This dual supply provides protection against total ischemic necrosis.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: The parotid duct, also known as Stensen's duct, traverses the masseter muscle and opens into the oral vestibule opposite the [___] tooth.
back:
• Maxillary (upper) second molar.
• It emerges from the anterior border of the gland.
• It pierces the buccinator muscle to enter the mouth.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Identify the specific portosystemic anastomosis site associated with the 'bare area' of the liver.
back:
• Communication between hepatic/portal tributaries and phrenic veins
• Systemic contribution: Inferior phrenic veins
• Interface: Diaphragmatic surface of the liver
• Clinically relevant for collateral flow bypassing the liver

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: A patient presents with fever and right upper quadrant pain following a perforated gall bladder. Imaging reveals a fluid collection between the diaphragm and the diaphragmatic surface of the liver. Identify the most likely anatomical space involved.
back: Right subphrenic space. • Potential space between the diaphragm and liver. • Separated into anterior and posterior by the falciform ligament. • Communicates with the right paracolic gutter.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Explain the mechanism by which respiratory movements facilitate the circulation and absorption of peritoneal fluid toward the diaphragm.
back:
Mechanisms include:
- Diaphragmatic contraction creates pressure gradients.
- Fluid is directed toward subphrenic spaces.
- Absorption occurs via subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries.
- Large surface area of diaphragmatic peritoneum assists rapid uptake.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
coreConcept: Branches and Distribution of the Celiac Trunk
front: List the three primary terminal branches of the celiac trunk and specify the embryological segment they collectively supply.
back:
• Branches: Left gastric, Splenic, and Common Hepatic arteries.
• Segment: Foregut.
• Extent: Lower esophagus to the level of the major duodenal papilla.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A patient undergoes a truncal vagotomy for refractory peptic ulcer disease. Predict the anatomical distribution of the posterior vagal trunk as it enters the abdomen.
back:
Enters on the posterior surface of the esophagus.
- Supplies the posterior stomach wall.
- Sends a large branch to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses.
- Distributes to the intestine up to the splenic flexure.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Distinguish between the superior and inferior attachments (origin/insertion) of the rectus abdominis muscle.
back: - Origin (Inferior): Pubic symphysis and pubic crest. - Insertion (Superior): Xiphoid process and costal cartilages of 5th, 6th, and 7th ribs. - Stabilizes the pelvis and flexes the trunk.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Contrast the primary lymphatic basins for the upper two-thirds of the lesser curvature versus the lower half of the greater curvature.
back:
* Upper lesser curvature: Left gastric nodes.
* Lower greater curvature: Right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) nodes.
* Both eventually converge at the celiac nodes.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Name the specific lymphatic trunk that collects efferent drainage from the celiac nodes before entering the cisterna chyli.
back:
* Intestinal lymph trunk.
* Formed by confluence of celiac and mesenteric efferents.
* Terminal vessel before the abdominal origin of the thoracic duct.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: In the lymphatic drainage of the stomach, all vessels eventually pass through the [___] lymph nodes situated around the root of the eponymous artery.
back:
* Celiac lymph nodes.
* Situated around the root of the celiac artery.
* They represent the final common drainage pathway for all gastric lymph before entering the intestinal trunk.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Explain the anatomical method used by surgeons to reliably locate the base of the appendix during an open appendectomy.
back:
* Identify the three teniae coli of the cecum.
* Trace these longitudinal muscle bands inferiorly.
* The bands converge at the exact site of the appendiceal base.
* Usually involves the posteromedial cecal wall.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Specify the vertebral level of the esophageal hiatus and the names of the nerves that traverse it alongside the esophagus.
back:
- T10 (10th Thoracic vertebra)
- Vagus nerves (Anterior and Posterior vagal trunks)
- Vital for gastric acid secretion and motility

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Identify the most common anatomical site for intussusception in children and the suspected role of lymphoid tissue in its pathogenesis.
back:
* Ileocolic junction
* Swelling of Peyer’s patches (lymphoid tissue)
* Leads to telescoping of the ileum into the cecum
* Compromises blood supply, potentially causing gangrene

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Contrast the sensory innervation of the peripheral versus the central parts of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum.
back:
- Central: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5); refers pain to shoulder.
- Peripheral: Lower six intercostal nerves; refers pain to the adjacent abdominal wall skin.
- Both utilize somatic sensory pathways.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Describe the functional mechanism that allows the greater omentum to be termed the 'Abdominal Policeman' during localized intra-abdominal infections.
back:
* High mobility allows it to migrate via intestinal peristalsis.
* Adheres to inflamed peritoneal surfaces using fibrin.
* Wraps around infected foci (e.g., appendicitis) to prevent generalized peritonitis.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: An elderly patient with acute cholecystitis develops localized necrosis and perforation of the gallbladder. Analyze the anatomical basis for why this organ is highly susceptible to gangrene.
back:
• Single arterial supply (Cystic artery).
• Lack of extensive collateral circulation.
• Inflammatory edema easily compresses the artery, leading to ischemia and necrosis.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Identify the primary nerve responsible for the sensory supply of the parietal peritoneum lining the pelvic walls.
back:
• Obturator nerve
• Branch of the lumbar plexus (L2-L4)
• Clinical check involves digital rectal or vaginal examinations.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Describe the coordinated mechanism of the palatopharyngeus muscle during the involuntary phase of swallowing.
back:
• Pulls the pharyngeal wall upward, forward, and medially
  • Shortens the pharynx to receive the food bolus
  • Approximates the palatopharyngeal arches to seal the pharyngeal isthmus

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A patient presents with pain localized to the transpyloric plane. Describe the anatomical location of the stomach's pylorus in relation to this plane and the midline.
back:
• Lies on the transpyloric plane
• Level of L1 vertebra
• Situated just to the right of the midline

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: The external spermatic fascia, the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, is anatomically derived from the [___].
back:
• Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle
• It is acquired as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: A 15-year-old male presents with periumbilical pain shifting to the right flank. He has no anterior abdominal tenderness but exhibits pain on extending his right hip. Identify the most likely anatomical position of his appendix.
back:
* Retrocecal position
* The inflamed appendix irritates the psoas major muscle
* Leads to a positive Psoas sign (pain on hip extension)

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Explain the sequence of venous drainage from the portal vein into the systemic circulation under normal physiological conditions.
back:
• Portal Vein → Liver Sinusoids
• Sinusoids → Central Veins
• Central Veins → Hepatic Veins (Right, Middle, Left)
• Hepatic Veins → Inferior Vena Cava

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the primary venous pathway of the gallbladder and the major circulatory system it joins.
back:
• Cystic vein
• Drains directly into the Portal vein or liver sinusoids
• Forms part of the portal circulation
• Smaller veins enter the visceral liver surface.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient presents with isolated weakness in tensing the soft palate while elevation remains intact. Contrast the motor innervation of the muscle responsible for palatal tension with those responsible for elevation.
back:
• Tensor veli palatini (Tension): Mandibular nerve (V3) via nerve to medial pterygoid.
• Levator veli palatini (Elevation): Vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Identify the specific lymphoid structures that form the inferior and lateral boundaries of Waldeyer's ring.
back: Inferior: Lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue. Lateral: Palatine tonsils and tubal tonsils. The tubal tonsils are located near the opening of the auditory tube. Together, they form a protective mucosal barrier.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Identify the surface projection and vertebral extent of the root of the small intestine mesentery.
back:
Root of the Mesentery

*   6-inch (15cm) long oblique line
*   Extends from duodenojejunal flexure (L2 level)
*   Ends at the right sacroiliac joint

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: Specify the exact termination point of the submandibular (Wharton’s) duct within the oral cavity.
back:
Sublingual caruncle.
- Located as a small papilla on either side of the lingual frenulum.
- Lies in the floor of the mouth, deep to the mucous membrane.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Specify the precise anatomical relationship of the common bile duct to the first part of the duodenum.
back:
• The duct passes posterior to the first part of the duodenum.
• It lies to the right of the gastroduodenal artery.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the three primary arteries that provide the rich vascular supply to the soft palate.
back:
• Greater palatine artery (from Maxillary).
• Ascending palatine artery (from Facial).
• Ascending pharyngeal artery (from External Carotid).

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The most frequent anatomical position of the vermiform appendix, occurring in approximately 64% of cases, is the [___] position.
back:
* Retrocecal position.
* Situated behind the cecum or ascending colon.
* Often lies within the retrocecal peritoneal recess.
* May be extraperitoneal in some variations.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The surface projection of the base of the appendix, used to guide surgical incisions, is known as [___].
back:
McBurney's Point.
- One-third the distance from the Right ASIS to the umbilicus.
- Corresponds to the base regardless of tip position.
- Primary site of maximum tenderness (somatic pain).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: In diverticulosis, the mucosal herniations typically occur between the teniae coli at sites where [___] pierce the circular muscle layer.
back:
* Blood vessels (vasa recta)
* Represent points of anatomical weakness
* Most common in the sigmoid colon
* Can lead to diverticulitis or perforation

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A patient with a history of dyspepsia presents with sudden, massive hematemesis. Imaging reveals an ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Which major vessel is most likely eroded?
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery
* Runs posterior to the first part of the duodenum
* Erosion leads to life-threatening hemorrhage
* Located near the common bile duct and portal vein

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Contrast the venous termination of the Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV) with the Inferior Mesenteric Vein (IMV).
back:
- SMV: Joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein. 
- IMV: Typically joins the splenic vein behind the body of the pancreas.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: A patient presents with a perforated posterior gastric ulcer. Identify the specific peritoneal space involved and the horizontal reflections that form its left lateral boundary.
back:
* Space: Lesser sac (Omental bursa)
* Gastrosplenic ligament (anteriorly)
* Splenorenal ligament (posteriorly)
* These ligaments enclose the splenic hilum.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: A 40-year-old male with liver cirrhosis presents with significant ascites. Explain how the vertical reflections of the peritoneum influence fluid collection when the patient is supine.
back: * Fluid gravitates to the hepatorenal pouch (Morison’s pouch) and pelvic cavity. * Morison's pouch is the lowest point of the upper abdominal cavity in the supine position. * Reflections of the coronary ligament define the bare area of the liver.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: A patient with cirrhosis presents with a palpable notch in the left hypochondrium. Describe the anatomical hemodynamic change responsible for this finding.
back:
• Increased pressure in Splenic vein
• Passive congestion of splenic pulp
• Results in Splenomegaly
• Splenic vein joins SMV to form portal vein.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: List the three main arterial sources providing blood supply to the soft palate.
back:
• Greater palatine artery (from Maxillary artery).
• Ascending palatine artery (from Facial artery).
• Ascending pharyngeal artery (from External Carotid artery).

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Name the two anatomical structures that serve as the immediate boundaries for the mesoappendix.
back:
* Terminal ileum and the vermiform appendix itself
* Forms a triangular fold of peritoneum
* Encloses the appendicular artery, vein, and lymphatic vessels

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Explain why eating acidic foods (gustatory stimulus) causes severe facial pain in acute parotitis versus facial sweating in Frey’s syndrome.
back:
- Parotitis pain: Salivary secretion increases pressure within the rigid, inelastic parotid capsule.
- Frey’s sweating: Misdirected parasympathetic fibers stimulate sweat glands rather than the parotid tissue.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Ligamentous Contrast in the Pelvic Inlet
front: Distinguish the composition of the inguinal ligament from the pectineal ligament found along the superior ramus of the pubis.
back: - Inguinal ligament: Folded border of external oblique aponeurosis - Pectineal (Cooper's) ligament: Thickened periosteum along the pectineal line - Lacunar ligament serves as the medial bridge between them

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the anatomical distribution of the celiac trunk versus the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) by identifying their specific transition point along the duodenum.
back: Celiac Trunk: Supplies the foregut down to the middle of the second part of the duodenum. SMA: Supplies the midgut starting from that point downwards. * Transition occurs at the major duodenal papilla.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Explain how the gallbladder modifies the bile received from the liver during the inter-digestive phase.
back:
* Stores bile while the Sphincter of Oddi remains closed
* Concentrates bile by absorbing water and electrolytes
* Mucosal microvilli increase the surface area for absorption
* Secretes mucus to protect and acidify the stored bile

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Describe the anatomical sequence of events that results in a large gallstone causing mechanical bowel obstruction at the ileocecal junction.
back:
• Formation of a cholecysto-duodenal fistula.
• Gallstone ulcerates into the duodenum.
• Stone travels distally.
• Impacts at the narrowest part (ileocecal junction).

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Specify the nerve primarily targeted during surgical vagotomy to reduce gastric acid secretion in chronic peptic ulcer disease.
back:
* Vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X).
* It provides parasympathetic secretomotor supply to gastric glands.
* Stimulation increases the production of hydrochloric acid and pepsin, which exacerbates peptic ulceration.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: Contrast the intra-oral drainage sites of the submandibular gland versus the sublingual gland.
back:
* Submandibular: Opens at the sublingual caruncle (base of frenulum) via Wharton's duct
* Sublingual: Opens via 8–20 small ducts (Rivinus) on the sublingual fold
* Submandibular is a single major duct; Sublingual has multiple minor ducts

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Describe the neuroanatomical mechanism behind involuntary 'guarding' in acute peritonitis.
back: ● Irritation of the parietal peritoneum triggers reflex spasms. ● The same segmental nerves (T7-L1) supply both the peritoneum and overlying muscles. ● Protective mechanism to rest the inflamed area.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the role of the marginal artery (of Drummond) in providing collateral circulation during a cadaveric demonstration of a mesenteric vascular block.
back:
• Forms a continuous anastomotic channel along the colon.
• Connects branches of the SMA (Middle Colic) and IMA (Left Colic).
• Provides bypass circulation if a major mesenteric vessel is obstructed.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: How does the hepatic branch of the anterior vagal trunk contribute to gastric motor control?
back:
• Origin: Arises from the anterior vagal trunk at the cardia.
• Path: Passes through the lesser omentum to the liver.
• Pyloric Branch: Sends fibers to the pylorus to regulate emptying.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A patient with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with distended, radiating veins around the umbilicus. This clinical sign, known as caput medusae, involves an anastomosis between the systemic veins and the [___].
back:
• Paraumbilical veins
• Travel within the falciform ligament
• Connect to the left branch of the portal vein

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Internal and External Small Intestine Differentiation
front: Explain how the visual appearance of the plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring) is used to differentiate the jejunum from the ileum on a cadaver.
back:
Jejunum: Plicae are larger, more numerous, and closely set.
- Ileum: Plicae are smaller, widely separated, and disappear in the distal segment.
- This reflects higher absorption surface area in the proximal small bowel.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: The hormone gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion, is primarily produced by the mucosa of the [___] of the stomach.
back:
* Pyloric antrum.
* This region contains cells that secrete the hormone into the bloodstream.
* Surgical removal (antrectomy) is performed to eliminate the hormonal stimulus for gastric acid secretion.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Contrast the anatomical consequences of a gallstone ulcerating through the gallbladder wall into the transverse colon versus the duodenum.
back:
* Transverse Colon: Stone enters the large bowel; usually passed naturally via the rectum
* Duodenum: Stone enters the small intestine
* Consequence: Large stones often lodge at the ileocecal junction
* Result: Potential intestinal obstruction known as gallstone ileus

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The right and left hepatic ducts emerge from the liver at the porta hepatis and unite to form the [___].
back: • Common hepatic duct • Approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm) long • Descends within the free margin of the lesser omentum

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the upper, middle, and lower thirds of the esophagus.
back:
• Upper 1/3: Deep cervical nodes
• Middle 1/3: Posterior mediastinal nodes
• Lower 1/3: Left gastric and celiac nodes.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Specify the peritoneal structures that form the boundaries of the epiploic foramen.
back: * Anterior: Free margin of lesser omentum (portal triad). * Posterior: Peritoneum covering the inferior vena cava. * Superior: Caudate lobe of the liver. * Inferior: First part of the duodenum.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which the soft palate prevents nasal regurgitation during swallowing.
back:
* Elevation by Levator Veli Palatini
* Tensing by Tensor Veli Palatini
* Contact with Passavant’s ridge (posterior pharyngeal wall)
* Complete closure of the pharyngeal isthmus

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Explain how the parasympathetic vagus nerves influence gastric activity and the anatomical rationale for performing a vagotomy in peptic ulcer disease.
back:
Vagal Influence (CN X):
- Provides secretomotor fibers to gastric glands, increasing acid and pepsin production.
- Stimulates peristalsis in the stomach wall.
- Vagotomy is performed to reduce hyperacidity by sectioning these stimulatory parasympathetic pathways.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: Identify the nerve that traverses the inguinal canal but enters through the side of the canal rather than the deep inguinal ring.
back:
* Ilioinguinal nerve (L1)
* Passes between internal and external oblique
* Emerges through the superficial inguinal ring

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Identify the muscle that forms the core of the anterior pillar of the fauces and describe its action on the oropharyngeal isthmus.
back:
• Palatoglossus
  • Elevates the root of the tongue and pulls the soft palate down
  • Narrows the oropharyngeal isthmus to separate the mouth from the pharynx

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: During surgery for an indirect inguinal hernia, a surgeon identifies a sac entering the canal via the deep ring. Identify the layer that provided the internal spermatic fascia for this sac.
back: * Transversalis fascia. * The deep ring is the site of evagination. * The sac is located lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Contrast the clinical examination findings of an inflamed retrocecal appendix with those of an appendix located in the pelvic position.
back:
* Retrocecal: Tenderness in flank; positive Psoas sign
* Pelvic: Tenderness on rectal or vaginal exam; positive Obturator sign
* Retrocecal is the most common variant; Pelvic is second

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: The lateral aspect of Waldeyer’s ring, located around the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube, is composed of the [___] tonsil.
back:
Tubal tonsil. 
- Situated near the torus tubarius. 
- Provides immune surveillance at the entry to the middle ear.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the anatomical formation of the portal vein as observed posterior to the neck of the pancreas on a cadaver.
back:
• Formed by union of Splenic Vein and Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV)
• Occurs at the level of the L2 vertebra
• Conveys nutrient-rich blood to the liver

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
coreConcept: Differential Pain Pathways in Biliary Disease
front: Contrast the anatomical basis of referred pain in simple biliary colic versus acute cholecystitis involving the central diaphragmatic peritoneum.
back:
* Biliary colic: Visceral pain referred to T7-T9 dermatomes (epigastrium/back).
* Cholecystitis: Somatic irritation of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) refers pain to the right shoulder.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: A surgeon chooses a pararectus incision along the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis. Explain the primary neurological risk associated with extending this incision longitudinally.
back:
Risk of segmental nerve injury.
- Nerves enter the rectus muscle from its posterior surface.
- Longitudinal extension often divides these nerves.
- Results in postoperative muscle weakness or atrophy.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Lymphatic drainage from the gallbladder primarily passes to the [___] node situated near the neck of the gland, eventually reaching the celiac nodes.
back:
* Cystic lymph node (Node of Lund/Mascagni)
* Drains to hepatic nodes in the porta hepatis
* Final drainage into the celiac group of nodes
* Important for staging gallbladder malignancies

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Contrast the anatomical basis of a volvulus with that of an intussusception in the large intestine.
back:
* Volvulus: Torsion of a mobile segment (e.g., sigmoid colon) around its mesentery, obstructing blood supply
* Intussusception: Telescoping of a proximal segment (e.g., terminal ileum) into an adjacent distal segment (e.g., cecum).

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific part of the duodenum that is retroperitoneal and lies in direct contact with the hilum of the right kidney.
back:
Second (Descending) part of the Duodenum
- Vertically oriented at L2-L3 levels.
- Contains the major duodenal papilla (Ampulla of Vater).
- Receives bile and main pancreatic ducts.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Contrast the arterial supply of the lesser curvature with that of the greater curvature of the stomach.
back:
• Lesser Curvature: Left gastric (celiac) and right gastric (hepatic) arteries
  • Greater Curvature: Left gastroepiploic (splenic) and right gastroepiploic (gastroduodenal) arteries

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: A surgeon exploring the epiploic foramen (opening of the lesser sac) identifies the portal triad in its anterior boundary. Name the specific structure forming this boundary.
back:
Free border of the Lesser Omentum

*   Contains: Bile duct, Hepatic artery, Portal vein
*   Posterior Boundary: Inferior Vena Cava
*   Superior Boundary: Caudate process of liver

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Identify the specific lymphatic anatomical landmark where advanced gastric carcinoma typically metastasizes to produce Troisier’s sign.
back:
• Virchow's node
• Left supraclavicular lymph node
• Located at the junction of the thoracic duct and left subclavian vein

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Trace the pathway of taste sensations from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue to the brainstem.
back:
* Lingual nerve → Chorda tympani (CN VII)
* Geniculate ganglion → Nervus intermedius
* Terminates in Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS)

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Define the 'Bare Area of the Liver' and its importance in the spread of infection.
back:
• Region on posterior liver surface devoid of peritoneum
• Bound by coronary and triangular ligaments
• In direct contact with the diaphragm
• Potential route for infection to spread to the thorax

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: List the five primary structures that form important posterior relations with the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver.
back: Posterior Liver Relations. • Right kidney (upper pole). • Right suprarenal gland. • Inferior vena cava. • Right colic (hepatic) flexure. • Second part of the duodenum.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Abrupt cessation of inspiration during deep palpation of the right upper quadrant is known as [___] sign.
back:
• Murphy’s Sign
• Highly suggestive of acute cholecystitis
• Occurs as the inflamed gallbladder touches the parietal peritoneum upon diaphragmatic descent.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A 45-year-old patient presents with a perforated anterior duodenal ulcer. Despite the upper abdominal origin, the patient reports intense pain in the right iliac fossa. Explain this anatomical manifestation.
back:
• Fluid tracks down the right lateral paracolic gutter
• Directed by the transverse colon
• Can lead to a mistaken diagnosis of acute appendicitis
• Involves irritation of the parietal peritoneum.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The dome-shaped portion of the stomach that projects upward and to the left of the cardiac orifice, typically identified by a gas bubble on radiographs, is the [___].
back:
* Fundus.
* Lies superior to the horizontal plane of the cardiac orifice.
* Related superiorly to the left dome of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: A 25-year-old male presents with a swelling in the groin that extends into the scrotum. On exploration, the hernial sac is found to be lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. Identify the type and its congenital origin.
back:
* Indirect Inguinal Hernia
* Origin: Persistent processus vaginalis
* Enters through the deep inguinal ring

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: A 40-year-old obese multiparous woman presents with a lump that protrudes through the linea alba just above the umbilicus. This is defined as a(n) [___] hernia.
back: Paraumbilical Hernia. • Different from congenital umbilical hernias. • Sac protrudes near the umbilical scar. • Often contains omentum or coils of small intestine.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Distinguish between the clinical manifestation of jaundice caused by a gallstone in the bile duct versus a tumor in the head of the pancreas.
back:
Clinical Contrast:

*   Gallstone: Typically 'painful' jaundice associated with biliary colic.
*   Pancreatic Tumor: Classically 'painless,' progressively worsening jaundice.
*   Both result in clay-colored stools due to biliary obstruction.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) opens into the vestibule of the mouth on a small papilla opposite the [___].
back:
* Crown of the upper second molar tooth
* Pierces the buccinator muscle
* Crosses masseter muscle superficial to it

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: A child with chronic mouth breathing and snoring is diagnosed with enlarged adenoids. Explain how this condition relates to the development of otitis media.
back: Enlarged adenoids (pharyngeal tonsils) can obstruct the auditory tube orifice. This prevents ventilation of the middle ear and causes fluid accumulation. The resulting stasis leads to recurrent infections (otitis media) and potential conductive hearing loss.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: During a submandibular gland excision, a surgeon must identify the hypoglossal nerve. Describe its positional relationship to the mylohyoid muscle and the submandibular duct.
back:
• Passes deep to the mylohyoid muscle
• Lies inferior to the submandibular duct
• Positioned on the lateral surface of the hyoglossus muscle.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
front: A 30-year-old male presents with a hernia. On examination, the mass exits the abdominal wall via a triangular defect superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. Name this structure and its origin.
back: * Superficial inguinal ring. * Origin: External oblique aponeurosis. * It transmits the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament in females.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Identify the deep arteries supplying the lateral abdominal wall derived from the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta.
back:
*   Lower two posterior intercostal arteries (descending thoracic aorta)
*   Four lumbar arteries (abdominal aorta)
*   Pass forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles
*   Supply the lateral part of the abdominal wall

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: A patient presents with an inability to protrude the tongue in the midline; instead, it deviates to the right. There is noticeable wasting and wrinkling of the right half of the tongue.
back:
• Diagnosis: Right-sided Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) hypoglossal nerve injury
• Deviation occurs toward the paralyzed side
• Caused by the unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the specific bony landmarks that provide attachment for the anterior portion of the soft palate.
back:
• Posterior border of the hard palate.
• Formed by the horizontal plates of the palatine bones.
• Also involves palatine processes of the maxillae.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The skeletal framework of the hard palate is formed anteriorly by the [___] processes of the maxillae.
back:
• Palatine processes.
• They form the anterior two-thirds of the hard palate skeletal base.
• Meet at the median palatine suture.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Anterolateral Abdominal Wall
front: The [___] artery, a branch of the external iliac artery, originates just above the inguinal ligament and enters the rectus sheath at the arcuate line to supply the anterior wall.
back: • Inferior epigastric artery. • Originates from the external iliac artery. • Enters the rectus sheath at the arcuate line. • Acts as a surgical landmark to differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: The submandibular gland is divided into a larger superficial part and a smaller deep part by the posterior border of the [___] muscle.
back:
Mylohyoid muscle.
- It forms the muscular floor of the mouth.
- The deep part of the gland lies in the sublingual space.
- Wharton's duct emerges from the deep part.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Distinguish between the cardiac and pyloric orifices in terms of their anatomical sphincteric structure.
back:
• Cardiac: Physiologic sphincter (no distinct muscle thickening)
  • Pyloric: True anatomic sphincter (thickened circular smooth muscle)

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
coreConcept: Metastatic Routes of Large Bowel Cancer
front: Distinguish between the primary lymphatic and venous routes of metastasis for a malignant tumor located in the ascending colon.
back:
* Lymphatic: Superior mesenteric nodes via paracolic/colic nodes
* Venous: Liver via the portal vein (superior mesenteric vein tributary)
* Portal spread usually occurs late in the disease

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: A patient exhibits intense pain when an examiner suddenly removes their hand from the abdominal wall. Name this sign and its neuroanatomical cause.
back:
*   Rebound Tenderness.
*   Mechanism: Somatic sensory fibers in the parietal peritoneum are extremely sensitive to sudden stretch or mechanical movement.
*   Indicates localized peritonitis.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: During a percutaneous liver biopsy, the needle is inserted in the midaxillary line through the 8th or 9th intercostal space. Identify the mandatory respiratory phase and its anatomical purpose.
back:
• Full expiration.
• Reduces the size of the costodiaphragmatic recess.
• Moves the lung border upward to prevent accidental pleural/pulmonary puncture.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Identify the specific appendiceal position that lies posterior to the terminal ileum and may lead to localized ileitis or diagnostic confusion with small bowel pathology.
back:
* Post-ileal position.
* Situated directly behind the terminal ileum.
* Can cause irritation of the ileal wall.
* Rare compared to retrocecal or pelvic types.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Distinguish the macroscopic mesenteric vascular patterns and plicae circulares between the jejunum and the ileum.
back:
* Jejunum: Few large arcades, long vasa recta, and dense plicae circulares.
* Ileum: Multiple complex arcades, short vasa recta, and sparse/absent plicae circulares.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Evaluate the anatomical rationale for using Fowler's position (propped up at 45°) in patients with acute peritonitis to prevent subphrenic abscesses.
back:
• Gravity directs infected exudate toward the pelvic cavity.
• The pelvic peritoneum has a much slower toxin absorption rate than the subphrenic region.
• This localization reduces systemic sepsis and prevents diaphragmatic lymphatic irritation.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
coreConcept: Physiology of the Lower Esophageal Sphincter
front: Explain the physiological role of the gastroesophageal sphincter despite the absence of a distinct anatomical muscular thickening.
back: * Functions as a tonic smooth muscle barrier. * Relaxes ahead of peristaltic waves for food entry. * Prevents gastric acid reflux under vagal and hormonal control.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A patient with acute cholecystitis reports sharp pain over the right shoulder. Deduce the anatomical pathway responsible for this specific somatic referral.
back:
• Inflammation irritates central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum
• Carried by the Phrenic nerve (C3–C5)
• Referred to Supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4)
• Example of somatic-to-somatic referred pain.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A 45-year-old male presents with right-sided tongue atrophy and deviation to the right side upon protrusion. This suggests a lesion of the [___].
back:
• Right Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
• Tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion
• Occurs due to the unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Explain the anatomical basis for referred ear pain (otalgia) in a patient suffering from acute palatine tonsillitis.
back: * Sensory supply to the tonsil is via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). * CN IX also supplies the middle ear via the tympanic nerve.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Specify the vertebral level and surface plane where the first part of the duodenum typically originates from the gastric pylorus.
back:
* Level: L1 vertebra.
* Plane: Transpyloric plane.
* This segment is uniquely mobile and intraperitoneal compared to the retroperitoneal distal parts.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Contrast the motor innervation of the palatoglossus muscle with that of the other extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus).
back:
- Palatoglossus: Innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X).
- Others: Innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: A patient experiences dull, poorly localized aching in the epigastrium. Visceral afferent fibers transmitting this pain from the stomach travel via which specific nerves to enter the spinal cord?
back:
• Greater splanchnic nerves.
• Spinal segments: T5 to T9.
• Referred Pain: Perceived in the epigastric dermatomes.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: All lymphatic drainage from the various regions of the stomach eventually converges upon the [___] lymph nodes situated around the root of the eponymous artery.
back:
• Celiac lymph nodes.
• Ultimate terminal group for gastric lymph.
• Located around the celiac trunk on the posterior abdominal wall.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: Distinguish between the drainage duct systems of the submandibular and sublingual glands.
back:
Submandibular: Single Wharton’s duct.
- Sublingual: Multiple small Rivinus ducts (8-20) and occasionally one major Bartholin’s duct.
- Bartholin’s duct often joins Wharton’s duct.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Distinguish between the portal and systemic components of the venous drainage in the upper and lower halves of the anal canal.
back:
*   Portal: Superior rectal vein (from inferior mesenteric)
*   Systemic: Middle and inferior rectal veins (from internal iliac/pudendal)
*   Site of portosystemic shunt causing internal hemorrhoids

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: State the primary arterial source for the jejunum and ileum and its drainage route into the systemic circulation.
back:
* Arterial: Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA).
* Venous: Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV).
* Drainage: Joins splenic vein to form the portal vein.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Fascial Origins of the Deep Inguinal Ring
front: Identify the specific abdominal wall layer that forms the margins of the deep inguinal ring.
back: * Transversalis fascia. * This fascia evaginates to form the internal spermatic fascia. * The ring is positioned midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the symphysis pubis.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A surgeon is performing an esophagectomy and needs to ligate the blood supply to the cervical portion. Which artery must be identified?
back:
• Inferior thyroid artery
• Derived from the thyrocervical trunk
• Supplies the segment from C6 to the thoracic inlet.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: Distinguish the rectus abdominis muscle from the pyramidalis muscle on an anatomical model.
back:
• Rectus Abdominis: Long vertical strap muscle with tendinous intersections (T6-L1 nerve supply)
• Pyramidalis: Small triangular muscle anterior to lower rectus (T12 supply)
• Pyramidalis tenses the linea alba

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Distinguish between the venous drainage of the upper and lower halves of the anal canal in the context of portal hypertension.
back:
* Upper Half: Drains via superior rectal vein to portal system (pressure increases).
* Lower Half: Drains via inferior rectal veins to systemic system (remains low pressure).

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: The fibrous band found in the free margin of the falciform ligament, representing the obliterated fetal umbilical vein, is the [___].
back:
• Ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver).
• It is a remnant of the left umbilical vein.
• Extends from the umbilicus to the visceral surface of the liver.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: List the structures that constitute the 'Floor' and the 'Roof' of the inguinal canal.
back:
* Floor: Inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament
* Roof: Arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with gastric carcinoma. Identify the primary nodal group that must be removed 'en bloc' because it serves as the final abdominal drainage site for the stomach.
back:
* Celiac lymph nodes.
* They are located on the posterior abdominal wall at the celiac trunk origin.
* Total gastrectomy involves removing these nodes along with the spleen and associated omenta.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: A 55-year-old male presents with a hard, fixed mass in the parotid region and a sudden onset of ipsilateral facial drooping with inability to close the eye. What is the most likely clinical implication of these findings?
back:
* Malignant parotid tumor
* Benign tumors (like pleomorphic adenoma) rarely cause facial nerve palsy
* Rapidly invasive growth involves the facial nerve (CN VII) within the gland substance

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Distinguish between the fetal origins of the ligamentum teres and the ligamentum venosum.
back:
• Ligamentum teres: Obliterated left umbilical vein (post-natal remnant).
• Ligamentum venosum: Obliterated ductus venosus.
• Both reside in fissures on the visceral surface of the liver.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Specify the parasympathetic and sympathetic nerve sources that regulate small intestinal motility.
back:
• Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve (CN X) increases motility and secretion
• Sympathetic: Greater and Lesser splanchnic nerves (T5-T11) decrease motility
• Synapse occurs in the Celiac and Superior Mesenteric plexuses

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A patient with cholelithiasis develops sudden epigastric pain and elevated serum amylase. Explain the anatomical basis for this secondary complication.
back:
* Gallstone impaction at the Ampulla of Vater
* Shared terminal pathway for bile and pancreatic juice
* Reflux of bile triggers acute pancreatitis

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Esophageal varices occur primarily at the site of a portal-systemic anastomosis where the esophageal branches of the [___] vein meet the esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein.
back: * Left gastric vein. * Located at the lower third of the esophagus. * Dilatation occurs due to portal hypertension (e.g., liver cirrhosis).

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the peritoneal attachments and ligaments associated with the lesser curvature versus the greater curvature of the stomach.
back:
Lesser Curvature:
- Attached to Lesser Omentum (Hepatogastric/Hepatoduodenal ligaments).
Greater Curvature:
- Attached to Gastrosplenic ligament (upper part).
- Attached to Greater Omentum (lower part).

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the Common Hepatic Duct and the Bile Duct regarding their formation and anatomical relations within the lesser omentum.
back:
* CHD: Formed by R/L hepatic ducts; more superior
* CBD: CHD + Cystic duct; more inferior
* CBD lies anterior to portal vein and right of hepatic artery

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: A 60-year-old male presents with a direct inguinal hernia bulging through the Hesselbach triangle. This typically occurs due to a weak posterior wall medially, specifically where the [___] and transversus abdominis aponeuroses fail to form a strong conjoint tendon.
back: • **Internal oblique** • Inserts onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. • Reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal behind the superficial ring.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The [___] duct is formed at the porta hepatis by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts.
back:
• Common hepatic duct
  • Length is approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm)
  • Descends within the free margin of the lesser omentum

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Identify the systemic vessels that anastomose with the colic veins in the retroperitoneal space (Veins of Retzius) during portal hypertension.
back:
• Tributaries of Renal veins
• Lumbar veins
• Phrenic veins
• Provides an alternative systemic bypass for bowel drainage.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: The lymphoid aggregation situated in the roof of the nasopharynx, forming the superior portion of Waldeyer's ring, is the [___].
back: Pharyngeal tonsil (Adenoids). It is located in the midline of the nasopharyngeal roof. It typically reaches maximum size in childhood and atrophies after puberty. Hypertrophy can lead to significant nasal obstruction and mouth breathing.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Compare the sensory innervation and pain localization of the parietal peritoneum versus the visceral peritoneum.
back:
Peritoneal Nerve Supply

*   Parietal: Somatic nerves; sensitive to pain/touch; precisely localized
*   Visceral: Autonomic nerves; sensitive to stretch/tearing; dull/poorly localized
*   Parietal inflammation causes rebound tenderness

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: Differentiate the clinical surface location of an inguinal hernia from a femoral hernia relative to the pubic tubercle.
back:
• Inguinal Hernia: Emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle
• Femoral Hernia: Emerges below and lateral to the pubic tubercle

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: A patient is diagnosed with an abscess in the hepatorenal pouch (Morison’s Pouch). Trace the vertical reflection that defines this space's posterior limit.
back:
* Hepatorenal pouch is a subhepatic space
* Posterior limit: Parietal peritoneum covering the right kidney
* It is the most dependent part of the abdominal cavity when supine.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Upper GIT
front: Identify the branch of the celiac trunk that provides blood supply to both the lower third of the esophagus and the lesser curvature of the stomach.
back: * Left gastric artery. * Anastomoses with the right gastric artery. * Runs in the lesser omentum.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: A patient with portal hypertension exhibits a 'Caput Medusae' pattern. This clinical sign is formed by the anastomosis between paraumbilical veins and which specific systemic veins of the abdominal wall?
back:
Superficial epigastric veins.
* Also involves superior and inferior epigastric veins.
* Located in the subcutaneous tissue.
* Represents umbilical portosystemic site.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Identify the two lobes of the liver that are functionally part of the left lobe despite being anatomically part of the right lobe.
back: * Quadrate lobe. * Caudate lobe. * These receive the left branches of the hepatic artery and portal vein and drain into the left hepatic duct.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A patient with a history of large gallstones presents with symptoms of small bowel obstruction. If a stone has ulcerated into the duodenum, identify the most likely site of impaction.
back:
Ileocecal junction.

*   Narrowest part of the small intestine.
*   The condition is known as Gallstone Ileus.
*   Caused by a cholecystoenteric fistula.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A 65-year-old diabetic patient presents with high fever, persistent RUQ pain, and rebound tenderness. Imaging reveals intramural gas in the gallbladder wall. Identify the most likely diagnosis and its anatomical risk.
back:
• Gangrenous cholecystitis (Gallbladder gangrene).
• Ischemia leads to wall necrosis and perforation.
• High mortality risk in elderly and diabetic patients.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: The potential space between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney, which is the most dependent part of the upper peritoneal cavity when supine, is the [___].
back:
• Hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch).
• Formed by the right posterior subphrenic space.
• Common site for the accumulation of infected peritoneal fluid or blood.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient presents with a loss of sensation specifically on the palatal mucosa adjacent to the upper molar teeth. Damage to which nerve is most likely responsible?
back:
• Greater palatine nerve.
• Originates from the pterygopalatine ganglion (V2).
• Supplies the mucosa and glands of the majority of the hard palate.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: A surgeon observes fluid tracking vertically between the ascending colon and the lateral abdominal wall. Identify the peritoneal feature facilitating this movement and its clinical danger.
back:
* Right lateral paracolic gutter.
* Connects the supracolic compartment to the right iliac fossa/pelvis.
* Risk: Can direct infected fluid from a perforated gallbladder to the pelvic cavity.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The common bile duct typically joins the main pancreatic duct to form the [___], which opens into the second part of the duodenum.
back:
• Hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
• Opens at the summit of the major duodenal papilla.

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: Describe how the 'shutter mechanism' of the inguinal canal prevents herniation during periods of high intra-abdominal pressure.
back:
• Contraction of internal oblique and transversus abdominis
• Lowers the arched roof toward the floor
• Compresses the canal contents
• Effectively closes the canal space

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: Contrast the fate of the superficial fatty layer (Camper's) versus the membranous layer (Scarpa's) as they descend into the scrotum.
back:
• Camper's: The fat is lost and replaced by smooth muscle (dartos muscle).
• Scarpa's: Persists as a distinct, separate membranous layer within the scrotal wall.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Identify the specific origin of the short gastric arteries and their anatomical destination.
back:
• Origin: Splenic artery (at the hilum)
  • Destination: Fundus of the stomach
  • Travels within the gastrosplenic ligament

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Identify the specific segment of the duodenum where acidic chyme is squirted from the pylorus, making it the most common site for peptic ulceration.
back:
First part of the duodenum (Duodenal Cap).
- Specifically the anterolateral wall.
- Receives the direct impact of acidic chyme.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific notch on the lesser curvature that anatomically demarcates the junction between the gastric body and the pyloric antrum.
back:
* Incisura Angularis (Angular Notch).
* A constant landmark on the right/superior border.
* Directs the transition into the tubular pyloric region.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the functional roles of intrinsic lingual muscles with extrinsic lingual muscles.
back:
*   Intrinsic: Alter tongue shape (no bony attachment).
*   Extrinsic: Alter tongue position (attached to mandible, hyoid, styloid, or palate).
*   Both are essential for speech and deglutition.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
coreConcept: Nerve supply to the Conjoint Tendon
front: A patient develops a direct inguinal hernia following a gridiron incision for appendectomy. The surgeon suspects iatrogenic injury to a nerve that supplies the lower fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, specifically the [___].
back: • Iliohypogastric nerve (L1). • Supplies lower fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis. • Action: These muscles form the conjoint tendon, which reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Distinguish the lymphatic drainage of the skin of the back above the iliac crest from the drainage below the iliac crest.
back:
*   Above iliac crest: Lymph drains superiorly to posterior axillary nodes
*   Below iliac crest: Lymph drains inferiorly to superficial inguinal nodes
*   This drainage pattern follows the same watershed principle as the umbilicus

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Explain how the anatomical position of the palatine tonsil differs from the pharyngeal tonsil during a clinical examination.
back: Palatine tonsils: Visible on oral examination between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. Pharyngeal tonsil: Located in the nasopharynx; requires posterior rhinoscopy or imaging to visualize. The palatine tonsil is oropharyngeal, while the pharyngeal tonsil is nasopharyngeal.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: Explain the role of the 'Shutter Mechanism' in protecting the inguinal canal during increased intra-abdominal pressure.
back:
* Arched fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis contract
* The roof flattens against the floor (inguinal ligament)
* Effectively closes the canal to prevent herniation

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is clinically located at the tip of the [___] costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.
back:
• Ninth (9th) costal cartilage
• Marks the intersection with the linea semilunaris
• Important landmark for Cholecystitis palpation (Murphy's sign).

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The fibrous framework of the soft palate, formed by the expanded tendons of the tensor veli palatini muscles, is the [___].
back:
• Palatine aponeurosis.
• Attached to the posterior border of the hard palate.
• Provides support for other palatal muscles.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Distinguish between the ligamentum teres and the ligamentum venosum regarding their fetal origins.
back: * Ligamentum Teres: Fibrous remnant of the fetal left umbilical vein. * Ligamentum Venosum: Fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus. * Both are found on the visceral surface of the liver.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: A 32-year-old pregnant patient presents with sharp midline abdominal pain and a palpable, tender mass below the umbilicus following a severe coughing fit. Identify the likely vessel ruptured within the rectus sheath.
back:
• Inferior epigastric artery or vein
• Bleeding usually occurs below the umbilicus where the posterior wall is absent.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: External Features of the Large Intestine
front: The small fatty tags of peritoneum filled with adipose tissue found exclusively on the external surface of the large intestine are called [___].
back:
● Appendices epiploicae (Omental appendices).
● Absent on the small intestine, rectum, and appendix.
● Help distinguish the colon from small bowel loops during surgery.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Distinguish between the anatomical relations of the 'Promontoric' position and the 'Paracecal' position of the appendix.
back:
Promontoric vs. Paracecal.
- Promontoric: Tip points toward the sacral promontory.
- Paracecal: Tip lies along the lateral side of the cecum.
- Both are less common than retrocecal or pelvic.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: A patient with a subphrenic abscess presents with referred pain in the right shoulder. Describe the anatomical basis for this clinical finding.
back:
Phrenic nerve irritation (C3-C5).
- Central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum is supplied by the phrenic nerve.
- Pain is referred to the C3-C4 dermatomes.
- Sensory fibers share segments with supraclavicular nerves.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the lymphatic drainage pathway for a malignant lesion originating in the soft palate.
back:
• Drains directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes.
• Primary target is the jugulodigastric node.
• Some drainage may pass through retropharyngeal nodes first.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Aggregated lymphoid follicles, characteristic of the distal small intestine and primarily located in the mucous membrane of the ileum, are termed [___].
back:
* Peyer's patches.
* Most prominent in the distal ileum along the antimesenteric border.
* Essential for intestinal immune surveillance and lymphoid defense.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: The peripheral portions of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum receive sensory innervation from the [___] nerves.
back:
*   Lower six thoracic (intercostal) nerves.
*   Matches the segmental supply of the peripheral diaphragm muscle.
*   Distinct from the central phrenic supply.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Distinguish between a primary infection of the palatine tonsil and a peritonsillar abscess based on physical findings.
back: Tonsillitis: Features inflamed, enlarged tonsils within their arches. Peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy): Collection of pus lateral to the capsule, displacing the tonsil medially and shifting the uvula to the opposite side. Quinsy typically presents with severe trismus.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: The most superficial muscle of the anterolateral abdominal wall, characterized by fibers running in a 'hands-in-pockets' (downward and medial) direction, is the [___].
back:
• External oblique muscle
• Originates from the lower eight ribs
• Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and superficial inguinal ring
• Primary rotator and lateral flexor of the trunk

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the anatomical mechanism by which the suspensory ligament of Treitz maintains the position of the duodenojejunal flexure.
back:
Ligament of Treitz
- A peritoneal fold containing skeletal and smooth muscle.
- Attaches the flexure to the right crus of the diaphragm.
- Marks the formal transition between the duodenum and jejunum.

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: Contrast the relationship of the hernial sac's neck to the inguinal rings and the inferior epigastric vessels in direct versus indirect hernias.
back:
• Indirect: Neck is lateral to vessels; enters via deep ring
• Direct: Neck is medial to vessels; bulges through posterior wall
• Indirect: Often reaches scrotum
• Direct: Neck is typically wide and stays in the groin

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
coreConcept: Signs of Lower Motor Neuron Lesion
front: A chronic, long-standing lesion of the hypoglossal nerve will result in the [___] and characteristic wrinkling of the tongue on the affected side.
back:
- Atrophy
- This occurs due to the loss of trophic motor input to the striated muscles of the tongue.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Identify the specific intraoral landmark for the opening of the parotid (Stensen's) duct.
back:
• Small papilla located in the vestibule
• Opposite the upper second molar tooth
• Saliva enters the mouth after the duct pierces the buccinator muscle

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: Anatomically justify why a transverse incision is often better tolerated than a vertical incision in terms of post-operative muscle function.
back: * Follows natural skin cleavage lines. * Usually involves only one segmental nerve. * Rectus muscle fibers are held by tendinous intersections. * Aponeurotic repair provides a strong closure without muscle fiber suturing.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Identify the retroperitoneal porto-systemic anastomosis involving the colic veins and their systemic counterparts.
back:
• Portal: Veins of retroperitoneal organs (Ascending/Descending colon)
• Systemic: Renal, Lumbar, and Phrenic veins
• Clinical: Important deep collateral route during portal vein obstruction

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A patient is undergoing an appendectomy. On the cadaver, identify the surface landmark and point of maximum tenderness for the appendix base.
back:
McBurney’s Point
- Located 1/3 of the distance from the right ASIS to the umbilicus.
- Corresponds to the base of the appendix.
- Teniae coli converge at this specific site.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Clinical Topography of the Inguinal Ligament
front: A surgeon performing a repair for an indirect inguinal hernia identifies the floor of the canal formed by a recurved aponeurotic band. Identify the muscle of origin and the lateral and medial attachments of this band.
back: - Muscle: External oblique aponeurosis. - Lateral attachment: Anterior superior iliac spine. - Medial attachment: Pubic tubercle.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the vascular relations of the bile duct as it descends from the lesser omentum to the retroduodenal area.
back:
• Lesser omentum: Lies anterior to the portal vein and to the right of the hepatic artery
  • Retroduodenal: Situated behind the first part of the duodenum and to the right of the gastroduodenal artery

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Discuss the developmental basis for the lengthy and curving anatomical course taken by the hypoglossal nerve in the neck.
back:
- The nerve supplies muscles derived from occipital myotomes.
- It must follow these myotomes as they migrate from the hindbrain area, around the pharynx, and into the floor of the mouth.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: On a prosected small intestine specimen, contrast the vascular arcade and vasa recta patterns used to differentiate the jejunum from the ileum.
back: * Jejunum: One or two large arcades with long vasa recta. * Ileum: Multiple tiers (3-4+) of small arcades with short vasa recta. * Aids in segment identification during surgery.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
