front: A dentist injects local anesthetic into the greater palatine foramen. To which specific teeth will the palatal gingival anesthesia extend anteriorly?
back:
* Up to the maxillary canine.
* The nasopalatine nerve must be blocked for the incisor region.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A patient presents with right iliac fossa pain. Contrast the anatomical pathway by which fluid from a perforated duodenal ulcer reaches this area versus the pain progression in acute appendicitis.
back:
* Ulcer: Fluid tracks via the right lateral paracolic gutter
* Appendicitis: Initial T10 referred pain shifts to localized RLQ somatic pain
* Ulcer fluid is directed by the transverse colon

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with dilated, radiating periumbilical veins. Name the clinical sign and the specific portal vessel traversing the falciform ligament.
back:
*   Caput Medusae
*   Paraumbilical veins
*   Shunts portal blood to superficial systemic epigastric veins

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Name the three anatomical boundaries of the Cystohepatic Triangle (Calot’s Triangle) used to identify the cystic artery.
back:
• Superior: Visceral surface of the liver
• Medial: Common hepatic duct
• Lateral: Cystic duct
• Contains the cystic artery and Calot's node.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: In the circular arrangement of Waldeyer’s ring, the [___] tonsils are specifically situated within the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
back:
Palatine tonsils. 
- Most commonly removed during tonsillectomy. 
- Covered by a fibrous capsule laterally.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Small, peritoneum-covered fatty tags unique to the external surface of the colon are specifically called [___].
back:
Appendices Epiploicae (Omental Appendices).
- Key external marker for large intestine.
- Absent on the small intestine, appendix, and rectum.
- Frequently contain small nutrient vessels.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Explain the peritoneal reflections that define the 'Bare Area' of the liver and identify the major vessel located here.
back:
* Demarcated by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament.
* Laterally bounded by right and left triangular ligaments.
* Contains the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC).

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Describe the functional difference in trunk rotation between the external oblique and internal oblique muscles.
back: - External Oblique: Rotates the trunk to the opposite side (contralateral). - Internal Oblique: Rotates the trunk to the same side (ipsilateral). - They work synergistically to perform diagonal rotation.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: The fan-shaped fold of peritoneum that reflects from the posterior abdominal wall to suspend the jejunum and ileum is the [___].
back: * Mesentery of the small intestine. * Its root extends obliquely from the L2 level to the right sacroiliac joint. * Transmits mesenteric vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: Detail the anatomical extension and structures incised during an abdominothoracic incision used for lower esophageal carcinoma.
back:
Abdominal and thoracic extension.
- Upper oblique or paramedian incision.
- Extended into the 7th, 8th, or 9th intercostal space.
- Transects costal arch and incises the diaphragm.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Deep Ring
front: Distinguish between the mid-inguinal point and the midpoint of the inguinal ligament regarding the anatomical projection of the deep inguinal ring.
back: * Deep ring: Projects at the mid-inguinal point. * Mid-inguinal point: Halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis. * Midpoint of ligament: Halfway between ASIS and pubic tubercle.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Gallbladder Fundus
front: The fundus of the gallbladder projects below the inferior border of the liver and comes into contact with the anterior abdominal wall at the level of the [___] costal cartilage.
back: The fundus of the gallbladder is located at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage. It is typically found where the lateral margin of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Distinguish the origins of the right and left gastric arteries as they appear on a cadaveric stomach along the lesser curvature.
back: * Left Gastric: Direct branch of the celiac trunk. * Right Gastric: Branch of the hepatic artery proper (or common hepatic). * They form an anastomotic arcade along the lesser curvature.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A patient with a gallstone impacted in the retroduodenal portion of the bile duct experiences a severe hemorrhage. Which specific artery running directly posterior to the first part of the duodenum is likely eroded?
back:
• Gastroduodenal artery
• Relation: The bile duct lies to its right
• Location: Both structures pass behind the 1st part of the duodenum

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Explain the surgical method used to identify the base of the appendix by tracing the longitudinal muscle bands of the large intestine.
back:
Convergence of Teniae Coli.
- Follow the three teniae coli of the cecum distally.
- They converge at the posteromedial aspect of the cecal wall.
- This point marks the fixed base of the appendix.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Explain the physiological trigger that causes the normally small portosystemic collateral channels to become pathologically enlarged in patients with hepatic cirrhosis.
back:
Portal Hypertension.
* Occurs when intrahepatic resistance increases.
* Forces blood through collateral pathways.
* Reverses normal flow toward systemic veins.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A patient with cholelithiasis presents with jaundice and epigastric pain. Identify the specific biliary site where a stone obstructs both bile and pancreatic outflow.
back:
● Hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
● Located in the second part of the duodenum
● Common site for biliary-pancreatic reflux if obstructed

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient cannot elevate the posterior tongue to close the oropharyngeal isthmus. Identify the involved muscle and its atypical innervation compared to other lingual muscles.
back:
• Muscle: Palatoglossus
• Nerve: Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus
• Other tongue muscles are innervated by CN XII

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Contrast the clinical presentation and neuroanatomical basis of pain arising from the parietal peritoneum versus the visceral peritoneum.
back:
Key distinctions:
- Parietal: Sharp, localized, somatic innervation (spinal nerves); sensitive to pressure/temp.
- Visceral: Dull, poorly localized (midline), autonomic innervation; sensitive to stretch/ischemia.
- Parietal irritation leads to guarding and rebound tenderness.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain how the 'secondary palate' is formed during the 8th to 12th weeks of intrauterine life.
back:
* Medial growth of palatal processes (from maxillary processes)
* Midline fusion of processes
* Fusion with the nasal septum and primary palate.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic epigastric pain presents with sudden, massive hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Identify the most likely eroded artery.
back:
• Gastroduodenal artery
• Significant risk due to its location posterior to the duodenal bulb
• Branch of the common hepatic artery

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A 45-year-old female presents with severe, spasmodic right upper quadrant pain after eating fried chicken. Identify the specific nerves that transmit this visceral pain to the T5–T9 spinal segments.
back:
Greater splanchnic nerves.

*   Transmit visceral afferents from the celiac plexus.
*   Pain is poorly localized and often felt in the epigastrium.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: A patient is diagnosed with an internal hernia involving a loop of small bowel trapped within the paraduodenal recess. Identify the specific vascular structure at risk in the anterior margin of this fold.
back: * Inferior mesenteric vein. * Located in the fold forming the paraduodenal recess. * Compression can lead to venous congestion or ischemia.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Describe the anatomical mechanism by which the cystic duct and gallbladder neck maintain patency during pressure changes.
back: • Spiral valve of Heister • Fold of mucous membrane within the neck and duct • Prevents kinking or collapse of the lumen • Ensures bidirectional flow for storage and emptying

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Ileocecal Region
front: An 18-month-old child presents with intermittent abdominal pain and 'currant jelly' stools. A portion of the ileum is found invaginated into the cecum. Identify this condition.
back:
### Intussusception
* Most common at the ileocecal junction.
* Telescoping of proximal gut into distal gut.
* Can lead to gangrene due to mesenteric vessel compression.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Distinguish the internal mucosal features of the duodenum's first part from its second and third parts.
back:
* First part (Cap): Smooth mucous membrane; lacks circular folds.
* 2nd/3rd/4th parts: Thrown into permanent circular folds (Plicae Circulares).
* Folds increase surface area for enzyme contact and absorption.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy: Gastric Relations and Hemorrhage
front: A 50-year-old patient with a chronic posterior gastric ulcer presents with massive internal bleeding. The ulcer has most likely eroded into the [___] artery.
back: ● Splenic artery. ● Runs along the superior border of the pancreas. ● Forms a major part of the stomach bed.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Describe the mechanism by which the oropharyngeal isthmus is narrowed to prevent food from returning to the mouth during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
back: The palatoglossus muscles contract, pulling the root of the tongue upward and the soft palate downward. This action, combined with the approximation of the palatoglossal arches, narrows the isthmus to propel the bolus.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Lymph from the upper part of the lesser curvature of the stomach predominantly drains into the [___] nodes.
back:
Left gastric nodes.
- These follow the left gastric artery.
- They are a primary site for proximal gastric cancer metastasis.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Anatomical Divisions of the Bile Duct
front: Explain the four-part sequence of the bile duct's descent toward the duodenum.
back:
• Supraduodenal: In lesser omentum
• Retroduodenal: Behind the 1st part of duodenum
• Infraduodenal: In groove behind pancreatic head
• Intraduodenal: Piercing the 2nd part of duodenum

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the venous drainage of the lower third of the esophagus with the drainage of the thoracic segment.
back: 1. Lower Third: Drains to portal system (Left gastric vein). 2. Thoracic Segment: Drains to systemic system (Azygos vein). 3. Clinical Link: Site of portal-systemic anastomosis.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Describe the autonomic pathway for visceral pain fibers originating from the stomach to the spinal cord.
back:
*   Route: Accompany sympathetic fibers through the celiac plexus.
*   Nerves: Travel via the greater splanchnic nerves.
*   Level: Enter the spinal cord at T5-T9 segments.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: Describe the specific anatomical layers and structures traversed during a midline incision through the abdominal wall.
back:
Linea alba approach.
- Skin and superficial fascia layers.
- Fibrous linea alba (fused aponeuroses).
- Transversalis fascia and extraperitoneal fat.
- Parietal peritoneum.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Identify the primary arterial supply for the supraduodenal part of the common bile duct.
back:
• Cystic artery (proximal portion)
• Right hepatic artery (middle portion)
• Posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal and gastroduodenal arteries (distal portion).

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Identify three anatomical factors that comprise the 'physiologic' sphincter mechanism at the gastroesophageal junction to prevent GERD.
back:
* Lower Esophageal Sphincter: Tonically active circular smooth muscle.
* Diaphragmatic Crura: External compression by the right crus.
* Angle of His: Acute angle between the esophagus and stomach fundus.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A 45-year-old male with persistent heartburn is diagnosed with a hiatal hernia. Identify the muscular structure of the diaphragm that normally forms the esophageal hiatus and its role.
back:
- Right crus of the diaphragm
- Forms a muscular sling around the esophagus
- Acts as an extrinsic physiological sphincter

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the role of gastric rugae in accommodating large meals within the stomach.
back:
• Longitudinal mucosal folds
• Flatten out during distension to increase volume capacity
• Provide temporary storage without increasing internal pressure

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: A 50-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with sudden-onset hematemesis. Identify the specific portal and systemic veins involved in this anastomosis.
back:
Esophageal anastomosis:
* Portal: Left gastric vein.
* Systemic: Azygos vein (via esophageal tributaries).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: At which vertebral level does the esophagus typically terminate by joining the stomach?
back: T11 (at the cardiac orifice of the stomach).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the venous drainage pathway of the thoracic segment of the esophagus.
back: * Drained by the azygos and hemiazygos veins. * Represents systemic venous drainage. * These vessels eventually empty into the superior vena cava.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: A 55-year-old patient with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with massive hematemesis. The dilated veins responsible for this hemorrhage involve a communication between the left gastric vein and which systemic venous system?
back:
Azygos system.
* Specifically the esophageal tributaries.
* Occurs in the lower third of the esophagus.
* Managed with Sengstaken-Blakemore tubes.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Explain the anatomical basis for why a pharyngeal infection might cause referred pain to the ear.
back: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) supplies the oropharynx (palatine tonsils) and the middle ear (tympanic plexus). Sensory impulses from a sore throat can be 'referred' to the ear along these shared nerve pathways, misleading the patient's perception of pain location.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Distinguish between the anatomical triggers for variceal formation versus the development of ascites in portal hypertension.
back:
• Varices: Opening of pre-existing porto-systemic collateral shunts.
• Ascites: Increased hydrostatic pressure causing fluid leak across visceral peritoneum.
• Both result from portal venous blockage.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Pathway of the Parotid Gland
front: In the parasympathetic pathway for parotid salivary secretion, preganglionic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) synapse in the [___] ganglion.
back:
• Otic ganglion
• Located in the infratemporal fossa
• Postganglionic fibers then travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to stimulate the gland's serous secretions

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: In addition to the standard circular and longitudinal layers, the stomach uniquely possesses an innermost [___] muscle layer.
back:
* Oblique Layer.
* Essential for the complex churning motion to form chyme.
* Most developed in the fundus and body regions.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: Contrast the neck position of a Direct versus an Indirect inguinal hernia relative to the inferior epigastric artery.
back:
* Indirect: Neck is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery
* Direct: Neck is medial to the inferior epigastric artery
* Direct hernias occur through Hesselbach's triangle

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Identify the anatomical relationship between the soft palate and Waldeyer’s ring during the involuntary phase of deglutition.
back:
- The soft palate is elevated by the levator veli palatini. 
- It seals against the posterior pharyngeal wall (pharyngeal isthmus). 
- This prevents food from entering the nasopharyngeal tonsillar region.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: A 55-year-old male with liver cirrhosis presents with sudden massive hematemesis. Endoscopy confirms dilated submucosal veins at the lower esophagus. Specify the veins forming this porto-systemic junction.
back:
• Portal side: Left gastric (coronary) vein.
• Systemic side: Esophageal branches of the azygos vein.
• Clinical Picture: Esophageal varices; rupture causes life-threatening bleeding due to high portal pressures.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The terminal part of the bile duct usually unites with the [___] to form the [___].
back:
* Main pancreatic duct (Duct of Wirsung).
* Hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater).
* Opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: The longitudinal depressions found between the lateral abdominal wall and the ascending or descending colon are termed the [___].
back:
Paracolic Gutters

*   Pathways for infected fluid/bile movement
*   Right gutter communicates with the subphrenic space
*   Essential for predicting abscess spread in supine patients

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Lower Esophagus
front: Specify the primary arterial supply to the abdominal portion of the esophagus, which is frequently involved in surgical resections.
back:
• Left gastric artery
• Arises from the celiac trunk
• Supplies the lower esophagus and lesser curvature of the stomach

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Name the four distinct parts of the duodenum in order from the pylorus to the duodenojejunal flexure.
back:
1. First Part: Superior (intraperitoneal start).
2. Second Part: Descending (contains biliary papillae).
3. Third Part: Horizontal (crosses Aorta/IVC).
4. Fourth Part: Ascending (ends at Treitz ligament).

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: In surgical anatomy, the neck of an indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal via the deep inguinal ring, which is situated [___] to the inferior epigastric artery.
back:
• Lateral
• Enters through the deep inguinal ring
• Often descends into the scrotum
• Caused by a congenital patent processus vaginalis

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: List the specific layers of the spermatic fascia that provide a covering for an indirect inguinal hernia but are bypassed by a direct inguinal hernia.
back:
• Internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia)
• Cremasteric fascia (internal oblique muscle)
• External spermatic fascia (external oblique aponeurosis)

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The [___] part of the duodenum is the only segment that is primarily intraperitoneal and is mobile, unlike the remaining retroperitoneal parts.
back:
• First part (Superior part)
• Approximately 2 inches long
• Proximal half is attached to the lesser omentum
• Lies at the level of L1 vertebra

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Contrast the jejunal mesentery with the ileal mesentery regarding the arrangement of arterial arcades and vasa recta.
back:
*   Jejunum: One or two large arcades with long, infrequent vasa recta
*   Ileum: Multiple tiers (3–4+) of smaller arcades with short, numerous vasa recta
*   Purpose: High-yield surgical landmark for identifying segments during laparotomy

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Describe the formation and clinical significance of the 'Marginal Artery' (of Drummond) along the large intestine.
back:
- Formation: Anastomosis of the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic, and left colic arteries. 
- Significance: Provides collateral circulation; protects the colon from ischemia if a major mesenteric vessel is occluded.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Contrast the specific portal and systemic vessels that contribute to the formation of internal hemorrhoids at the anorectal junction.
back:
Portal: Superior rectal vein.
Systemic: Middle and inferior rectal veins.
* Anastomosis occurs at the anal canal.
* Systemic veins drain to internal iliac.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Specify the vertebral level and the horizontal abdominal plane that corresponds to the location of the gastric pylorus.
back:
• L1 Vertebra
• Transpyloric Plane
• Intersection of the tips of the 9th costal cartilages

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with caput medusae. This portosystemic shunt occurs because the [___] veins, tributaries of the portal vein, dilate and communicate with systemic veins.
back: * Paraumbilical veins. * They run along the ligamentum teres. * They connect the left portal vein branch to the superficial epigastric veins.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: In the setting of portal hypertension, the clinical sign characterized by distended veins radiating from the umbilicus is known as [___].
back:
• Caput medusae.
• Anatomical Basis: Anastomosis between paraumbilical veins (portal) and superficial epigastric veins (systemic).
• Pathophysiology: Retrograde flow through the ligamentum teres when portal flow is obstructed.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Distinguish the attachments and major vascular contents of the gastrosplenic omentum (ligament) versus the lesser omentum.
back:
Peritoneal Folds:
- Gastrosplenic Omentum: Connects upper greater curvature to the spleen; contains short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.
- Lesser Omentum: Connects lesser curvature and proximal duodenum to the liver; contains gastric vessels and the portal triad.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: A patient presents with a tongue that deviates to the left when protruded during a physical examination. This finding indicates a lesion of the [___] hypoglossal nerve.
back:
- Left (Ipsilateral)
- The tongue points toward the side of the nerve injury due to unopposed action of the healthy side.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Contrast the surface features and precise oropharyngeal location of the palatine tonsil with the nasopharyngeal tonsil.
back: ● Palatine: Located in the tonsillar sinus (between arches); contains deep, stratified squamous-lined crypts ● Nasopharyngeal: Located in the nasopharyngeal roof; contains mucosal folds and ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: The point of convergence for the three [___] on the cecum serves as the reliable anatomical landmark for locating the base of the appendix during surgery.
back:
* Teniae coli
* Converge at the appendiceal base
* Provide a continuous longitudinal muscle coat
* Essential for identification in retrocecal variants

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Identify the two most common anatomical locations for the tip of the appendix as encountered in clinical practice.
back:
• Retrocecal (behind the cecum)
• Pelvic (descending into the true pelvis)
• Other less frequent sites include subcecal, pre-ileal, and post-ileal.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A 60-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). CT reveals a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which portion of the biliary tree is likely obstructed?
back:
• The third (intrapancreatic) part of the bile duct
• It runs in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A 60-year-old female presents with symptoms of small bowel obstruction. Radiography reveals a large gallstone in the intestinal lumen. Identify the most likely route and site of obstruction.
back:
* Route: Cholecystoduodenal fistula (ulceration through the gallbladder wall).
* Site: Ileocecal junction (narrowest part of the small bowel).
* This condition is known as Gallstone Ileus.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Detail the clinical importance of the Suspensory Muscle of the Duodenum (Ligament of Treitz).
back:
* Marks the duodenojejunal flexure.
* Anatomical boundary dividing Upper GI bleeding from Lower GI bleeding.
* Attached to the right crus of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Explain the functional role of the Greater Omentum in limiting the spread of localized abdominal infections.
back:
• Acts as the 'Abdominal Policeman'
• Highly mobile; migrates to sites of inflammation
• Adheres to infected viscera (e.g., appendix)
• Walls off infection to prevent generalized peritonitis

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A clinician performs a lateral abdominal paracentesis. The needle must be inserted lateral to the [___] artery to avoid severe iatrogenic hemorrhage.
back: ● Inferior epigastric artery. ● Located medial to the deep inguinal ring. ● Injury causes rectus sheath hematoma or intraperitoneal bleeding.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the primary lymphatic station for the gallbladder and its specific surgical landmark.
back:
• Cystic lymph node (Node of Lund)
• Located at the junction of the neck and cystic duct
• Efferents drain to hepatic nodes
• Ultimately reaches the celiac nodes.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Contrast the typical locations of pain in peritonitis caused by a pelvic appendix versus a subphrenic abscess.
back: • Pelvic Appendix: Tenderness above symphysis pubis; localized by rectal examination. • Subphrenic Abscess: Pain in hypochondrium; often referred to shoulder (C3-C5).

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Distinguish the origin of the testicular artery from that of the inferior epigastric artery relative to the cord's path.
back:
• Testicular Artery: Arises from the Abdominal Aorta (L2 level).
• Inferior Epigastric: Arises from the External Iliac artery; used as a landmark medial to the deep ring.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Distinguish between the mesentery of the small intestine and the transverse mesocolon in terms of their posterior wall attachments.
back: * Mesentery of Small Intestine: Attaches along an oblique line from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocolic junction. * Transverse Mesocolon: Attaches horizontally across the anterior surface of the pancreas.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: The peritoneal compartment located posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum, communicating with the greater sac via the epiploic foramen, is the [___].
back:
• Lesser sac (omental bursa)
• Provides space for stomach distension
• Bound posteriorly by the pancreas and left kidney.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: During a physical exam, the physician asks the patient to say 'Ah.' The uvula is seen to deviate towards the left. Which nerve is likely damaged?
back:
• Right Vagus nerve (CN X).
• The uvula deviates towards the healthy side (away from the lesion).
• Caused by unopposed action of the contralateral levator veli palatini.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: Explain the clinical importance of suturing the membranous layer (Scarpa's fascia) during the closure of an abdominal surgical wound.
back:
• Increases the mechanical strength of the healing wound.
• Prevents stretching and widening of the skin scar.
• Ensures a more cosmetically acceptable result post-operatively.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A 45-year-old female with gallstones presents with acute right upper quadrant pain that radiates to her right shoulder. Explain the anatomical basis for this specific referral of pain.
back: Inflammation irritates the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). Pain is referred to the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4), which share the same spinal segments and supply the skin of the shoulder.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Identify the two major peritoneal folds that contain the primary lymph node groups for the lesser and greater curvatures respectively.
back:
- Lesser Omentum: Contains gastric nodes.
- Greater Omentum: Contains gastro-omental nodes.
- Gastrosplenic Ligament: Contains pancreaticosplenic nodes for the fundus.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: The posterior wall of the rectus sheath is entirely absent below the level of the [___], where the muscle sits directly on the transversalis fascia.
back:
• Arcuate line (linea semicircularis)
• This occurs approximately at the level of the anterior superior iliac spine.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Analyze the anatomical rationale for why an appendix in the 'retrocecal' position may produce a positive Psoas sign.
back:
The appendix lies posterior to the cecum, resting on the Psoas Major.
- Inflammation irritates the muscle.
- Pain is elicited by passive extension of the right hip, which stretches the muscle.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: A 24-year-old male presents with right-sided abdominal pain. On examination, extending the right hip (Psoas sign) exacerbates the pain, but the abdominal wall lacks significant tenderness. This clinical picture suggests the appendix is in the [___] position.
back:
• Retrocecal position
• Most common anatomical variant
• The cecum buffers the inflamed appendix from the anterior abdominal wall, masking typical guarding.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Identify the large artery running along the upper border of the pancreas that is most susceptible to erosion by a posterior gastric ulcer.
back:
• Splenic artery
• Branch of the celiac trunk
• Erosion leads to potentially fatal intraperitoneal hemorrhage
• Located in the posterior wall of the lesser sac.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: The [___] veins, which travel within the falciform ligament, connect the left branch of the portal vein to the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
• Paraumbilical veins
• Remains of the fetal umbilical vein pathway
• Connects to systemic epigastric venous system
• Pathological dilation creates the Caput Medusae sign

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Contrast the clinical consequences of a perforation on the anterior stomach wall versus the posterior wall.
back:
• Anterior: Contents leak into the greater sac, causing generalized peritonitis.
• Posterior: Contents enter the lesser sac (omental bursa).
• Complication: Posterior leaks can form pseudocysts or erode the pancreas.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Distinguish the fetal origins of the Ligamentum Teres and the Ligamentum Venosum.
back:
• Ligamentum Teres: Remnant of the left umbilical vein.
• Ligamentum Venosum: Remnant of the ductus venosus.
• Ductus venosus shunted blood from the umbilical vein to the IVC.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Outline the systematic lymphatic drainage of the jejunum and ileum starting from the intestinal wall.
back:
• Lymph enters lacteals in villi
• Passes through mesenteric lymph nodes (located within the mesentery)
• Terminates in the Superior Mesenteric Nodes
• Eventually enters the Cisterna Chyli

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Physiologic and Anatomic Sphincters of the Stomach
front: Explain the role of the pyloric sphincter in regulating gastric emptying into the duodenum.
back:
Anatomic sphincter formed by thickened circular muscle.
- Controls chyme outflow.
- Stimulated (contracted) by sympathetic fibers.
- Inhibited (relaxed) by vagal fibers and gastrin.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Identify the primary regional lymph nodes that receive drainage from the jejunum and ileum, and state their final destination.
back:
* Superior mesenteric lymph nodes.
* Located around the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
* Efferents drain into the intestinal lymph trunk and cisterna chyli.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the anatomical nature of the pyloric sphincter with that of the cardiac (gastroesophageal) junction.
back:
• Pylorus: True anatomical sphincter (thickened circular muscle)
• Cardiac: Physiologic sphincter (diaphragmatic crura and muscle tone)
• Pylorus regulates emptying; Cardia prevents acid reflux

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: Identify the specific anatomical site of protrusion characteristic of a Spigelian hernia.
back: Linea semilunaris. • Protrudes through the aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis. • Usually occurs at the level of the arcuate line, lateral to the rectus sheath.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: In the lower third of the esophagus, a vital porto-systemic anastomosis is formed between the [___] vein, a tributary of the portal vein, and the esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein.
back:
• Left gastric (coronary) vein
• Dilates during portal hypertension to form esophageal varices
• Rupture results in life-threatening hematemesis

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A patient with suspected cholecystitis experiences a sudden arrest of inspiration upon deep palpation of the right subcostal region. Identify the organ involved and the anatomical mechanism of this sign.
back: The gallbladder is assessed. As the patient breathes in, the diaphragm descends, pushing the inflamed gallbladder against the examiner's fingers. This causes sharp pain and a reflex halt in inspiration, known as Murphy's sign.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: A 6-year-old child presents with chronic mouth breathing, snoring, and recurrent middle ear infections. Examination reveals a mass in the roof of the nasopharynx.
back: ● Adenoids (Pharyngeal Tonsil Hypertrophy) ● Enlargement obstructs the posterior nasal choanae ● Blocks the auditory tube orifice, leading to secondary otitis media ● Common indication for surgical adenoidectomy in children.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: The parotid duct (Stensen’s duct) enters the vestibule of the oral cavity by piercing the [___] muscle and opening onto a papilla opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth.
back:
* Buccinator muscle
* The duct crosses the masseter muscle superficially before piercing the buccinator
* It is approximately 5 cm long

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific point in the gastrointestinal tract where the blood supply shifts from the celiac trunk territory to the superior mesenteric artery territory.
back:
Middle of the second part of the duodenum.
• Corresponds to the entry of the bile duct.
• Represents the embryological junction of the foregut and midgut.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: A 15-year-old male with periumbilical pain and fever shows relief of pain when flexing the right hip, but severe pain upon hip extension. Identify the likely anatomical position of the appendix.
back:
Retrocecal position
*   Appendix is coiled behind the cecum
*   Irritates the psoas muscle, causing a positive psoas sign
*   Often lacks classic anterior abdominal tenderness

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Distinguish between the anatomical and physiological sphincters of the esophagus.
back:
- Anatomic: No distinct thickening of circular muscle is present.
- Physiologic: Region of high pressure maintained by smooth muscle tone and diaphragmatic support.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
coreConcept: Neurovascular Relations of the Submandibular Gland
front: A patient experiences loss of general sensation and taste on the anterior 2/3 of the tongue after a deep biopsy in the floor of the mouth. Which nerve, found medial to the submandibular gland, is affected?
back:
* Lingual nerve
* Carries chorda tympani fibers (taste) and V3 fibers (general sensation)
* It is the most medial and intimate nerve relation of the gland

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: A patient with advanced gastric cancer presents with an enlarged left supraclavicular node (Troisier sign). Through which major lymphatic vessel did the malignant cells reach this location?
back:
* Thoracic duct.
* Cancer cells ascend via the intestinal trunk and cisterna chyli.
* Lodges at the junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Distinguish the anatomical attachments of the lesser omentum from those of the greater omentum.
back:
• Lesser Omentum: Connects lesser curvature of stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver.
• Greater Omentum: Connects greater curvature of stomach to the transverse colon, hanging over intestines.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: The [___] gutters provide clinical pathways for the migration of infected fluid or bile from the upper abdomen to the pelvis in supine patients.
back:
• Paracolic gutters
• Lateral to the ascending and descending colons
• Right gutter is common route for fluid from perforated gallbladders
• Directs exudate toward the rectovesical or recto-uterine pouches

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, except for the [___].
back:
- Palatoglossus
- This specific muscle is supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The bile duct terminates by piercing the medial wall of the [___] part of the duodenum.
back:
* Second (descending) part
* Joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla
* Opens at the major duodenal papilla

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: In the presence of portal hypertension, the paraumbilical veins anastomose with the [___] veins, leading to the clinical appearance of caput medusae.
back: The superficial epigastric (and/or superior/inferior epigastric) veins.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Identify the specific sites in the colonic wall where diverticula primarily occur and explain why.
back:
* Sites: Between the teniae coli
* Reason: Points of relative weakness where vasa recta (blood vessels) pierce the circular muscle
* Commonality: Most frequent in the sigmoid colon

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the functional mechanism of the genioglossus muscle during tongue movement.
back:
• Bilateral contraction: Protrudes the tongue tip
• Known as the 'safety muscle'
• Prevents the tongue from falling backward and obstructing the airway

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: Distinguish between the deep and superficial inguinal rings based on their location and fascial origins.
back:
* Deep Ring: Opening in transversalis fascia; 0.5 inch above mid-inguinal point
* Superficial Ring: Defect in external oblique aponeurosis; above and medial to pubic tubercle

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: The primary anatomical landmark used to differentiate the origins of direct and indirect inguinal hernias is the [___] artery.
back:
• Inferior epigastric artery
• Indirect hernias are lateral to it
• Direct hernias are medial to it

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Zones of the Stomach
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the fundus and upper left greater curvature with that of the right portion of the greater curvature.
back:
- Fundus/Left: Drains to pancreaticosplenic (splenic) nodes via short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels.
- Right Greater Curvature: Drains to right gastro-omental and subpyloric nodes.
- Both eventually reach the celiac nodes.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Lesser Peritoneal Sac
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach. Identify the specific peritoneal compartment where the leaked gastric contents initially collect.
back: * Lesser sac (Omental bursa). * Positioned behind the stomach and lesser omentum. * Communicates with the greater sac via the epiploic foramen.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: External Features of the Large Intestine
front: The three distinct longitudinal bands of smooth muscle characteristic of the large intestine, which converge at the base of the appendix, are known as [___].
back:
Teniae Coli.
- Formed by the outer longitudinal muscle layer.
- Their shorter length relative to the colon creates haustrations (sacculations).
- Absent on the appendix and rectum.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Contrast the anatomical pathways for visceral gallbladder pain versus somatic pain from localized cholecystitis.
back:
• Visceral: Via celiac plexus and greater splanchnic nerves (T7-T9); felt in the epigastrium.
• Somatic: Irritation of the anterior abdominal wall parietal peritoneum; felt in the right upper quadrant.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A surgeon identifies the base of the appendix during an emergency appendectomy by tracing the convergence of the three longitudinal muscle bands of the cecum known as [___].
back:
● Teniae coli.
● They converge at the base of the appendix to form a complete longitudinal muscle coat.
● They are a hallmark feature of the large intestine.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma involving the lesser curvature of the stomach. Metastatic spread via lymphatics from this specific region primarily involves which node group?
back:
Gastric lymph nodes (Left and Right).
- Specifically left gastric nodes for the upper lesser curvature.
- Right gastric nodes for the lower lesser curvature.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: A patient develops localized sweating and flushing over the parotid region while eating, following a previous history of parotid surgery. This phenomenon is caused by the misdirected regeneration of [___] fibers.
back:
* Frey’s syndrome (auriculotemporal syndrome)
* Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers erroneously join sympathetic fibers supplying sweat glands
* Symptoms occur during gustatory stimuli (eating)

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Specify the portal and systemic components that form the retroperitoneal (Retzius) anastomosis.
back:
* Portal: Veins of retroperitoneal organs (e.g., ascending/descending colon, duodenum).
* Systemic: Renal, lumbar, and phrenic veins.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Describe the anatomical basis and vertebral level for the difference in height between the right (hepatic) and left (splenic) colic flexures.
back:
### Colic Flexures
* **Right Flexure:** Lower, below the right lobe of the liver.
* **Left Flexure:** Higher (L1 level), attached to the diaphragm via the **phrenicocolic ligament**.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: In the free margin of the lesser omentum, the hepatic portal vein is situated [___] to both the hepatic artery and the bile duct.
back:
• Posterior
• Forms the posterior boundary of the portal triad
• Lies anterior to the epiploic foramen (of Winslow)

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 24-year-old male presents with periumbilical pain that later shifts to the right iliac fossa. Contrast the nerve pathways involved in this shift from visceral to somatic pain.
back:
Appendix Pain Transition
- Visceral: Afferents travel with sympathetic nerves to T10 (periumbilical).
- Somatic: Irritation of the parietal peritoneum by the inflamed appendix.
- Somatic pain is precisely localized to the right iliac fossa.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Explain the mechanism of Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating) following a penetrating injury to the parotid region.
back:
• Damage to the auriculotemporal nerve.
• Misdirected regrowth of parasympathetic fibers to sympathetic sweat glands.
• Results in sweating on the cheek during eating (salivatory stimulus).

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The dome-shaped part of the stomach located superior to the level of the cardiac orifice, usually visualized on X-ray containing a gas bubble, is the [___].
back: Fundus

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: Describe the pathway of the lower five intercostal nerves as they transition from the thoracic cage to supply the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
- Pass posterior to the costal cartilages.
- Enter the neurovascular plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
- Pierce the rectus sheath and muscle to reach the skin.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific anatomical site where the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct Typically discharge their contents into the small intestine.
back:
● Major duodenal papilla.
● Located on the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum.
● Marks the junction between the foregut and midgut.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Explain the underlying pathophysiology of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating) following a parotidectomy.
back:
- Damaged parasympathetic fibers of the auriculotemporal nerve regenerate.
- They mistakenly reinnervate facial sweat glands (sympathetic).
- Result: Sweating and flushing during meals instead of salivation.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Organs such as the kidneys and suprarenal glands, which develop and remain posterior to the parietal peritoneum, are classified as [___] structures.
back:
• Primarily retroperitoneal
• Only their anterior surfaces are covered by peritoneum
• Supported by perirenal and pararenal fat.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Metastatic deposits from a primary sigmoid colon tumor are frequently found in the left lobe of the liver. Account for this distribution based on portal venous dynamics.
back:
• 'Streaming' of blood in the portal vein
• IMV/Splenic blood tends to enter the left hepatic lobe
• SMV blood tends to enter the right hepatic lobe

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the arterial supply of the cervical portion of the esophagus with that of the abdominal portion.
back:
• Cervical: Branches of the inferior thyroid arteries.
• Abdominal: Left gastric artery and left inferior phrenic artery.
• The thoracic portion is supplied by bronchial and esophageal aortic branches.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: Specify the muscular boundaries of Petit’s triangle, which serves as the site for a lumbar hernia.
back: Base: Iliac crest. • Anterior: Posterior border of external oblique. • Posterior: Anterior border of latissimus dorsi. • Floor: Internal oblique muscle.

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: Identify the specific spinal nerves that provide cutaneous innervation to the skin of the epigastrium.
back:
- T7, T8, and T9 thoracic nerves.
- T7 corresponds to the xiphoid process.
- Derived from the anterior rami of lower thoracic segments.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is primarily formed by the transversalis fascia, which is reinforced medially by the [___].
back:
• Conjoint tendon (Falx inguinalis)
• Formed by the union of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses
• Strengthens the posterior wall medially
• Acts as a primary structural defense against direct inguinal herniation

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Describe how the anatomical features of the parotid fascia contribute to the severe pain experienced during acute parotitis.
back:
* The gland is enclosed in a tough, unyielding fibrous capsule
* Derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
* Inflammation causes rapid pressure increase within this tight sheath, stretching sensory nerves

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: How do the anterior and posterior vagal trunks contribute to gastric secretory function?
back:
• Parasympathetic innervation
  • Secretomotor to gastric glands (HCl and pepsinogen)
  • Motor to gastric wall muscle; inhibitory to pyloric sphincter

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Spermatic Cord
front: A patient with a testicular tumor shows para-aortic lymphadenopathy. Which specific cord structures facilitate this metastatic spread?
back:
• Testicular lymph vessels
• Drainage follows the testicular artery back to the lumbar (para-aortic) nodes at the L1 level.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: In Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD), persistent acid exposure can lead to [___], a condition where squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium, increasing adenocarcinoma risk.
back: * Barrett's esophagus. * Occurs at the lower end of the esophagus. * Requires surveillance for malignant transformation.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish between the arterial sources supplying the cervical and thoracic segments of the esophagus.
back: * Cervical: Branches of the inferior thyroid arteries. * Thoracic: Esophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Pancreatic Relations of the Bile Duct
front: A 65-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice. Imaging reveals a mass in the head of the pancreas. The specific segment of the biliary tree most likely compressed is the [___].
back: • Third part of the bile duct • Situated in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head • Compression leads to retrograde bile backup (obstructive jaundice)

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The esophagus begins at the lower border of the [___] cartilage, corresponding to the level of the C6 vertebra.
back: * Cricoid cartilage. * Extends approximately 25 cm in length. * Ends at the cardiac orifice of the stomach at vertebral level T11.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Describe the course and termination of the Inferior Mesenteric Vein (IMV) in relation to the portal system.
back:
• Course: Ascends on the left of the IMA, behind the body of the pancreas.
• Termination: Usually joins the Splenic Vein (rarely the SMA).
• Distribution: Drains the hindgut (distal colon and upper rectum).

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Contrast the anatomical source of bleeding in esophageal varices with the typical mucosal change seen in chronic GERD.
back: * Varices: Rupture of dilated submucosal veins at the portal-systemic junction. * GERD: Columnar metaplasia of the distal esophageal squamous mucosa (Barrett's esophagus).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The descending (second) part of the duodenum features a small rounded elevation called the [___], which serves as the common opening for the bile and main pancreatic ducts.
back:
*   Major duodenal papilla
*   Location: Halfway down the medial border
*   Significance: Junction between the embryological foregut and midgut derivatives

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: How does the structural arrangement of the portal triad at the porta hepatis facilitate liver function?
back:
• Triad consists of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct.
• Arteries/veins enter to provide oxygen and nutrients.
• Bile ducts exit to transport hepatic secretions to the duodenum.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the anatomical structure within the cystic duct that prevents its collapse and name its embryological significance.
back:
Spiral valve (Spiral fold of Heister).

*   Maintains patency of the cystic duct.
*   Ensures two-way flow of bile during gallbladder filling and emptying.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Distinguish the innervation of the central diaphragmatic peritoneum from that of the peripheral diaphragmatic peritoneum.
back:
*   Central: Phrenic Nerve (C3-C5).
*   Peripheral: Lower six intercostal nerves.
*   Clinical: Central irritation refers to the shoulder; peripheral refers to the abdominal wall.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Explain how the lymphoid tissues of Waldeyer's Ring provide immunological protection for the upper respiratory tract.
back: ● Immunological Surveillance ● Acts as the first line of defense against inhaled or ingested pathogens ● Comprised of pharyngeal, tubal, palatine, and lingual tonsils ● Facilitates the production of IgA for mucosal immunity.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Explain how the hepatic portal system differs from the systemic venous circulation regarding its destination and terminal vessel type.
back:
• Carries nutrient-rich blood from the GIT to the liver
• Begins in GIT capillaries and ends in liver sinusoids
• Does not drain directly into the heart

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The lymphatic vessels from the jejunum and ileum, which carry absorbed lipids as chyle, drain primarily into the [___] lymph nodes.
back:
* Superior Mesenteric lymph nodes.
* Located around the origin of the Superior Mesenteric Artery.
* Efferents contribute to the intestinal lymph trunk.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: A 65-year-old male presents with an acquired groin swelling. During surgery, the sac is noted to bulge directly through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. What is the diagnosis?
back: Direct Inguinal Hernia. * Caused by weakness of the abdominal muscles (Hesselbach's triangle). * Characterized by a wide necked sac. * Rarely extends into the scrotum compared to the indirect type.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The [___] of the gallbladder is its distal, rounded portion that projects beyond the inferior border of the liver.
back:
● Fundus
● Completely surrounded by peritoneum
● Located at the intersection of the right semilunar line and costal margin

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A patient presents with mid-abdominal colicky pain referred to the umbilicus. Determine the neuroanatomical basis for this referred pain localization.
back:
* T10 spinal segment.
* Visceral afferents from the midgut travel with sympathetic nerves.
* Pain is referred to the corresponding T10 dermatome at the umbilicus.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: A patient develops an acutely tender, non-fluctuant mass within the rectus sheath after a violent bout of coughing. Identify the anatomical source of the bleeding.
back: * Inferior epigastric vessels. * Usually occurs below the umbilicus. * Caused by vessel stretching/tearing during muscle contraction. * Contained by the rectus sheath walls.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A 48-year-old female presents with severe right upper quadrant pain and referred pain in her right shoulder. Explain the neuroanatomical basis for the shoulder tip pain.
back:
* Inflammation irritates the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum.
* Phrenic nerve (C3–C5) carries these pain impulses.
* Pain is referred to the supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4), which share common spinal segments.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: A patient suffers a mid-face laceration one fingerbreadth below the zygomatic arch. Clear fluid leaks from the wound during eating. Identify the structure damaged.
back:
- Parotid Duct (Stensen's duct).
- Injury leads to a salivary fistula.
- Surgical repair requires cannulation to prevent ductal stenosis.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Identify the primary lymphatic drainage route for a malignant tumor located in the ascending colon.
back:
* Paracolic nodes to ileocolic and right colic nodes
* Ultimately drains to the superior mesenteric lymph nodes
* Follows the superior mesenteric arterial supply
* Late metastasis may occur via the portal vein to the liver.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Specify the segmental level of the phrenic nerve and its significance in peritoneal pain.
back:
- Segments C3, C4, and C5.
- Innervates central diaphragmatic peritoneum.
- Key in diagnosing subdiaphragmatic irritation through shoulder tip pain.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Lymphatic drainage from the "bare area" of the liver is unique because it passes through the diaphragm to reach the [___] lymph nodes.
back: * Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes. * Other liver lymph drains to hepatic nodes in the porta hepatis. * Final common drainage is to the celiac lymph nodes.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Describe the anatomical path of the 'Root of the Mesentery' and its significance for the small intestine.
back:
* A 6-inch diagonal attachment from L2 (left) to the right sacroiliac joint.
* Crosses the horizontal duodenum, aorta, and IVC.
* Permits passage of superior mesenteric vessels to the mobile jejunum and ileum.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The common bile duct is formed by the union of the [___] and the common hepatic duct.
back:
• Cystic duct
• Union occurs within the right free margin of the lesser omentum.

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: Contrast the orientation of the 'four-quadrant' system with the 'nine-region' system regarding their primary central intersecting points.
back:
* Four-Quadrant System: Intersects at the umbilicus using one vertical and one horizontal line
* Nine-Region System: Defined by two vertical mid-inguinal lines and two horizontal planes (subcostal and intertubercular)

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the role of the right crus of the diaphragm in preventing gastroesophageal reflux.
back:
• Acts as an external 'pinch-cock' sphincter
• Compresses the esophagus during inspiration
• Maintains the angle of His (acute angle at the junction).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
coreConcept: Vascular Relations of the Third Duodenal Part
front: A thin 20-year-old female presents with postprandial vomiting and epigastric pain. Imaging shows the third part of the duodenum compressed between the Aorta and the Superior Mesenteric Artery. Diagnosis?
back:
* Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome.
* Also called Wilkie's syndrome.
* Caused by a loss of the mesenteric fat pad, narrowing the aortomesenteric angle.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A patient with chronic GERD is found to have Barrett’s esophagus. Explain the anatomical and histological significance of this finding.
back:
- Metaplasia of lower esophageal lining.
- Squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium.
- Caused by persistent irritation from acidic gastric contents.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Contrast the arterial supply transition zone at the second part of the duodenum with the transition at the distal transverse colon.
back:
- Duodenum (2nd part): Transition from Celiac artery (Superior Pancreaticoduodenal) to SMA (Inferior Pancreaticoduodenal). 
- Transverse Colon: Transition from SMA (Middle Colic) to IMA (Left Colic).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the innervation mechanism that coordinates esophageal peristalsis.
back:
• Vagus nerve (Parasympathetic): Primary motor supply
• Recurrent laryngeal nerves: Supply upper striated muscle
• Myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus: Coordinates intrinsic smooth muscle contraction.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Contrast the anatomical factors leading to Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) versus the pathophysiology of Achalasia.
back:
- GERD: Incompetent lower esophageal sphincter (LES) or hiatal hernia allowing acid reflux.
- Achalasia: Hypertonic/non-relaxing LES due to plexus degeneration causing proximal stasis.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
coreConcept: Differential Clinical Signs for Appendix Positions
front: Contrast the specific physical exam maneuvers used to detect an inflamed retrocecal appendix versus a pelvic appendix.
back:
* Retrocecal: Positive Psoas sign (pain on hip extension).
* Pelvic: Positive Obturator sign (pain on internal rotation of flexed hip).
* Pelvic position also presents with rectal/vaginal tenderness.

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: In clinical surface anatomy, the vertical lines used to divide the abdomen into nine regions pass through the [___].
back: * Midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and the symphysis pubis (mid-inguinal point)

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: While most lingual muscles are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve, the [___] muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve).
back:
*   Palatoglossus.
*   Acts to elevate the posterior tongue.
*   Closes the oropharyngeal isthmus during swallowing.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Contrast Biliary Colic with Acute Cholecystitis regarding the nature of the pain and systemic inflammatory findings.
back:
Differential Points:

*   Biliary Colic: Temporary spasm (minutes/hours); no fever or leukocytosis.
*   Acute Cholecystitis: Persistent pain (days); involves parietal peritoneum; presents with fever, leukocytosis, and Murphy's sign.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Explain the role of the spiral valve (of Heister) located within the neck and cystic duct of the gallbladder.
back:
• A continuous spiral fold of mucous membrane.
• Function: Keeps the cystic duct lumen open at all times.
• Facilitates the filling and emptying of the gallbladder without collapse.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: A patient requires wide abdominal exposure. Why might a transverse incision be preferred over a vertical one regarding postoperative complications and nerve injury?
back:
Minimal nerve damage.
- Incision runs parallel to segmental nerves (T7-L1).
- Rarely damages more than one nerve segment.
- Lower risk of postoperative weakness or visceroptosis.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: A 55-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law). Imaging reveals a mass in the head of the pancreas. Identify the structure most likely compressed to cause these symptoms.
back:
Bile Duct (Common Bile Duct).

* Located in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head.
* Compression prevents bile flow into the duodenum.
* Results in obstructive jaundice and retrograde gallbladder distention.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the cervical part of the esophagus with that of the abdominal part.
back: * Cervical: Drains into deep cervical nodes. * Abdominal: Drains into left gastric and celiac nodes. * Thoracic segment primarily drains to posterior mediastinal nodes.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish between the venous drainage of the upper and lower thirds of the esophagus.
back: • Upper third: Drains into inferior thyroid veins (Systemic). • Lower third: Drains into the left gastric vein (Portal). • The middle third drains into azygos veins.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: Distinguish between the anatomical boundaries of an internal hernia and an incisional hernia.
back: Internal: Protrusion into a peritoneal recess (e.g., lesser sac). • Incisional: Protrusion through a previous surgical scar. • Incisional is often caused by wound infection or nerve damage.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Parotid Duct
front: Clinically, the parotid duct runs forward across the masseter muscle approximately one fingerbreadth below the [___].
back:
• Zygomatic arch
• It travels superficially over the masseter muscle
• Clinically vulnerable to facial lacerations and requires surgical repair to prevent salivary fistulas

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The esophagus begins at the level of the [___] vertebra, marking its transition from the pharynx at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.
back:
• C6 (Sixth Cervical) vertebra.
• It is continuous with the laryngeal part of the pharynx above.
• This site corresponds to the first physiological constriction.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: In short, obese individuals, the stomach tends to be high and transversely arranged, a morphology known as a [___] stomach.
back:
• Steer-horn stomach.
• Contrasts with the J-shaped stomach of tall, thin individuals.
• Position varies with habitus and respiration.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A 45-year-old female presents with sudden, severe epigastric pain radiating to the right infrascapular region after a meal of fried food. Identify the clinical condition and the spinal segments mediating this pain.
back:
* Biliary colic.
* Visceral afferent fibers travel via the greater splanchnic nerves to the T7-T9 segments of the spinal cord.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A patient with long-standing gallstones presents with small bowel obstruction and air in the biliary tree. Predict the most likely anatomical route for this complication.
back:
* Gallstone ileus via a cholecystoduodenal fistula.
* A large stone ulcerates into the duodenum.
* Typically obstructs at the narrow ileocecal junction.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: The fan-shaped, double-layered fold of peritoneum that attaches the coils of the jejunum and ileum to the posterior abdominal wall is the [___].
back: * Mesentery of the small intestine. * Extends from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocecal junction. * Transmits superior mesenteric vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Contrast the clinical presentation and underlying pathophysiology of biliary colic with that of acute cholecystitis.
back:
* Colic: Transient cystic duct obstruction by a stone; produces spasmodic, midline/epigastric pain.
* Cholecystitis: Persistent obstruction causing inflammation; constant right-sided pain, fever, and positive Murphy's sign.
* Gallbladder wall thickening is typically seen in cholecystitis.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
