front: Describe the formation and primary functional role of the common bile duct.
back:
* Formed by the junction of the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct.
* Measures approximately 3 inches (8 cm) in length.
* Transports bile from the liver and gallbladder to the second part of the duodenum.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: Define the contents and structural cause of a congenital umbilical hernia (exomphalos).
back: Failure of midgut to return to the abdomen. • Contents remain in the extraembryonic coelom. • The hernia is covered by the umbilical cord structures.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Explain the hormonal mechanism that triggers gallbladder contraction and bile release into the duodenum during the digestion of a fatty meal.
back:
* Fatty food in the duodenum stimulates Cholecystokinin (CCK) release.
* CCK travels via the bloodstream to the gallbladder wall.
* Causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the Sphincter of Oddi.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The base of the vermiform appendix is located on the surface of the abdominal wall at [___], situated one-third of the way along the line connecting the right ASIS to the umbilicus.
back:
McBurney’s point
*   Corresponds to the attachment site on the posteromedial cecum
*   Surgical landmark for appendectomy incisions

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Describe the functional role of the Sphincter of Oddi during the inter-digestive period versus the post-prandial state.
back:
* Inter-digestive: Contracts to divert bile into the gallbladder for storage
* Post-prandial: Relaxes via CCK stimulation
* Facilitates bile entry into the second part of the duodenum

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: A patient with a subphrenic abscess reports pain at the tip of the right shoulder. Explain the anatomical basis for this referred pain.
back:
• Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum.
• C3-C5 spinal segments also supply the supraclavicular nerves.
• The brain interprets peritoneal irritation as originating from the shoulder skin.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The skeletal framework of the hard palate is formed anteriorly by the palatine processes of the maxillae and posteriorly by the [___] of the palatine bones.
back: Horizontal plates of the palatine bones.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Complete the clinical observation: In a hypoglossal nerve injury, the tongue deviates [___] the side of the lesion because the [___] muscle fails to pull that side forward.
back:
• Toward
• Genioglossus
• Unopposed side pushes the tongue toward the weak side.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: The stomach is anatomically located primarily in the [___], left hypochondrium, and umbilical regions of the abdomen.
back:
• Epigastrium
  • Left hypochondrium
  • Umbilical region

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Direct Tributaries of the Portal Vein
front: Identify the two specific gastric tributaries that typically drain directly into the main trunk of the hepatic portal vein rather than its formative branches.
back:
• Left Gastric Vein
• Right Gastric Vein
• Both accompany the lesser curvature of the stomach

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A child presents after swallowing a small battery. Endoscopy reveals the object is stuck at the narrowest anatomical point of the esophagus, roughly 15cm from the incisors. Identify this constriction.
back: Pharyngoesophageal junction (at the level of the cricoid cartilage/C6).

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A patient with acute cholecystitis experiences referred pain in the right shoulder. Explain the anatomical pathway responsible for this symptom.
back:
• Irritation of the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum.
• Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) carries pain impulses.
• Referred to shoulder via supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4).

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: A 45-year-old male with lower lobar pleurisy presents with sharp pain referred to the epigastric skin. This clinical phenomenon occurs because the [___] nerves provide sensory innervation to both the thoracic pleura and the abdominal wall.
back: • Lower five intercostal nerves (T7-T11) • Shared segmental innervation allows thoracic pain to manifest in abdominal dermatomes • Clinical Significance: Pleurisy may mimic an acute surgical abdomen

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: The specific dermatome that provides sensory coverage to the skin surrounding the umbilicus is [___].
back:
- T10 (Tenth thoracic nerve).
- Represents the mid-point of the anterior abdominal wall.
- Useful for localizing spinal cord lesions.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Distinguish between the clinical presentation of 'Caput Medusae' and 'Caval-Caval' shunts on the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
• Caput Medusae: Portal-systemic; radiates from umbilicus
• Caval-Caval: Systemic-systemic; involves lateral thoracic/superficial epigastric
• Caval-Caval indicates IVC or SVC obstruction
• Caput Medusae specifically indicates portal hypertension

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Explain the anatomical method used by a surgeon to definitively locate the appendix when it is not immediately visible upon opening the peritoneum.
back:
Trace the Teniae Coli
*   Three longitudinal muscle bands of the cecum converge at the base
*   Provides a continuous longitudinal muscle coat for the appendix
*   Essential for finding retrocecal or ectopic tips

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Identify the visceral structures related anteriorly to the second (descending) part of the duodenum.
back:
*   Fundus of the gallbladder
*   Right lobe of the liver
*   Transverse colon and coils of small intestine

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: Contrast the anatomical location of the superficial and deep inguinal rings relative to the inferior epigastric artery.
back: * Deep Inguinal Ring: Located lateral to the artery. * Superficial Inguinal Ring: Located medial to the artery's vertical plane. * This landmark differentiates indirect from direct hernias.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Identify the deep peritoneal space between the liver and right kidney that serves as the most dependent part of the abdominal cavity when supine.
back:
• Hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch).
• Also known as the right posterior subphrenic space.
• Primary site for fluid or blood accumulation detected during trauma ultrasound (FAST scan).

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A surgeon is performing a cholecystectomy and identifies a vessel within the hepatobiliary triangle (of Calot). Identify this artery and its most common parent vessel.
back:
Cystic Artery.
• Most commonly arises from the Right Hepatic Artery.
• Lies within the boundaries formed by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and liver.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: The anatomic and physiologic valve controlling the outflow of gastric contents into the duodenum is the [___].
back:
• Pyloric sphincter
• Formed by thickened circular smooth muscle
• Receives motor sympathetic fibers and inhibitory vagal fibers
• Relaxes reflexly as the stomach fills.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Analyze the 'internal' physiological factors that maintain the gastroesophageal barrier to prevent acid reflux.
back:
- Tonic contraction of circular smooth muscle
- Vagal nerve (parasympathetic) control
- Hormonal influence (e.g., Gastrin)
- Intra-abdominal esophageal length and pressure

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Define 'adhesiostomy' and identify the primary risk associated with untreated peritoneal adhesions.
back: ● Adhesiostomy: Surgical separation of fibrous scar tissue. ● Primary risk: Intestinal obstruction. ● Can also cause chronic pelvic pain or secondary infertility.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: What is the specific anatomical relationship that allows the spread of infection from the peritoneal cavity to the pleural cavity?
back: • Diaphragmatic lymph vessels. • Pass through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal nodes. • Can cause pleural effusion or empyema. • Often occurs with subphrenic abscesses.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Explain how bile flow into the duodenum is regulated by the Sphincter of Oddi during the inter-digestive (fasting) state.
back:
• The sphincter remains tonically contracted.
• Bile is diverted into the gallbladder for storage and concentration via the cystic duct.

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
coreConcept: Pathophysiology of Direct vs. Indirect Hernias
front: A 65-year-old male presents with a painless bulge in the groin that appears only upon standing. The protrusion occurs medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through a weakness in the [___].
back:
• Posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Transversalis fascia)
• Diagnosis: Direct Inguinal Hernia
• Protrudes through Hesselbach’s triangle
• Associated with acquired abdominal wall weakness

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A post-operative patient is nursed in a strictly supine position. Analyze why the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) is a frequent site for abscess formation in this patient.
back:
• In the supine position, Morison’s pouch is the most dependent part of the upper peritoneal cavity.
• Infected fluid gravitates here from the right paracolic gutter.
• It is separated from the pelvis by the pelvic brim.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Describe the biological mechanism by which the gallbladder modifies bile during storage.
back:
● Concentrates bile by absorbing water and electrolytes
● Selectively absorbs bile salts to maintain acidity
● Secretes mucus to protect the mucosal lining

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Contrast the portal and systemic venous contributions at the retroperitoneal sites known as the Veins of Retzius.
back:
• Portal: Veins of retroperitoneal organs (colic, splenic, mesenteric)
• Systemic: Renal, lumbar, and phrenic veins
• Location: Where retroperitoneal viscera contact the posterior wall
• Provides a hidden collateral pathway

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: On a cadaveric model, the portal vein is identified forming posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the [___] and the [___].
back: * Superior mesenteric vein (SMV). * Splenic vein. * Carries 70% of the liver's blood supply, rich in absorbed nutrients from the GIT.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Ileocecal Region
front: A 10-month-old infant presents with 'red currant jelly' stools and an abdominal mass. This clinical finding most likely involves a telescoping of the bowel at [___].
back:
The Ileocolic Junction.
- Known as Intussusception.
- Usually involves the terminal ileum invaginating into the cecum.
- Common due to the relative size difference and mobility of segments.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Contrast the vascular territories supplied by the Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) and the Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA) along the transverse colon.
back: * SMA: Supplies the proximal two-thirds (midgut) * IMA: Supplies the distal one-third (hindgut) * The transition point occurs near the splenic (left colic) flexure

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
coreConcept: Posterior anatomical relations of the gallbladder
front: Distinguish the posterior relations of the gallbladder fundus from the posterior relations of its neck.
back: The fundus is related posteriorly to the transverse colon. The neck and cystic duct are related posteriorly to the first and second parts of the duodenum, just above the head of the pancreas.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Trace the horizontal reflection of the peritoneum as it transitions from the lateral abdominal wall to the ascending and descending colons.
back: * Reflects from the parietal wall to cover the anterior and lateral surfaces of the colon. * Creates the right and left paracolic gutters. * These gutters serve as conduits for fluid movement between the upper abdomen and pelvis.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Explain the anatomical pathway that leads to the clinical appearance of Caput Medusae during portal obstruction.
back:
• Retrograde flow through Paraumbilical veins (ligamentum teres)
• Anastomoses with superficial epigastric veins
• Visible as radiating subcutaneous veins from the umbilicus.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Distinguish between the small and large intestine based on the presence of teniae coli and appendices epiploicae.
back:
• Teniae coli: Three longitudinal muscle bands unique to the large intestine
• Appendices epiploicae: Small fatty tags found only on the colon/cecum
• Small intestine: Features continuous longitudinal muscle and no fatty tags.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: In portal hypertension, the [___] veins connect the left branch of the portal vein to the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall, leading to caput medusae.
back:
• Paraumbilical veins
• Travel within the falciform ligament
• Accompany the ligamentum teres
• Anastomose with systemic superficial epigastric veins

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Explain the role of Cholecystokinin (CCK) in the physiological delivery of concentrated bile into the duodenum.
back:
Mechanism of CCK:

*   Released from duodenal mucosa in response to fatty foods.
*   Stimulates gallbladder wall contraction.
*   Causes relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Explain the secretomotor pathway of the parotid gland starting from the inferior salivary nucleus.
back:
* Preganglionic: Via Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), tympanic branch, and lesser petrosal nerve
* Relay: Otic ganglion
* Postganglionic: Via the auriculotemporal nerve to the gland

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: In the anatomical organization of the anterolateral abdominal wall, the [___] spinal nerve dermatome is the primary sensory level supplying the skin of the umbilicus.
back: • T10 dermatome • T7 serves the epigastrium; L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) serves the suprapubic and inguinal regions • Crucial for sensory mapping and localizing spinal cord injuries

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: A patient with chronic liver disease presents with dilated, tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae). This represents a portal-systemic shunt between the paraumbilical veins and the [___] veins.
back:
• Superficial epigastric veins.
• Occurs as blood from the left portal vein branch shunts through the ligamentum teres.
• A key clinical indicator of portal hypertension and systemic venous congestion.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Explain the anatomical communication pathway between the greater sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa).
back:
• Commingled via the epiploic foramen (opening of the lesser sac).
• Lesser sac lies posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum.
• Greater sac is the main compartment of the peritoneal cavity.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: List the three specific anatomical sites where the esophagus is narrowed and may resist the passage of a nasogastric tube.
back: * At the pharyngoesophageal junction (cricopharyngeus muscle). * Where the arch of the aorta and left bronchus cross. * At the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Venous Tributaries of the Portal System
front: Contrast the anatomical termination of the inferior mesenteric vein (IMV) with that of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV).
back:
• IMV: Usually joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic body
• SMV: Joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Contrast the anatomical structures forming the anterior relations of the stomach with those constituting the posterior 'stomach bed'.
back:
Gastric Relations:
- Anterior: Left lobe of liver, diaphragm, and anterior abdominal wall.
- Posterior (Stomach Bed): Pancreas, splenic artery, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, spleen, and transverse mesocolon.
- Note: The lesser sac separates the stomach from its posterior relations.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Distinguish the lymphatic territories of the right gastric nodes from the left gastric nodes.
back:
Right Gastric: Drains the lower part of the lesser curvature.
Left Gastric: Drains the cardia and upper part of the lesser curvature.
Both: Follow the lesser curvature of the stomach.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: A 50-year-old cirrhotic male presents with 'Caput Medusae.' Identify the specific portal and systemic vessels whose communication produces this clinical sign.
back:
• Portal: Paraumbilical veins (ligamentum teres)
• Systemic: Superficial epigastric/thoracoepigastric veins
• Radiate from the umbilicus due to portal hypertension
• Utilizes the anterior abdominal wall network

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Identify the specific histological metaplasia occurring at the lower esophagus as a long-term complication of chronic acid exposure in GERD.
back:
• Barrett's Esophagus
• Stratified squamous epithelium replaced by simple columnar (intestinal) epithelium
• Significant precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The 'safety muscle' of the tongue, which is the primary extrinsic muscle responsible for protrusion and preventing airway obstruction, is the [___].
back:
* Genioglossus muscle.
* Attachments: Superior genial tubercle of mandible to the body of hyoid and tongue substance.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which the soft palate prevents food from entering the nasopharynx during deglutition.
back:
• Tensing: Tensor veli palatini tightens the palatine aponeurosis.
• Elevation: Levator veli palatini raises the palate against the posterior pharyngeal wall.
• Seal: Contraction of palatopharyngeus helps seal the pharyngeal isthmus.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring, which is positioned [___] to the inferior epigastric artery.
back: Lateral. • It follows the path of a persistent processus vaginalis. • It is considered congenital in origin. • It can extend into the scrotum or labium majus.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Detail the anatomical path taken by blood when the liver is bypasssed via the 'Bare Area' porto-systemic anastomosis.
back: Blood from the hepatic portal tributaries in the liver substance shunts directly to the phrenic veins (systemic) of the diaphragm where the liver lacks a peritoneal covering.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: The superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall consists of an outer fatty layer and a deeper, thin membranous layer specifically known as [___].
back:
• Scarpa's fascia
• Fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh approximately 1 cm below the inguinal ligament
• Continues into the perineum as Colles' fascia
• Provides a critical layer for surgical suture to prevent skin scar stretching

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Distinguish between the anterior and posterior peritoneal relations of the gallbladder body.
back:
* Anterior (Superior): Adherent to the liver's gallbladder fossa; devoid of peritoneum
* Posterior (Inferior): Covered by visceral peritoneum; relates to the transverse colon
* Proximity: Also relates to the first/second parts of the duodenum
* Fundus: Usually completely surrounded by peritoneum

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
coreConcept: Referred Visceral Pain of the Gallbladder
front: A 45-year-old female presents with episodic right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain that radiates to the epigastrium following fatty meals. Specify the spinal segments that carry the visceral afferent fibers for this pain.
back:
• T7–T9 spinal segments
• Fibers accompany sympathetic nerves
• Pass through the celiac plexus and greater splanchnic nerves
• Pain is initially dull and poorly localized.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: A 40-year-old obese female presents with sudden, episodic right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the back after eating a fatty meal. There is no fever or jaundice. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Biliary Colic
• Caused by gallbladder contraction against a stone obstructing the cystic duct
• Pain is typically transient, lasting less than 6 hours.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the vascular arcade patterns and the length of vasa recta between the jejunal and ileal mesentery as seen in a dissected specimen.
back:
Jejunal: 1–2 simple arcades with long, infrequent vasa recta.
- Ileal: 3–4+ complex tiers of arcades with shorter, more numerous vasa recta.
- Ileal mesentery also contains significantly more fat extending to the bowel wall.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: Describe the specific distal attachment of Scarpa’s fascia that creates a potential closed space for extravasated fluid in the lower abdomen.
back:
• Fuses with the fascia lata (deep fascia of the thigh).
• Attachment is exactly one fingerbreadth below the inguinal ligament.
• Creates a space continuous only with the scrotum and perineum.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Contrast the typical anatomical path of fluid spread following a perforation of the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum versus the posterior wall of the stomach.
back:
- Anterior Duodenum: Escapes into the greater sac (right paracolic gutter).
- Posterior Stomach: Escapes into the lesser sac (omental bursa).

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Contrast the direction of venous blood flow in the abdominal wall during portal hypertension versus Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) obstruction.
back:
* Portal Hypertension: Blood radiates away from the umbilicus (Caput Medusae).
* IVC Obstruction: Blood flows vertically upward from the lower abdomen toward the axillary vein.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) traverses the masseter muscle and opens into the vestibule of the oral cavity opposite the [___].
back:
• Upper second molar tooth
• Pierces the buccinator muscle to enter the vestibule
• Facilitates drainage of serous salivary secretions

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: A patient with a subphrenic abscess presents with sharp pain referred to the right shoulder. This clinical phenomenon is mediated by the [___] nerve.
back:
*   Phrenic Nerve (C3, C4, C5).
*   Supplies the central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum.
*   Shares segmental origin with supraclavicular nerves supplying the shoulder skin.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A patient presents with a midgut volvulus. List the three hallmark external features that allow a radiologist to distinguish large bowel from small bowel on a plain abdominal film.
back:
● Teniae coli (three longitudinal bands).
● Haustrations (sacculations caused by teniae shortening).
● Appendices epiploicae (fatty peritoneal tags).

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Segments and Relations of the Bile Duct
front: A patient presents with obstructive jaundice; ultrasound shows a stone lodged in the bile duct behind the duodenum. Contrast the posterior relations of the duct at this retroduodenal site with its relations in the lesser omentum.
back: • Retroduodenal: Posterior to the first part of the duodenum and anterior to the IVC • Supraduodenal (Lesser Omentum): Anterior to the right margin of the portal vein

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: Specify the vertebral levels for the intercristal plane and the intertubercular plane respectively.
back:
* Intercristal plane: L4 (highest point of iliac crests)
* Intertubercular plane: L5 (tubercles of iliac crests)

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Distinguish between the distal attachments of the palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus muscles.
back: Palatoglossus: Originates from the palatine aponeurosis and inserts into the side of the tongue. Palatopharyngeus: Originates from the aponeurosis and hard palate, inserting into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the most common arterial supply to the gallbladder and specify its typical parent vessel.
back:
* Cystic Artery.
* Usually a branch of the Right Hepatic Artery.
* Typically found within the cystohepatic triangle (Calot’s triangle) during cholecystectomy.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Describe the anatomical relationship of the superior mesenteric artery as it crosses the third part of the duodenum and its clinical significance.
back:
* SMA passes anterior to the horizontal duodenal part.
* Originates from the aorta posteriorly.
* May cause SMA syndrome (vascular compression of the duodenum).

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Describe the neuro-anatomical mechanism by which the vagus nerves stimulate gastric acid production and influence pyloric sphincter tone.
back:
• Stimulates acid and pepsin via gastric glands
• Increases motor activity in the stomach wall
• Provides inhibitory fibers to the pyloric sphincter

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: During a pancreatectomy, a surgeon identifies a tortuous vessel running along the superior border of the pancreatic body. Identify this vessel and its terminal destination.
back:
• Vessel: Splenic Artery.
• Origin: Celiac trunk.
• Termination: Hilum of the spleen via the splenorenal ligament.
• Note: It supplies the pancreas via multiple small branches.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Specify the autonomic nerve supply responsible for carrying visceral pain fibers from the gallbladder to the spinal cord.
back:
* Celiac plexus (Sympathetic and Parasympathetic/Vagus)
* Visceral afferent pain fibers accompany sympathetic nerves
* Enter the spinal cord at T7-T9 segments
* Referred pain initially felt in the epigastric region

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Name the two most common anatomical positions for the tip of the vermiform appendix and how a 'retrocecal' position affects clinical examination.
back:
• Positions: Retrocecal (behind cecum) and Pelvic (hanging in pelvis)
• Clinical masking: Retrocecal appendices may show absent guarding/tenderness because the appendix is shielded from the anterior peritoneum.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the specific vertebral level where the esophagus terminates and the name of its junction with the stomach.
back: * Level: T11 vertebra. * Junction: Cardiac orifice (Gastroesophageal junction). * Situated approximately 1.25 cm below the diaphragm.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Retroperitoneal portosystemic communications, often called the Veins of [___], connect the colic and splenic veins with the renal and lumbar veins.
back:
Retzius.
* Found at retroperitoneal organ sites.
* Includes duodenum and ascending/descending colon.
* Systemic component: Lumbar/Renal/Phrenic veins.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Systemic spread of large bowel cancer to the liver primarily occurs via the [___] venous system.
back:
* Portal venous system
* Drains blood from the mesenteric veins to liver sinusoids
* Liver is the most common site for secondary malignant deposits
* Follows initial lymphatic spread

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A 45-year-old female with cholecystitis experiences referred pain in her right shoulder. Irritation of which nerve's parietal peritoneal distribution causes this finding?
back:
● Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5)
● Irritation of subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum
● Pain referred to C3-C4 dermatomes via supraclavicular nerves

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: The paratonsillar space, situated between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle, contains the [___] vein.
back: ● External Palatine (Paratonsillar) Vein ● Descends from the soft palate to the pharyngeal venous plexus ● Located in loose areolar tissue ● Common cause of venous hemorrhage during tonsillectomy procedures.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Formation of the Hepatic Portal Vein
front: The hepatic portal vein is formed behind the [___] of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
back: - Neck of the pancreas. - Occurs at the second lumbar (L2) vertebral level. - Collects venous blood from the abdominal gastrointestinal tract and spleen.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the autonomic nerve components that supply the gallbladder and the primary plexus from which they are derived.
back: It is supplied by sympathetic and parasympathetic (vagus) fibers. These nerves are derived from the celiac plexus. Vagal stimulation causes gallbladder contraction, while sympathetic fibers are largely vasomotor to the cystic vessels.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the highest-situated flexure of the large intestine and the ligament that secures it to the diaphragm.
back: * Left colic (splenic) flexure. * Phrenicocolic ligament. * It is positioned higher, more posterior, and deeper than the right hepatic flexure.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific branch of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) that descends into the pelvis to supply the upper rectum.
back:
• Superior Rectal Artery
• Terminal continuation of the IMA
• Anastomoses with middle and inferior rectal arteries

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Identify the specific nerve that provides the primary sensory supply to the parietal peritoneum lining the pelvic cavity.
back:
*   Obturator Nerve (L2-L4).
*   Clinical Significance: Allows detection of pelvic inflammation (e.g., pelvic appendix) via rectal or vaginal examination.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Contrast the anatomical boundaries of the Greater Peritoneal Sac with those of the Lesser Peritoneal Sac (Omental Bursa).
back: * Greater Sac: Main compartment extending from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor. * Lesser Sac: Smaller space located strictly behind the stomach and lesser omentum. * Connectivity: Linked only via the epiploic foramen.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Contrast the palatine tonsil with the lingual tonsil regarding their specific anatomical locations and their relationship to the sulcus terminalis.
back: * Palatine: Located in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. * Lingual: Located on the posterior third of the tongue, posterior to the sulcus terminalis.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Contrast the anatomical distribution of the Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) with the Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA) regarding the segments of the large intestine they supply.
back:
• SMA (Midgut): Cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
• IMA (Hindgut): Distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: State the specific peritoneal compartment into which an ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum would most likely perforate.
back:
* Lesser sac (omental bursa)
* Lies immediately posterior to the first inch of the duodenum
* Can lead to adhesions to the pancreas
* Pancreatic erosion often causes referred back pain

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: During an emergency appendectomy, the surgeon must ligate the appendicular artery within the mesoappendix. This vessel is a branch of the [___] artery.
back:
Posterior cecal artery. 
- The posterior cecal is a branch of the ileocolic artery. 
- The appendicular artery is a functional end artery.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: In a cadaveric dissection, the primary artery supplying the midgut—stretching from the second part of the duodenum to the distal transverse colon—is the [___].
back:
Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA). 
• Originates from the aorta at L1 level.
• Passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum.
• Supplies derivatives of the embryonic midgut.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Contrast the diagnostic utility of a digital rectal examination in a patient with a pelvic appendix versus one in the retrocecal position.
back:
• Pelvic appendix: Elicits exquisite tenderness on the right side of the rectum
• Retrocecal appendix: Typically yields a negative rectal exam as it lies superior and posterior to the pelvis.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: A patient presents with a history of a midline incision through the linea alba. Contrast this with a transrectus incision regarding the management of the rectus abdominis muscle.
back:
No damage vs. Muscle splitting.
- Midline: Travels through the linea alba; no muscle fibers are cut.
- Transrectus: The muscle is split longitudinally.
- Result: Transrectus denervates the medial portion of the split muscle.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Identify the anatomical boundaries of the parotid bed that define the gland's position below the ear.
back:
* Superior: External auditory meatus and temporomandibular joint
* Posterior: Mastoid process and sternocleidomastoid muscle
* Anterior: Ramus of the mandible and masseter muscle

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: A 40-year-old male presents with a posterior gastric ulcer eroding into the space behind the stomach. Name the potential space involved and its left lateral boundary.
back:
* Lesser sac (Omental bursa).
* Boundary: Gastrosplenic ligament (anteriorly) and Splenorenal ligament (posteriorly).
* These reflections seal the sac from the greater sac on the left side.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Contrast the venous drainage pathways of the superior rectal vein with those of the middle and inferior rectal veins.
back:
• Superior rectal vein: Drains into the portal system via the inferior mesenteric vein.
• Middle/Inferior rectal veins: Drain into the systemic system via internal iliac and internal pudendal veins.
• Clinical Significance: This site of anastomosis produces anorectal varices during portal hypertension.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Identify the boundaries of the epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow) that permit communication between the two peritoneal sacs.
back:
• Anterior: Free border of lesser omentum (portal triad)
• Posterior: Inferior Vena Cava
• Superior: Caudate lobe of liver
• Inferior: First part of duodenum.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A newborn is found to have a bifid uvula and a cleft involving only the soft palate. This developmental failure involves the incomplete fusion of the [___].
back:
• Palatal processes of the maxillary processes.
• Occurs at the posterior aspect of the secondary palate.
• Typically develops between the 8th and 11th weeks.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Analyze why an inflamed retrocecal appendix might fail to produce classic rebound tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa.
back:
* Appendix is separated from the anterior parietal peritoneum by the cecum
* Prevents somatic nerve irritation of the anterior abdominal wall
* Results in silent abdominal signs despite active inflammation

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A 45-year-old female presents with severe right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the right shoulder. Explain the neurological basis for the shoulder-specific referred pain.
back: * Irritation of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). * Supplies the central diaphragmatic peritoneum. * Referred via the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4).

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Identify the specific arterial branch providing the most significant vascular supply to the palatine tonsil.
back: ● Tonsillar branch of the Facial Artery ● Primary arterial supply to the tonsillar parenchyma ● Reaches the organ by piercing the superior constrictor muscle ● Accompanied by smaller branches from the lingual and ascending pharyngeal arteries.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: The circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue at the entrance of the pharynx, consisting of the pharyngeal, tubal, palatine, and lingual tonsils, is termed [___].
back: * Waldeyer’s lymphatic ring. * Serves as a primary immunological barrier for the respiratory and digestive tracts.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A 2-year-old child presents with sudden abdominal pain and 'red currant jelly' stools. Imaging shows the ileum telescoping into the cecum. Explain the most common trigger for this anatomical event.
back:
* Enlargement of Peyer's patches (lymphoid tissue) in the terminal ileum
* Acts as a 'lead point' for peristalsis to pull into the cecum
* Common at the ileocolic junction due to caliber differences between intestines.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Formation of the Common Hepatic Duct
front: The Common Hepatic Duct is formed by the union of the [___] and [___] at the porta hepatis.
back:
* Right hepatic duct
* Left hepatic duct
* Joins the cystic duct inferiorly to form the bile duct

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Contrast the clinical manifestation of a perforated ulcer on the anterior wall versus the posterior wall of the stomach.
back:
* Anterior wall ulcers: Perforate into the greater sac, causing generalized peritonitis.
* Posterior wall ulcers: Perforate into the lesser sac or erode the pancreas.
* Posterior erosion typically presents with referred back pain.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Identify the histological transformation at the lower esophagus caused by chronic GERD and its clinical significance.
back:
- Barrett’s Esophagus: Squamous to columnar metaplasia
- Response to chronic acid irritation
- Increased risk for esophageal adenocarcinoma

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: To ensure optimal healing and minimal scarring, abdominal surgical incisions should ideally follow the natural [___], where collagen fibers in the dermis run parallel to the horizontal plane of the trunk.
back: - Lines of cleavage (Langer’s lines) - Based on dermal collagen fiber orientation - Incisions along these lines heal with minimal scarring - Run horizontally around the trunk

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Identify the four structures that form the immediate boundaries of the Epiploic Foramen (Opening of Winslow).
back: * Anterior: Free edge of lesser omentum (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct). * Posterior: Inferior Vena Cava. * Superior: Caudate lobe of the liver. * Inferior: First part of the duodenum.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Describe how the gallbladder carries out its biological function of concentrating bile during the interdigestive period.
back: The columnar epithelium of the gallbladder absorbs water and electrolytes from the stored bile. Permanent mucosal folds and microvilli increase surface area, allowing bile to be concentrated by five to ten times.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Identify the specific anatomical layers a cannula must traverse during a midline abdominal paracentesis via the linea alba.
back:
• Skin and superficial fascia (Camper’s and Scarpa’s)
• Linea alba (fibrous intersection)
• Transversalis fascia and extraperitoneal fat
• Parietal peritoneum
Note: The bowel is pushed away by the cannula.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Terminal Bifurcation of the Portal Vein
front: Identify the exact anatomical landmark where the hepatic portal vein enters the liver and bifurcates into its terminal segments.
back:
• Porta hepatis (Hilum of the liver)
• Bifurcates into Right and Left portal branches
• Enclosed within the hepatoduodenal ligament

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Specify the primary arterial source for the gallbladder and the vessel from which it typically originates within the cystohepatic triangle.
back: The cystic artery is the primary blood supply. It most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery, a branch of the hepatic artery proper, usually within the cystohepatic triangle of Calot.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain how the anatomical relationship between the tensor veli palatini and the pterygoid hamulus facilitates palatal tension.
back:
• The muscle tendon turns 90 degrees around the hamulus.
• The hamulus acts as a pulley.
• Converts vertical muscle contraction into horizontal tension across the aponeurosis.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Retroduodenal Bile Duct
front: Identify the primary vascular and enteric structures related to the second part of the bile duct as it descends from the lesser omentum.
back:
* Posterior to the first part of the duodenum
* Right of the gastroduodenal artery
* Anterior to the portal vein

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Specify the boundaries of the epiploic foramen (opening of the lesser sac) in relation to the biliary system.
back:
* Anterior: Free border of the lesser omentum containing the bile duct, hepatic artery, and portal vein.
* Posterior: Inferior Vena Cava.
* Superior: Caudate process of the liver.
* Inferior: First part of the duodenum.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: Identify the neurovascular plane where the lower thoracic nerves and epigastric vessels are found when dissecting the lateral abdominal wall.
back:
• Plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles
• Houses the lower six thoracic nerves (T7-T12)
• Contains the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
• Parallel to the intercostal neurovascular bundle

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Specify the embryological origin of the falciform ligament and its role in connecting the liver to the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
• Derived from the ventral mesentery
• Contains the ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein)
• Reflects onto the liver to form the coronary ligaments.

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: The horizontal plane that passes through the lowest points of the costal margins (10th costal cartilages), corresponding to the L3 vertebral level, is the [___] plane.
back:
* Subcostal plane
* Landmarks: 10th costal cartilages
* Vertebral level: L3

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: How does the anatomical extent of the inguinal canal differ between a newborn and an adult?
back:
* Newborn: Short canal; rings almost overlap (directly posterior)
* Adult: Oblique passage (4 cm long)
* Growth: Deep ring moves laterally over time

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: A 45-year-old female presents with acute right upper quadrant pain that radiates to her right shoulder. Explain the anatomical pathway for this referred pain.
back:
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum.
• Mediated by the Phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
• Referred to the shoulder via supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) due to shared spinal segments.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which the visceral peritoneum perceives pain compared to the parietal peritoneum.
back:
- Visceral: Sensitive only to stretch and tearing; mediated via autonomic afferents.
- Parietal: Sensitive to pain, temperature, touch, and pressure; mediated via somatic nerves.
- Distension of a viscus causes dull, poorly localized visceral pain.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
coreConcept: Common Anatomical Site of Gastric Ulcers
front: Peptic ulcers originating in the stomach most frequently involve the alkaline-producing mucosa located along the [___].
back:
• Lesser curvature
• Specifically near the incisura angularis
• This site is frequently exposed to acidic chyme

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Identify the three specific locations of the tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis.
back: 1. Level of the xiphoid process. 2. Level of the umbilicus. 3. Halfway between the xiphoid and umbilicus. - They are firmly attached only to the anterior rectus sheath.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: The celiac trunk, the primary artery supplying the embryological foregut, originates from the abdominal aorta at the level of the [___] vertebra.
back: * T12 vertebra * It is the first major unpaired visceral branch of the abdominal aorta * Branches into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Distinguish the 'Stomach Bed' (posterior relations) from the structures related to the anterior surface of the stomach.
back: ● Anterior: Diaphragm, left lobe of liver, anterior abdominal wall. ● Posterior (Bed): Pancreas, splenic artery, left kidney, left suprarenal, spleen, transverse mesocolon.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Distinguish between the anatomical causes of 'internal hemorrhoids' and 'caput medusae' in a patient with a blocked portal vein.
back: * Hemorrhoids: Dilation of the anorectal anastomosis (Superior vs. Middle/Inferior rectal veins). * Caput Medusae: Paraumbilical veins shunting to the superficial epigastric veins. * Both involve portal-systemic shunting.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: In the anatomical management of massive variceal bleeding, a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube provides counterpressure. Identify the two specific regions where the balloons are inflated to stop hemorrhage.
back:
Gastric fundus and lower esophagus.
* Gastric balloon: Anchors the tube and compresses gastric varices.
* Esophageal balloon: Directly compresses submucosal esophageal varices.
* Anatomy: Targets the portal-systemic venous junction.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Contrast the vascular arcade patterns and vasa recta characteristics found in the mesentery of the jejunum versus the ileum.
back:
• Jejunum: Fewer, larger arcades with long vasa recta
• Ileum: Multiple rows of smaller, complex arcades with short vasa recta
• Jejunum has less mesenteric fat allowing better visualization of vessels

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
coreConcept: Valveless Nature of the Portal System
front: The portal vein radicles and its tributaries are unique compared to most systemic veins because they lack [___], enabling retrograde congestion in cirrhosis.
back:
• Valves
• Allows blood to bypass the liver
• Facilitates the engorgement of collateral bypass pathways.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Detail the specific motor innervation of the cremasteric muscle found within the spermatic cord.
back:
• Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2)
• Responsible for the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Contrast the anatomical location and communication of the greater peritoneal sac versus the lesser sac (omental bursa).
back:
Peritoneal Sac Compartments

*   Greater Sac: Main compartment from diaphragm to pelvis
*   Lesser Sac: Behind stomach and lesser omentum
*   Communication: Linked solely via the epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow)

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the surface landmark and corresponding vertebral level for the fundus of the gallbladder.
back:
● Intersection of the right 9th costal cartilage and lateral border of rectus abdominis
● Transpyloric plane level
● L1 vertebral level

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
coreConcept: Submandibular Gland Parts and Duct Origin
front: The submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) emerges from the anterior end of the [___] part of the gland and opens at the sublingual caruncle.
back:
* Deep part
* It runs forward between the mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles
* It is crossed twice by the lingual nerve (triple relation)

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: List the spinal segments that provide sensory innervation to the parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall.
back:
*   Lower six thoracic nerves (T7-T12).
*   First lumbar nerve (L1).
*   L1 is supplied via iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Distinguish between the Major and Minor Duodenal Papillae regarding the specific ducts they receive.
back:
* Major: Receives Bile Duct and Main Pancreatic Duct
* Minor: Receives Accessory Pancreatic Duct (if present)
* Major is located inferior to the minor papilla

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: Explain the role and management of the rectus abdominis muscle during a standard paramedian incision to maintain its nerve supply.
back:
Lateral retraction of the muscle.
- Anterior rectus sheath is incised one inch from midline.
- The muscle is freed and moved laterally.
- Protects nerves entering from the lateral aspect.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Most duodenal ulcers occur in the first part of the duodenum, specifically on the [___] wall, where acidic gastric chyme first impacts the mucosa.
back:
• Anterolateral wall
• Found within the first inch (2.5 cm)
• Clinical consequence: Perforation of this site leads to acid leakage into the greater peritoneal sac.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: Contrast the utility of a McBurney's incision versus a right paramedian incision in a suspected appendicitis case where the diagnosis is uncertain.
back:
Limited vs. Exploratory exposure.
- McBurney: Strictly for appendectomy; offers limited surgical field.
- Paramedian: Preferred for diagnostic doubt.
- Allows wider exploration of abdominal viscera and pelvis.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: At the lower end of the esophagus, identify the specific [___] vein (portal) that anastomoses with the azygos vein (systemic) to create a site for potential varices.
back:
• Left gastric vein (portal)
• Anastomoses with esophageal tributaries of azygos vein
• Clinically significant for life-threatening hematemesis
• Occurs in the lower third of the esophagus

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Vascular Relations of the Deep Inguinal Ring
front: During a cadaveric dissection, you are asked to demonstrate the deep inguinal ring. Which vascular landmark serves as the medial boundary to this ring?
back: * Inferior epigastric vessels. * The deep ring is positioned lateral to these vessels. * This anatomical relationship is critical for distinguishing indirect from direct inguinal hernias during surgical procedures.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Identify the fibrous structure that serves as the 'skeleton' of the soft palate and the muscle whose expanded tendon forms it.
back: Palatine aponeurosis. It is formed by the expanded tendon of the Tensor veli palatini. It attaches to the posterior border of the hard palate and provides support for the other palatal muscles.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A 55-year-old male with a tumor in the uncinate process of the pancreas shows signs of venous congestion in the small intestine. Which specific vessel's junction is likely compromised?
back:
• Superior Mesenteric Vein (SMV)
• The SMV joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck
• Compression here obstructs drainage from the midgut

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Contrast the innervation of the parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall with that of the posterior abdominal wall.
back:
• Both: Segmental spinal nerves supplying overlying skin/muscles.
• Anterior: Lower six thoracic (T7-T12) and L1 (iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal).
• Posterior: Corresponding segmental lumbar nerves.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Identify the fetal remnant that may provide a portosystemic shunt if it remains patent between the left portal vein and the inferior vena cava.
back:
Ligamentum venosum.
* Remnant of the fetal ductus venosus.
* Situated in the fissure of the liver.
* Connects portal to systemic systems.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Describe the physiological process by which the gallbladder concentrates hepatic bile during storage.
back:
• Active absorption of water and electrolytes (sodium/chloride) by the mucosa.
• Secretion of mucus into the lumen.
• Results in a 5- to 10-fold concentration of organic bile constituents.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Contrast the anatomical mechanisms of Volvulus versus Intussusception regarding how they compromise intestinal patency.
back:
• Volvulus: Twisting of a mobile segment (e.g., sigmoid) around its own mesentery
• Intussusception: Invagination of a proximal segment into the distal lumen
• Result: Both cause mechanical obstruction and strangulation of blood vessels.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals dilated veins in the distal esophagus. Identify the specific portal and systemic vessels involved in this anastomosis.
back:
• Portal: Left gastric vein
• Systemic: Esophageal branches of Azygos vein
• Clinical Outcome: Esophageal varices which are prone to rupture.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient bites the lateral margin of their tongue. Which nerve is responsible for the sharp, localized pain felt in the anterior two-thirds?
back:
*   Lingual nerve.
*   Branch of the Mandibular division (V3) of Trigeminal nerve.
*   Carries general somatic sensation (pain, touch, temperature).

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: A patient with suspected peritonitis exhibits 'guarding' (reflex muscle rigidity). Explain the anatomical relationship between the cutaneous nerves and the underlying musculature that causes this.
back:
- Segmental nerves (T7-L1) provide dual innervation to the parietal peritoneum and the abdominal muscles.
- Inflammation of the peritoneum triggers a reflex motor response in the same spinal segment.
- Leads to involuntary muscle contraction to protect viscera.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the role of the Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) in the sensory mechanism of the tongue.
back:
* Supplies both general sensation and taste to the posterior one-third.
* Supplies the vallate papillae (located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis).

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The small intestine is anchored to the posterior abdominal wall by a fan-shaped fold of peritoneum known as the [___].
back:
● Mesentery of the small intestine.
● It carries superior mesenteric vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
● Extends from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocecal junction.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 65-year-old male with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, severe periumbilical pain and a 'silent abdomen.' Occlusion of the major vessel supplying the midgut is suspected. Identify this vessel.
back:
• Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA)
• Supplies from the distal duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon
• Arises at the L1 vertebral level

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Distinguish between the mucosal environments where gastric ulcers typically develop compared to the areas producing acid and pepsin.
back:
• Ulcers: Typically occur in alkaline-producing mucosa (antrum/lesser curvature)
• Acid/Pepsin Production: Occurs in the body and fundus
• Gastrin (hormonal control) is produced in the antral mucosa
• Chronic ulcers invade muscular and peritoneal coats.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: In a patient with portal hypertension, distinguish between the venous shunts causing esophageal varices and those causing rectal varices.
back:
• Esophageal: Left gastric (portal) to azygos (systemic)
• Rectal: Superior rectal (portal) to middle/inferior rectal (systemic)
• Esophageal varices pose high risk of hematemesis
• Rectal varices present as internal hemorrhoids

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Portal hypertension leads to esophageal varices because the left gastric vein, which receives esophageal tributaries, drains directly into the [___] vein.
back:
• Portal vein
• High portal pressure reverses flow into the systemic azygos system
• Causes superficial venous dilatation in the esophageal submucosa

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third of the esophagus is likely to show initial lymphatic metastasis in the [___] nodes.
back: Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Explain why pain from the parietal peritoneum is precisely localized compared to the vague sensation of visceral peritoneal pain.
back:
• Parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic nerves (T7-L1)
• These nerves also supply overlying skin and muscle
• Visceral peritoneum lacks somatic innervation, responding only to stretch.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain how the unique muscular architecture of the stomach facilitates mechanical digestion compared to the rest of the alimentary canal.
back:
• Presence of an inner oblique muscle layer
• Works with circular and longitudinal layers for churning
• Facilitates the mechanical breakdown of food into chyme

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Explain the vertical continuity of the peritoneum as it reflects from the liver to the stomach and then to the pelvic floor.
back: * Liver to stomach: Lesser omentum. * Stomach to transverse colon: Greater omentum. * Transverse colon to wall: Transverse mesocolon. * Pelvic floor: Reflects over pelvic organs to form the rectovesical or rectouterine (Douglas) pouches.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the boundaries of the cystohepatic triangle (of Calot) and its primary surgical significance during cholecystectomy.
back:
* Boundaries: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior liver surface.
* Significance: Contains the cystic artery; identification is crucial to avoid ductal injury.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Identify the primary cranial nerve that provides the motor component to the pharyngeal plexus for the innervation of the musculus uvulae.
back: Vagus nerve (CN X). It supplies the motor fibers to the pharyngeal plexus, which innervates all muscles of the soft palate with the exception of the tensor veli palatini.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the nerve supply of the esophagus, distinguishing between the origins of the esophageal plexus and the innervation of the cricopharyngeus.
back:
• Esophageal Plexus: Formed by the vagus nerves (parasympathetic) and sympathetic trunks.
• Cricopharyngeus: Innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
• Vagus promotes peristalsis and gland secretion.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: List the three specific anatomical locations where the esophagus is normally constricted.
back: • Pharyngo-esophageal junction (C6/15cm from incisors). • Crossing of the aortic arch and left bronchus (T4-T5/25cm). • Diaphragmatic hiatus (T10/40cm).

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: Distinguish the anatomical landmarks and vertebral levels of the subcostal plane from the intertubercular plane.
back:
* Subcostal: Lowest costal margin (10th cartilage) at L3
* Intertubercular: Iliac tubercles at L5

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: On a cadaveric liver model, the [___] artery is identified as the branch of the common hepatic artery that descends behind the first part of the duodenum, posing a hemorrhage risk in posterior duodenal ulcers.
back:
Gastroduodenal Artery.
• Terminal branch of the common hepatic artery.
• Divides into the right gastro-omental and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Aponeurotic Openings of the Inguinal Canal
front: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening located in the aponeurosis of the [___] muscle.
back: * External oblique. * The superficial ring is a triangular defect in its aponeurosis. * It serves as the exit for the spermatic cord and is located just above the pubic tubercle.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Explain the mechanism by which portal hypertension leads to the clinical presentation of internal hemorrhoids.
back: High portal pressure causes retrograde flow into the superior rectal vein. It dilates the anastomosis with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic) in the anal canal, forming varicosities.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: A posterior wall ulcer in the first part of the duodenum typically causes severe hemorrhage by eroding the [___] artery.
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery
* Branch of the hepatic artery
* Lies directly posterior to the duodenal cap
* Erosion leads to massive hematemesis or melena

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Contrast the anatomical consequences of a perforated ulcer on the anterior stomach wall versus the posterior stomach wall.
back:
• Anterior: Leakage into greater sac causes generalized peritonitis
• Posterior: Leakage into lesser sac; may erode splenic artery or pancreas
• Posterior ulcers often present with referred back pain

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the neurovascular contents passing through the incisive foramen versus those in the greater palatine foramen.
back:
• Incisive Foramen: Nasopalatine nerve and terminal branch of Great Palatine artery.
• Greater Palatine Foramen: Greater palatine nerve and greater palatine artery.
• Both facilitate palatal neurovascular supply.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: Differentiate the composition of the posterior rectus sheath at the level of the umbilicus versus the level of the symphysis pubis.
back: * Umbilicus level: Formed by internal oblique and transversus aponeuroses. * Symphysis level: Posterior wall is absent; only transversalis fascia and peritoneum exist. * Demarcated by the arcuate line.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Explain the anatomical basis for why inflammation of the parietal peritoneum leads to reflex 'guarding' of the abdominal musculature.
back:
*   Shared Innervation: The parietal peritoneum and overlying muscles are supplied by the same segmental spinal nerves (T7-L1).
*   Protective Reflex: Irritation triggers motor neurons, causing involuntary muscle contraction to stabilize the area.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is located opposite the tip of the [___] costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.
back:
• Ninth (9th) costal cartilage.
• Corresponds to the transpyloric plane (L1).
• Clinically identified at the intersection of the linea semilunaris and the costal margin.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Distinguish the 'pre-ileal' and 'post-ileal' positions of the appendix tip in relation to the terminal part of the small intestine.
back:
Pre-ileal vs. Post-ileal
*   Pre-ileal: Tip lies anterior to the terminal ileum
*   Post-ileal: Tip lies posterior to the terminal ileum
*   Both are less common than retrocecal/pelvic positions

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Contrast the anatomical mechanism of bowel obstruction caused by peritoneal adhesions with that caused by an internal hernia.
back: ● Adhesions: Fibrous scar tissue binding bowel loops post-surgery/infection. ● Internal Hernia: Bowel trapped in pre-existing peritoneal recesses (e.g., lesser sac or paraduodenal recess). ● Both lead to kinking and ischemia.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A patient presents with epigastric pain and jaundice. Imaging shows a gallstone lodged at the hepatopancreatic ampulla. Explain the anatomical basis for the potential development of acute pancreatitis in this scenario.
back: A stone at the ampulla can cause bile to reflux into the pancreatic duct. This initiates premature activation of pancreatic enzymes, leading to autodigestion of the gland.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
coreConcept: Rectus Sheath Contents and Clinical Anatomy
front: A athlete presents with acute pain and a non-fluctuant mass in the lower abdominal wall following a strenuous workout. If the diagnosis is a rectus sheath hematoma, the bleeding most likely originates from the [___], which are key neurovascular contents of the sheath.
back: • Inferior epigastric vessels. • Other Contents: Rectus abdominis, Pyramidalis, Superior epigastric vessels, and terminal rami of T7-T12 nerves. • Formation: Below the arcuate line, all three aponeuroses form the anterior wall, leaving the posterior wall deficient.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: A surgical resident is identifying the structures in the inguinal canal of a female patient. Name the primary homologue to the spermatic cord and its destination.
back:
* Round ligament of the uterus
* Extends from the uterus to the labium majus
* Accompanied by the ilioinguinal nerve

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Describe the specific pathway of lymphatic drainage from the palatine tonsils to the deep cervical nodes.
back: ● Jugulodigastric Pathway ● Vessels pierce the superior constrictor muscle and pharyngobasilar fascia ● Drain directly into the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph node ● Node is palpated below and behind the angle of the mandible.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific external features that distinguish the large intestine from the small intestine upon inspection of a cadaveric specimen.
back:
Large Intestine Identification
- Teniae coli (longitudinal bands).
- Haustra (sacculations).
- Appendices epiploicae (fatty tags).
- Generally larger caliber and fixed (ascending/descending) parts.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A 60-year-old male with portal hypertension undergoes a procedure where the portal vein is anastomosed to the IVC. Contrast the contents of the portal vein versus the hepatic veins in this patient.
back: * Portal Vein: Carries nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood into the liver sinusoids. * Hepatic Veins: Carry processed deoxygenated blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Name the four primary high-yield anatomical sites for portosystemic anastomosis discussed in UHS Board anatomy.
back:
• Lower esophagus (Gastroesophageal)
• Anal canal (Anorectal)
• Umbilicus (Paraumbilical)
• Retroperitoneal/Posterior wall (Retzius and Bare Area)
• Each involves a portal tributary meeting a systemic vein

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: A 45-year-old male complains of a painful lump under the tongue that swells every time he eats. Palpation reveals a hard mass in Wharton’s duct. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
Sialolithiasis (Salivary Calculus).
