- Most common in the submandibular duct due to its tortuous, upward course.
- Causes post-prandial pain and gland swelling.
- Stones are typically radio-opaque.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Describe the anatomical components of the 'stomach bed' that are in direct relation to the posterior gastric surface.
back:
* Diaphragm and Spleen.
* Left Kidney and Suprarenal gland.
* Pancreas and Splenic Artery.
* Transverse Mesocolon.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The appendicular artery, which supplies the entire organ, is a branch of the posterior cecal artery and travels within the [___].
back:
• Mesoappendix
• A triangular fold of peritoneum
• Attaches to the mesentery of the small intestine.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the surgical importance of the 'Cystohepatic Triangle' (Calot's Triangle) during a cholecystectomy procedure.
back:
• Contains the cystic artery and possible accessory bile ducts.
• Boundaries: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and liver surface.
• Clear dissection prevents accidental ligation of the right hepatic artery.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Intrapancreatic Course of the Bile Duct
front: A 55-year-old male with a tumor in the head of the pancreas develops obstructive jaundice. Which specific segment of the biliary tree is most likely compressed?
back:
* Third (intrapancreatic) part of the bile duct.
* Lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head.
* Compression prevents bile flow into the duodenum, leading to jaundice.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Identify the arterial source of the superior epigastric artery and its specific entry point into the rectus sheath.
back:
*   Terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery
*   Enters rectus sheath between sternal and costal diaphragmatic origins
*   Descends posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle
*   Anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Detail the anatomical relationship of the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum that predisposes it to compression in 'Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome.'
back:
*   Position: Crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta at the L3 level
*   Overlying Structure: SMA and Superior Mesenteric Vein pass anterior to the duodenum
*   Mechanism: The duodenum is trapped in the acute angle between the SMA and the aorta

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Meckel's diverticulum is an anatomical remnant of the [___] duct, typically located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
back:
• Vitellointestinal (Vitelline) duct
• Location: Approximately 2 feet (61 cm) from the ileocecal junction
• Clinical note: May contain ectopic gastric mucosa leading to ulceration or hemorrhage.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: The anorectal porto-systemic anastomosis involves the [___] vein from the portal system and the middle/inferior rectal veins from the systemic system.
back:
• Superior Rectal vein
• Drains the upper half of the anal canal
• Systemic side: Internal iliac and internal pudendal tributaries
• Clinical: Leads to internal hemorrhoids

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Submandibular Duct Relation
front: Explain the anatomical 'triple relation' or loop between the lingual nerve and the submandibular duct.
back:
* Lateral: Nerve is lateral to the duct initially
* Inferior: Nerve loops under the duct from lateral to medial
* Medial: Nerve ascends medial to the duct to reach the tongue

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Explain the primary biological function of Waldeyer’s ring at the junction of the respiratory and digestive tracts.
back:
Immunological barrier. 
- Samples inhaled and ingested antigens. 
- Initiates immune responses at the aero-digestive portal. 
- Produces lymphocytes and antibodies (IgA) for local defense.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Identify the portal vessel that travels within the falciform ligament to reach the anterior abdominal wall to form the Caput Medusae sign.
back:
Paraumbilical veins.
* Connect left portal vein branch to umbilicus.
* Anastomose with superficial epigastric veins.
* Radiate from umbilicus in cirrhosis.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with massive hematemesis. Identify the specific venous anastomosis involved and its components.
back: • Portosystemic anastomosis. • Left gastric vein (portal tributary). • Esophageal branches of the azygos vein (systemic tributary). • Rupture causes esophageal varices.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Formation of the Common Hepatic Duct
front: The common hepatic duct is formed at the porta hepatis by the union of the [___] and [___] hepatic ducts.
back:
* Right and left hepatic ducts.
* Emerge from the respective lobes of the liver.
* Found within the porta hepatis.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: The first part of the duodenum, often referred to as the superior part, is approximately 2 inches long and is situated at the level of the [___] vertebra.
back:
* L1 (First Lumbar) vertebra.
* Lies on the transpyloric plane.
* Mobile in its first inch; the rest is retroperitoneal.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: Specify the vertebral level of origin for the inferior mesenteric artery and the primary segment of the gut it distributes to.
back: * L3 vertebra level * Supplies the hindgut * Distribution includes from the distal transverse colon to the upper half of the anal canal

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Name the anatomical structures forming the portal vein and its primary location behind the pancreas.
back:
• Formed by Splenic and Superior Mesenteric veins
• Location: Posterior to the neck of the pancreas
• Length: Approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
• Enters: Liver via the porta hepatis

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the role and anatomical formation of the marginal artery (of Drummond) as visualized along the concave margin of the large intestine.
back: * Formed by anastomoses of colic arteries (SMA and IMA). * Runs from the ileocecal junction to the superior rectum. * Provides critical collateral circulation during mesenteric artery occlusion.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Identify the primary venous drainage route of the liver and its termination point.
back:
• Drains via three or more hepatic veins.
• Hepatic veins emerge from the posterior surface of the organ.
• Terminate directly into the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC).

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Identify the venous structure within the spermatic cord responsible for heat exchange and specify its primary drainage on the left side.
back:
* Pampiniform plexus.
* Drains into the left renal vein.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: A 50-year-old male with chronic dyspepsia presents with sudden, massive hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals a deep ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach body. Erosion of which artery is the most likely cause of hemorrhage?
back:
• Splenic artery.
• Major component of the stomach bed.
• Runs along the superior border of the pancreas behind the stomach.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: During a liver biopsy, the needle is inserted through the 8th or 9th intercostal space. Why is the patient instructed to hold their breath in full expiration?
back:
• Reduces the size of the costodiaphragmatic recess.
• Elevates the diaphragm and lung away from the biopsy site.
• Minimizes the risk of lung or pleural penetration.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Relational Anatomy of the Bile Duct
front: Contrast the anatomical relations of the first part of the bile duct with the second part regarding the duodenum and major vascular structures.
back: The first part descends in the right free margin of the lesser omentum anterior to the portal vein. The second part lies posterior to the first part of the duodenum.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the two specific ducts that unite to form the bile duct (common bile duct) and name their location within the lesser omentum.
back:
* Cystic Duct and Common Hepatic Duct.
* Located in the right free margin of the lesser omentum.
* Lies anterior to the portal vein and right of the hepatic artery.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A 50-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with massive hematemesis. Explain the anatomical basis of the bleeding vessels.
back:
- Portal hypertension reverses flow from the portal vein to the left gastric vein.
- Submucosal esophageal veins dilate into varices.
- Rupture results in severe upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine is a vertical-oblique reflection extending from the duodenojejunal flexure to the [___].
back:
* Right sacroiliac joint (at the ileocecal junction).
* Approximately 15 cm (6 inches) long.
* Crosses the third part of the duodenum and the abdominal aorta.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the primary arterial source of the cystic artery and its typical relationship to the biliary ductal system.
back:
* Arises from the right hepatic artery
* Typically found within the Cystohepatic Triangle (Calot’s Triangle)
* Boundaries: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and liver inferior surface
* Critical structure to ligate during cholecystectomy

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Distinguish between the anatomical characteristics of the upper versus lower esophageal sphincters.
back:
- Upper: Anatomic sphincter (Cricopharyngeus muscle)
- Lower: Physiologic sphincter (no distinct muscle thickening)
- Lower relies on diaphragmatic and intrinsic muscle tone

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: General sensation from the mucous membrane of the soft palate is primarily mediated by the [___] and [___] nerves.
back:
• Lesser palatine nerves (from Maxillary Nerve/V2).
• Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
• These carry the sensory limb of the gag reflex.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the role of the gastroesophageal junction in preventing acid reflux, despite the absence of an anatomical sphincter.
back:
• Functions as a physiological sphincter.
• Regulated by the circular smooth muscle of the esophagus.
• Reinforced by the right crus of the diaphragm and the angle of His.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which the arrival of fatty food in the duodenum leads to the clinical onset of biliary colic.
back:
• Fat triggers Cholecystokinin (CCK) release from the duodenum.
• CCK causes gallbladder contraction against an obstructed cystic duct.
• Increased intraluminal pressure results in visceral pain.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: A 55-year-old male with confirmed adenocarcinoma of the gastric antrum presents with an enlarged left supraclavicular node. Explain the lymphatic route taken by malignant cells from the stomach to reach this specific site.
back: • Drainage via celiac nodes to the cisterna chyli. • Ascent through the thoracic duct. • Entry into the venous system at the left venous angle. • Retrograde spread to the supraclavicular (Troisier's) node.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
coreConcept: Vascular origins of the abdominal wall
front: The inferior epigastric artery, a major vessel of the anterior abdominal wall, arises from the [___] artery just superior to the inguinal ligament.
back:
*   External iliac artery
*   Originates just superior to the inguinal ligament
*   Ascends to enter the rectus sheath via the arcuate line
*   Anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: External Features of the Large Intestine
front: The small, fatty, peritoneum-covered tags uniquely attached to the outer surface of the colon are called [___].
back: * Appendices epiploicae (Omental appendices). * They are absent on the small intestine, cecum, and rectum. * They often contain small nutrient blood vessels.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Contrast the peritoneal reflections forming the gastrosplenic ligament and the splenorenal ligament regarding their contents.
back: * Gastrosplenic: Connects stomach to spleen; contains short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. * Splenorenal: Connects spleen to left kidney; contains splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Describe the anatomical basis of a 'positive Murphy’s sign' during a physical examination for suspected cholecystitis.
back:
Mechanism:

*   Diaphragmatic contraction during deep inspiration pushes the inflamed gallbladder downward.
*   The gallbladder contacts the palpating hand at the 9th costal cartilage.
*   Sharp pain causes sudden 'inspiratory arrest.'

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Identify the muscular structures that comprise the anterior and posterior pillars of the tonsillar fossa.
back: * Anterior: Palatoglossus muscle (within the palatoglossal arch). * Posterior: Palatopharyngeus muscle (within the palatopharyngeal arch).

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: A patient with advanced liver cirrhosis presents with a radiating pattern of dilated superficial veins around the umbilicus. Identify the anatomical vessels responsible for this clinical finding.
back:
*   Anastomosis between paraumbilical veins and superficial systemic veins
*   Paraumbilical veins (portal tributaries) accompany the ligamentum teres
*   Indicates severe portal hypertension, often due to hepatic cirrhosis

category: Describe the planes and quadrants of abdomen
front: Identify the abdominal region located centrally, directly below the xiphoid process and above the umbilical region.
back:
* Epigastric region (Epigastrium)
* Contents typically include the stomach and part of the liver

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A 40-year-old male presents with epigastric pain and severe internal bleeding. Radiography confirms a posterior duodenal ulcer. Name the major vessel found immediately posterior to the first part of the duodenum prone to erosion.
back:
Gastroduodenal artery.
- Descends behind the first part of the duodenum.
- Erosion causes severe hemorrhage.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Distinguish the common hepatic duct from the bile duct based on length and primary drainage role.
back:
• Common Hepatic: ~1.5 inches; drains liver directly to cystic junction
• Bile Duct: ~3 inches (8 cm); conveys combined hepatic/cystic bile to duodenum

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
coreConcept: Vascular Differences Between Jejunum and Ileum
front: Contrast the vascular architecture of the jejunal mesentery with that of the ileal mesentery regarding arterial arcades and vasa recta.
back:
* Jejunum: Few (1-2) large arcades; long, infrequent vasa recta.
* Ileum: Multiple (3-5) small, complex arcades; short, numerous vasa recta.
* Jejunum appears redder due to higher overall vascularity.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Identify the portal and systemic vessels involved in the retroperitoneal anastomoses (Veins of Retzius) of the ascending colon.
back:
*   Portal: Tributaries of the colic veins
*   Systemic: Lumbar, renal, and phrenic veins
*   Occur where retroperitoneal organs contact the posterior abdominal wall

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Contrast the physical examination findings of a 'Psoas sign' with an 'Obturator sign' regarding the specific location of the appendiceal tip.
back:
Psoas Sign vs. Obturator Sign.
- Psoas: Pain on hip extension; indicates retrocecal position (psoas major irritation).
- Obturator: Pain on internal rotation of flexed hip; indicates pelvic position (obturator internus irritation).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic peptic ulcers presents with sudden-onset hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals a deep erosion on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Identify the most likely vessel involved.
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery.
* Lies immediately posterior to the first duodenal segment.
* Significant risk for massive hemorrhage upon ulcer perforation.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Developmental Anatomy of the Inguinal Canal
front: Explain how the relationship between the deep and superficial rings changes from a newborn to an adult, and its mechanical purpose.
back: * In infants, the rings overlap, creating a short, straight path. * Adult growth moves the deep ring laterally, creating an oblique passage. * This obliquity reinforces the wall against high intra-abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: List the key components of the 'Stomach Bed' related to the posterior surface of the pancreas.
back:
* Anterior surface of the pancreatic body.
* Lesser sac (separates stomach from pancreas).
* Splenic artery (runs along the upper border of the pancreas).
* Transverse mesocolon.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Explain the dual blood supply mechanism of the liver, specifying the approximate percentage of blood volume and oxygenation levels provided by each source.
back:
• Portal Vein (70%): Low oxygen, nutrient-rich blood from GI tract.
• Hepatic Artery (30%): High oxygen, branch of the celiac trunk.
• Both mix in hepatic sinusoids before draining into hepatic veins.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the origin and termination of the short gastric arteries.
back:
Origin: Splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen.
- Course: Pass through the gastrosplenic ligament.
- Termination: Supply the fundus of the stomach.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Describe the topographical orientation of the bile duct relative to the hepatic artery and portal vein within the lesser omentum.
back:
• Position: Right free margin of lesser omentum
• To the left: Hepatic artery
• Posteriorly: Portal vein
• Landmark: Anterior to the epiploic foramen

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the superficial fascia (Scarpa’s) and the deep fascia of the anterior abdominal wall in terms of surgical utility.
back:
• Scarpa's: Strong, membranous, and capable of holding sutures for wound strength.
• Deep Fascia: Only a thin, flimsy layer of connective tissue covering the muscles.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Organs that are almost completely surrounded by visceral peritoneum and are typically suspended from the body wall by a mesentery are classified as [___].
back:
Intraperitoneal organs. 
- Includes the stomach, jejunum, ileum, and spleen.
- They are mobile and connected to other structures via peritoneal folds.
- They occupy the potential space of the peritoneal cavity.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Explain the role of the pyloric sphincter in regulating gastric contents.
back:
• Controls chyme outflow into the duodenum
  • Maintains tonic contraction to prevent reflux
  • Regulated by vagal relaxation and sympathetic contraction

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Describe the anatomical contribution of the right crus of the diaphragm to the antireflux mechanism.
back:
- Acts as an external physiological sphincter.
- Compresses the esophagus at the esophageal hiatus.
- Augments the internal lower esophageal sphincter (LES) during increased intra-abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: Distinguish the contents of the posterior wall of the rectus sheath above the costal margin from its contents at the level of the umbilicus.
back:
• Above costal margin: 5th, 6th, and 7th costal cartilages
• At umbilicus: Posterior lamina of IO and TA aponeurosis

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: During abdominal paracentesis, a full urinary bladder may reach as high as the [___], necessitating catheterization before the procedure to avoid perforation.
back: • Umbilicus. • Bladder rises out of pelvis when distended. • Emptying ensures it remains a pelvic organ. • Minimizes risk of accidental trocar injury.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A surgeon during laparotomy identifies a loop of small bowel in the upper left quadrant characterized by a thick wall, long vasa recta, and only one or two simple arterial arcades. Identify this segment.
back: * Jejunum. * It has a wider diameter and redder appearance than the ileum. * The mesentery typically contains less fat, creating translucent 'windows' near the gut wall.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: In the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, portal venous blood shunts into the systemic circulation at the lower esophagus via the anastomosis between the [___] vein and the azygos vein.
back:
Left gastric (coronary) vein.
* Portal component: Left gastric vein.
* Systemic component: Azygos and hemiazygos veins.
* Significance: High portal pressure causes these submucosal veins to dilate and potentially rupture.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Explain the mechanical role of the tensor veli palatini in middle ear pressure regulation during the act of deglutition.
back:
• Muscle fibers originate from the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube
  • Contraction pulls the lateral wall of the tube open
  • Allows air to enter the middle ear, equalizing pressure

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Describe the embryological origin and typical location of an ileal diverticulum (Meckel's).
back:
* Remnant of vitellointestinal duct
* Located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum
* Approximately 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocecal junction
* May contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Describe the mechanism by which the spermatic cord acquires its three distinct fascial coverings during fetal development.
back:
* The testis follows the gubernaculum through the abdominal wall.
* It pulls tubular extensions (fasciae) from the transversalis fascia, internal oblique, and external oblique aponeurosis.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The [___] artery, usually a branch of the right hepatic artery, provides the primary arterial supply to the gallbladder.
back:
● Cystic artery
● Often located within the Cystohepatic Triangle (Calot triangle)
● Arises from the right hepatic artery in the majority of cases

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The [___] curvature of the stomach forms the right border of the organ and serves as the attachment site for the [___].
back:
• Lesser curvature
• Lesser omentum
• Suspends the stomach from the liver's visceral surface

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with massive hematemesis. Explain the vascular pathophysiology behind this clinical presentation.
back:
*   Portal hypertension forces blood into the left gastric vein
*   Blood shunts to systemic esophageal veins (azygos)
*   Dilation and rupture of these varices occur

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: How does a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve affect the first (voluntary) stage of deglutition?
back:
• Impairs bolus formation
• Tongue cannot effectively push the bolus against the hard palate
• Difficulty moving food from the oral cavity into the oropharynx.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Distinguish the mucosal surface of the first part of the duodenum from that of the second part.
back:
• First part: Smooth mucosa (no circular folds; often called 'duodenal cap')
• Second part: Contains prominent plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes)
• Second part also features the major and minor duodenal papillae

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Describe the anatomical relationship and fixation of the duodenum that makes its third part susceptible to compression in a blunt crush injury.
back:
● Retroperitoneal fixation.
● It runs horizontally across the rigid lumbar vertebrae (L3).
● Compression occurs between the anterior abdominal wall and the vertebral column.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Outline the sequential anatomical step occurring in the biliary tree once Cholecystokinin triggers gallbladder contraction.
back: Bile enters the cystic duct, passes into the bile duct, travels behind the duodenum and through the pancreas, and finally enters the duodenal lumen via the major papilla.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: The [___] omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and folds back to attach to the transverse colon.
back:
Greater Omentum

*   Four-layered peritoneal fold laden with fat
*   Functions as the "abdominal policeman"
*   Moves via peristalsis to seal off infection foci

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: A 4-year-old male presents with a scrotal swelling that increases in size during crying and reduces during sleep. Identify the most likely embryological defect responsible for this condition.
back:
• Patency of the processus vaginalis
• Allows abdominal contents to enter the scrotum
• Leads to indirect inguinal hernia

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: The fibrous band extending from the xiphoid process to the symphysis pubis, formed by the fusion of aponeuroses from all three flat muscles, is the [___].
back:
• Linea alba
• Wider above the umbilicus than below
• Contains the umbilical scar
• Preferred site for rapid midline surgical incisions

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Contrast the developmental classification of the kidneys with that of the ascending colon regarding their peritoneal relationship.
back:
• Kidneys: Primarily retroperitoneal (always behind the sac)
• Ascending colon: Secondarily retroperitoneal
• Colon was initially intraperitoneal but fused posteriorly during development
• Both lack a posterior mesentery in adults

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Identify the specific lymph node group receiving drainage from the pyloric region along the inferior gastric border.
back:
Subpyloric (pyloric) lymph nodes.
- Located near the gastroduodenal artery.
- Drainage continues to hepatic and eventually celiac nodes.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Identify the artery contained within the mesoappendix and specify its parent vessel of origin.
back:
* Appendicular artery
* Originates from the posterior cecal artery
* Parent vessel is the ileocolic artery, a branch of the Superior Mesenteric

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the anatomical route and vertebral level where the esophagus traverses the diaphragm to enter the abdomen.
back: * Passes through the right crus of the diaphragm. * Level: T10 vertebra. * Accompanied by the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of parotid gland and its duct, mentioning the structures entering and exiting the gland
front: Explain the pathway of the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that stimulate saliva production in the parotid gland.
back:
• Preganglionic: CN IX via the tympanic branch and lesser petrosal nerve.
• Relay: Synapse in the Otic ganglion.
• Postganglionic: Travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to the gland.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: The sickle-shaped peritoneal fold that connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, containing the ligamentum teres in its free border, is the [___].
back: * Falciform ligament. * Derived from the ventral mesentery. * Divides the liver into anatomical right and left lobes on its anterior surface.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Contrast the anatomical positions of the bile duct, hepatic artery, and portal vein within the free margin of the lesser omentum.
back:
• Bile duct: Lateral and anterior
• Hepatic artery: Medial and anterior
• Portal vein: Posterior to both structures.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Gastric Tributaries of the Portal System
front: Identify the direct tributaries of the hepatic portal vein that run along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
back: * Left Gastric Vein. * Right Gastric Vein. * These drain directly into the main portal vein trunk or its formative branches.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Distinguish between the Lesser and Greater Curvatures of the stomach regarding their peritoneal attachments.
back:
* Lesser Curvature: Attached to the Lesser Omentum (Hepatogastric ligament).
* Greater Curvature: Attached to the Greater Omentum and Gastrosplenic ligament.
* Lesser is shorter and forms the right border.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Hypertrophy of the pharyngeal tonsil in children is commonly referred to as [___].
back: Adenoids. This condition is characterized by mouth breathing, snoring, and a 'nasal' voice. It is often associated with tubal obstruction and middle ear problems. Diagnosis is confirmed by viewing the nasopharynx via a mirror or endoscope.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: How does the greater omentum clinically function as the 'abdominal policeman' during a localized infection like appendicitis?
back: ● It migrates to the site of inflammation via peristalsis. ● Peritoneal surfaces adhere to the infected organ. ● Effectively walls off the focus to prevent generalized peritonitis.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Anastomotic Vascular Supply of the Lesser Curvature
front: Contrast the blood supply of the lesser curvature provided by the celiac trunk's direct and indirect branches.
back:
Left Gastric Artery:
- Direct branch of the celiac trunk.
- Supplies upper lesser curvature.
Right Gastric Artery:
- Branch of the hepatic artery (indirect).
- Supplies lower lesser curvature.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: A patient exhibits a brisk elevation of the testis when the medial thigh is stroked. Identify the efferent nerve branch involved in this reflex.
back:
* Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
* The reflex is the cremasteric reflex (L1-L2).

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Explain the biological mechanism of the 'shutter-like' action of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis during increased intra-abdominal pressure.
back: - Muscles arch over the inguinal canal. - Upon contraction, they flatten the roof toward the floor (inguinal ligament). - This virtually closes the canal, preventing the herniation of abdominal viscera.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: The pancreas is primarily a retroperitoneal organ located in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions, specifically crossing the [___] plane at the level of the L1 vertebra.
back:
Transpyloric.

* Intersects the L1 vertebral body.
* Marks the position of the pancreatic neck.
* Passes through the hila of the kidneys and the pylorus.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Lesser Curvature
front: Identify the two primary arteries that form an anastomosis along the lesser curvature of the stomach and state their respective origins.
back:
Lesser Curvature Supply:
- Left Gastric Artery: Direct branch of the celiac trunk.
- Right Gastric Artery: Branch of the hepatic artery (proper).
- These vessels run within the layers of the lesser omentum.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
coreConcept: Formation of the Hepatic Portal Vein
front: Explain the anatomical formation of the hepatic portal vein, including the vessels involved and the specific site of union.
back:
- Formed by the union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein. 
- Occurs behind the neck of the pancreas. 
- Located at the level of the L2 vertebra.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A 55-year-old patient with liver cirrhosis presents with severe vomiting of bright red blood. Explain the anatomical pathway of the venous blood causing this hemorrhage.
back:
- Obstruction of portal vein flow
- Retrograde flow into left gastric vein
- Dilatation of submucosal esophageal venous plexus
- Rupture of portosystemic anastomotic vessels

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Distinguish between the falciform ligament and the coronary ligament based on their anatomical attachments to the liver.
back:
Peritoneal Ligaments of Liver

*   Falciform: Connects liver to anterior wall; contains ligamentum teres
*   Coronary: Connects liver to diaphragm; encloses the 'bare area'
*   Both are two-layered peritoneal folds

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the critical procedural landmark for palpating a calculus in the submandibular duct within the oral cavity.
back:
*   Floor of the mouth.
*   Medial to the sublingual fold.
*   Orifice is at the summit of the papilla lateral to the lingual frenulum.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: External features of the large intestine
front: The characteristic three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle found on the outer surface of the colon, which converge at the base of the appendix, are known as the [___].
back:
Teniae coli
- Consist of thickened longitudinal smooth muscle.
- Shortening of these bands creates haustra (sacculations).
- Serve as a surgical guide to the appendix base.

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
front: Distinguish the surface anatomical location of the "Midpoint of the Inguinal Ligament" from the "Midinguinal Point.".
back: * Midpoint of Inguinal Ligament: Between ASIS and pubic tubercle. * Midinguinal Point: Between ASIS and symphysis pubis. * Per source text, the deep ring projects at the midinguinal point.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: Explain the anatomical route and destination of exocrine secretions through the main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung).
back:
* Begins in the tail and traverses the entire gland length.
* Joins the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater).
* Opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
coreConcept: Fascial Coverings of the Spermatic Cord
front: Contrast the anatomical layer that forms the cremasteric fascia with the layer that forms the internal spermatic fascia.
back:
• Cremasteric fascia: Derived from the Internal Oblique muscle and its fascia.
• Internal spermatic fascia: Derived from the Transversalis fascia.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Identify the specific anatomical region in the neck where the hypoglossal nerve is found as it passes downward and forward toward the tongue.
back: - The carotid triangle of the neck.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the functional role and appearance of the gastric rugae as seen during internal inspection of the stomach.
back:
* Longitudinal mucosal folds that flatten during distension.
* Facilitate stomach expansion without increasing internal pressure.
* Most prominent along the greater curvature and body.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Distinguish between the anatomical efficacy of the 'Abdominal Policeman' in an infant versus an adult during a localized infection like appendicitis.
back:
• Adult: The greater omentum is long and mobile; it wraps around and seals the infection site.
• Infant: The omentum is short and thin; it cannot effectively localize infections, leading to rapid generalized peritonitis.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The celiac trunk, providing the primary arterial supply to the embryonic foregut, arises from the abdominal aorta at the level of the [___] vertebra.
back: * T12 vertebra. * Supplies the stomach, liver, spleen, and upper duodenum. * Major branches include the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: Analyze how the transversalis fascia contributes to the structural integrity of the femoral sheath in the inguinal region.
back:
• Forms the anterior wall of the femoral sheath.
• Extends 1.5 inches into the thigh behind the inguinal ligament.
• Encloses femoral vessels but excludes the femoral nerve.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: The superficial inguinal ring is formed as a triangular-shaped defect in the aponeurosis of the [___] muscle.
back: * External oblique. * Situated superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. * Its margins (crura) give attachment to the external spermatic fascia.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Contrast the anatomical relations of the gallbladder's fundus with its posterior surface.
back:
● Fundus: Contacts anterior abdominal wall at the 9th right costal cartilage
● Posterior Surface: Relates to the transverse colon and second part of the duodenum

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the parent vessel and embryonic gut segment supplied by the superior mesenteric artery as it passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum.
back: * Arises from the abdominal aorta (L1). * Supplies the midgut derivatives. * Includes the gut from the distal duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Name the anatomical structure that guards the common opening of the bile and pancreatic ducts into the second part of the duodenum.
back:
Sphincter of Oddi (Hepatopancreatic Sphincter).
- Surrounds the Ampulla of Vater.
- Located at the summit of the Major Duodenal Papilla.
- Regulates flow of bile and pancreatic enzymes.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: Explain the role of the conjoint tendon in providing structural integrity to the inguinal canal region.
back:
• Formed by fused aponeuroses of internal oblique and transversus abdominis
• Attaches to the pubic crest and pectineal line
• Reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal
• Positioned directly behind the superficial inguinal ring

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: At the umbilicus, the [___] veins, which are tributaries of the portal vein, anastomose with the superficial epigastric veins of the systemic circulation.
back:
• Paraumbilical veins
• Clinical Sign: Caput medusae
• Context: Radiating dilated veins on the abdominal wall due to portal hypertension.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 4-week-old male presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting and a palpable "olive-shaped" mass in the epigastrium. The anatomical feature of the stomach involved in this condition is the [___].
back:
* Pyloric Sphincter.
* An anatomic sphincter formed by thickened circular smooth muscle.
* Located at the L1 level (transpyloric plane).

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Describe the porto-systemic communication occurring across the diaphragm at the 'bare area' of the liver.
back:
• Portal: Hepatic sinusoids/portal radicles
• Systemic: Phrenic and Intercostal veins
• Significant in establishing systemic bypass without variceal rupture.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Contrast the venous pathways utilized in portal hypertension (Caput Medusae) versus those seen in inferior vena cava (IVC) obstruction.
back:
*   Caput Medusae: Paraumbilical-superficial systemic anastomosis radiating from the umbilicus
*   IVC Obstruction: Thoracoepigastric vein formation (lateral thoracic to superficial epigastric)
*   Blood flows cephalad to bypass the obstructed vena cava

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: At the lower end of the esophagus, the [___] vein (a portal tributary) anastomoses with the systemic azygos vein to form a clinically significant portal-systemic site.
back:
- Left gastric vein
- Specifically its esophageal branches
- Dilation here leads to esophageal varices in portal hypertension

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the primary arterial arcades supplying the greater curvature of the stomach and their parent vessels.
back:
• Right gastro-omental (from Gastroduodenal artery)
• Left gastro-omental (from Splenic artery)
• Short gastric arteries (from Splenic artery) supply the fundus

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: In large bowel cancer, the primary route of initial spread is via the lymphatics, while distant metastasis most commonly involves the [___] through the portal circulation.
back:
* Liver.
* Venous drainage from the colon enters the portal venous system.
* Lymphatic spread follows the arterial supply to regional mesenteric nodes.

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: To perform an effective nerve block for the L1 segment, the anesthetic should be infiltrated 1 inch superior to the [___].
back:
- Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS).
- Targets both the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
- Performed along the spinoumbilical line.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Distinguish the vermiform appendix from the adjacent coils of the ileum based on longitudinal muscle arrangement.
back:
• Appendix: Possesses a complete, uniform longitudinal muscle coat
• Ileum: Possesses a continuous longitudinal layer but lacks the convergence of teniae found at the cecal junction.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: A patient presents with a suspected hepatic tumor in the caudate lobe. Anatomically, this lobe is considered a functional part of which primary liver division?
back:
• Left lobe of the liver.
• Receives blood from the left hepatic artery and left portal vein.
• Drains bile into the left hepatic duct.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: The hallmark of [___] is the degeneration of the parasympathetic myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus, leading to aperistalsis and dysphagia.
back:
- Achalasia of the cardia
- Results in proximal esophageal dilation
- Characterized by 'bird-beak' distal narrowing on imaging

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A clinician performing esophagoscopy notes resistance approximately 25–28 cm from the incisor teeth. This specific anatomical narrowing is caused by the [___].
back:
• Arch of the aorta and the left main bronchus.
• This represents the second physiological constriction.
• It occurs at the level of the T4/T5 vertebrae.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: During a difficult tonsillectomy, an injury occurs to the muscle forming the bed of the tonsillar fossa. Identify the muscle and the major artery lying immediately lateral to it.
back: * Muscle: Superior constrictor muscle. * Artery: Facial artery (loop) or Internal carotid artery (postero-lateral).

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Explain the role of Cholecystokinin (CCK) in the physiological emptying of the gallbladder upon the entry of fatty chyme into the duodenum.
back:
• Released by duodenal endocrine cells
• Stimulates smooth muscle contraction in gallbladder wall
• Relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to allow bile flow.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the role of the tensor veli palatini in soft palate dynamics and its specific nerve supply.
back:
• Tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube
• Wraps around the pterygoid hamulus
• Innervated by Nerve to Medial Pterygoid (V3 branch)
• Only palate muscle not supplied by CN X

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: A patient with a posterior gastric ulcer experiences sudden back pain. Which peritoneal space is most likely initially contaminated by leaking gastric contents?
back:
• Lesser sac (omental bursa)
• Fluid can later enter the greater sac via the epiploic foramen
• Posterior wall relates to the pancreas and splenic artery.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: The efferent vessels from the celiac lymph nodes unite with those of the superior mesenteric nodes to form the [___], which is the primary contributor to the cisterna chyli.
back:
Intestinal Lymph Trunk.
- Collects lymph from the foregut and midgut.
- Lies on the posterior abdominal wall.
- Empties into the cisterna chyli at the L1-L2 level.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The esophagus traverses the diaphragm at the level of the [___] vertebra to enter the abdominal cavity.
back: T10 (Tenth thoracic vertebra).

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: The peripheral part of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum is innervated by the [___] nerves.
back:
• Lower six thoracic nerves
• Also known as the intercostal nerves
• Irritation here refers pain to the lower chest or abdominal wall.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: The primary clinical sign of generalized peritonitis, where pain is significantly exacerbated upon the sudden release of manual pressure on the abdominal wall, is [___].
back:
• Rebound Tenderness.
• This indicates the underlying parietal peritoneum is inflamed.
• It is often accompanied by 'guarding' (reflex spasm of abdominal muscles).

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Contrast the venous drainage of the gallbladder with its parasympathetic nerve supply.
back:
● Venous: Cystic vein drains directly into the portal vein
● Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve (CN X) stimulates contraction and bile secretion

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: To locate the base of the appendix during a laparotomy, a surgeon should trace the three [___] until they converge into a continuous longitudinal muscle layer.
back:
• Teniae coli
• These bands meet at the cecal apex
• This convergence marks the constant anatomical origin of the appendix.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: The [___] hepatic duct is formed by the convergence of the right and left hepatic ducts within the porta hepatis.
back:
• Common hepatic duct
• Approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm) long
• Descends within the free margin of the lesser omentum

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Outline the sequential lymphatic drainage of the gallbladder starting from the cystic lymph node.
back:
• Cystic lymph node (near the gallbladder neck).
• Hepatic lymph nodes (along the hepatic artery).
• Celiac lymph nodes (pre-aortic nodes at the celiac trunk origin).

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Explain the relationship between the four anatomical gastric lymphatic zones and their corresponding arterial supplies.
back:
* Area 1 (Left Gastric Art.): Left gastric nodes.
* Area 2 (Hepatic Art.): Right gastric/pyloric nodes.
* Area 3 (Splenic Art.): Pancreaticosplenic nodes.
* Area 4 (Gastroduodenal Art.): Right gastro-omental nodes.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: List the 'Rule of 2s' used to characterize the anatomical features of an ileal (Meckel's) diverticulum.
back:
* 2 inches long; 2 feet from ileocecal valve
* 2% of population; presents by age 2
* 2 types of ectopic tissue: gastric and pancreatic
* 2:1 male to female ratio

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 52-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals dilated veins at the gastroesophageal junction. These varices represent a portal-systemic anastomosis between the [___] vein and the systemic azygos system.
back: Left Gastric Vein. * Component of the portal venous system. * Anastomoses with esophageal branches of the azygos vein. * Portal hypertension causes retrograde flow and variceal formation at the lower third of the esophagus.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: A surgeon requires rapid access to the abdominal cavity during an emergency laparotomy without sectioning muscle fibers or nerves. Identify the preferred incision site.
back: * Midline incision through the Linea Alba. * Anatomical basis: Fibrous fusion of aponeuroses with minimal vascularity. * Extends from xiphoid process to symphysis pubis. * Avoids major neurovascular injury.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific part of the small intestine that is C-shaped, retroperitoneal, and lacks a mesentery, and describe its relationship to the pancreas.
back:
### Duodenum
* Specifically the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th parts are retroperitoneal.
* The C-shaped loop encircles the **Head of the Pancreas**.
* The 1st part is the only mobile segment.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Describe how the gallbladder mucosa carries out its function of bile concentration.
back:
• Microvilli increase surface area
• Actively absorbs water and electrolytes
• Thrown into honeycombed permanent folds
• Selectively absorbs bile salts to keep bile acidic.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Contrast the anatomical consequences of a gallstone ulcerating into the duodenum versus one causing a complete obstruction of the cystic duct.
back: Duodenal ulceration can lead to gallstone ileus, where a stone obstructs the ileocecal junction. Cystic duct obstruction typically causes biliary colic and distension of the gallbladder, potentially leading to acute cholecystitis or mucocele.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the upper part of the greater curvature with that of its lower part.
back:
Upper: Drains to short gastric and left gastroepiploic nodes, then to splenic nodes.
Lower: Drains to right gastroepiploic nodes, then to subpyloric/hepatic nodes.
Both: Terminate in celiac nodes.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
front: Explain the anatomical watershed principle that determines the direction of superficial lymphatic drainage in the anterolateral abdominal wall.
back:
*   The umbilicus serves as the primary watershed line
*   Lymph above the umbilicus drains to axillary (pectoral) nodes
*   Lymph below the umbilicus drains to superficial inguinal nodes

category: Locate the position of superficial and deep inguinal rings on simulated subject or Cadaver
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Deep Inguinal Ring
front: The deep inguinal ring is located approximately 0.5 inches superior to the inguinal ligament at the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the [___].
back: * Symphysis pubis. * Per clinical source text, this midinguinal point marks the deep ring site. * It is an oval opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: During a surgical repair of a cleft palate, a surgeon identifies a transverse suture line separating the anterior 2/3 from the posterior 1/3 of the bony roof. Identify the bones meeting here.
back:
• Palatine processes of maxillae (Anteriorly).
• Horizontal plates of palatine bones (Posteriorly).
• Junction site is the transverse palatine suture.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
front: A 65-year-old female presents with a painful, irreducible lump in the groin located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Femoral Hernia. • Protrudes through the femoral canal. • Higher risk of strangulation due to its narrow neck. • More common in females due to a wider pelvis.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: List the three critical structures contained within the free margin of the lesser omentum.
back:
• Hepatic artery proper (left)
• Common bile duct (right)
• Portal vein (posterior)
• Together they form the portal triad at the porta hepatis

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 3-week-old male infant presents with projectile, non-bile-stained vomiting and an olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium. Identify the hypertrophied anatomical structure.
back:
• Pyloric Sphincter
• Hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer
• Causes mechanical gastric outlet obstruction (Pyloric Stenosis)

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Explain the primary anatomical mechanism that holds the liver in position within the upper abdominal cavity.
back: * Attachment of the hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava (IVC). * Intra-abdominal pressure and abdominal muscle tone. * Peritoneal ligaments play only a minor supportive role.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Identify the two primary arteries that form an anastomosis along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
back:
* Left gastric artery (branch of celiac artery).
* Right gastric artery (branch of hepatic artery).
* These vessels run within the lesser omentum to supply the right and left aspects of the curvature.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Distinguish between the mucosal appearance of the first part of the duodenum and the second part during endoscopy or dissection.
back:
First Part (Duodenal Cap): Smooth mucosa, lacking plicae circulares.
- Second Part: Characterized by circular folds and the Major Duodenal Papilla.
- Smoothness in the first part facilitates rapid passage of acidic chyme.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Describe how the vertical reflection of the falciform ligament partitions the subphrenic space.
back:
* Extends vertically from the anterior abdominal wall to the liver
* Contains the ligamentum teres in its free edge
* Divides the subphrenic space into right and left anterior compartments.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Explain the anatomical relationship that leads to life-threatening hemorrhage from a posterior duodenal ulcer.
back:
• Structure involved: Gastroduodenal artery
• Relationship: Runs directly posterior to the first part of the duodenum
• Clinical result: Erosion of the arterial wall causes massive hematemesis or melena.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: A surgeon uses a double-layered peritoneal fold to "plug" a perforated gastric ulcer and localize infection. Identify this mobile structure known as the "abdominal policeman."
back:
• Greater Omentum.
• Connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon.
• Highly mobile; adheres to inflamed areas to seal off and localize intraperitoneal infections.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The palatine aponeurosis, which forms the structural framework of the soft palate, is the expanded tendon of the [___] muscle.
back:
• Tensor veli palatini.
• It tenses the palate to allow elevation.
• It is uniquely innervated by the Nerve to Medial Pterygoid (Mandibular Nerve/V3).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The esophagus begins at the lower border of the [___] cartilage, which corresponds to the vertebral level of C6.
back:
• Cricoid cartilage
• Marks the junction with the pharynx
• Approximately 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: The portal vein, which drains most of the GIT, is formed by the junction of the [___] and the [___] behind the neck of the pancreas.
back: * Splenic vein * Superior mesenteric vein (SMV) * Collects nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood for processing by the liver

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A 55-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with abdominal distension and 'shifting dullness.' Explain the anatomical basis for this percussion finding.
back: ● Intraperitoneal fluid moves to dependent regions due to gravity. ● Air-filled bowel loops float to the top. ● Changing patient position shifts the fluid level relative to the abdominal wall.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Explain the neuroanatomical defect responsible for the failure of the gastroesophageal sphincter to relax in Achalasia.
back:
- Degeneration of Auerbach’s (myenteric) plexus
- Loss of inhibitory ganglionic cells in the esophageal wall
- Persistent tonic contraction of the physiologic sphincter
- Results in proximal esophageal dilatation

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Explain the venous mechanism leading to internal hemorrhoids during portal hypertension in terms of vascular drainage.
back:
• Superior rectal vein (portal) experiences retrograde flow
• Blood shunts to middle/inferior rectal veins (systemic)
• Systemic path involves internal iliac/pudendal veins
• Results in dilation of the submucosal anorectal plexus

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: In the presence of infection, the [___] acts as the 'abdominal policeman' by adhering to inflamed viscera and sealing off the focus of peritonitis.
back: • Greater omentum. • Moves via peristaltic activity. • Uses fibrin deposition to adhere. • Localizes infection to prevent generalized peritonitis.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Explain the role of the Plicae Circulares (Valvules of Kerckring) in small intestine physiology.
back:
* Permanent mucosal folds that do not flatten with distension.
* Increase surface area for nutrient absorption.
* Most numerous and closely set in the jejunum; absent in the distal ileum.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Explain the role of visceral afferent nerves in the sensation of pain from the visceral peritoneum.
back:
• Respond only to stretch and tearing, not touch or temperature.
• Travel with sympathetic fibers to the central nervous system.
• Mediate dull, poorly localized midline pain.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Identify the specific anatomical points where mucosal herniation typically occurs in colonic diverticulosis.
back:
* Occurs between the teniae coli.
* Sites where nutrient arteries (vasa recta) pierce the circular muscle layer.
* Most commonly affects the sigmoid colon due to high intraluminal pressure.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the specific artery supplying the vermiform appendix and name its immediate parent vessel as seen within the mesoappendix.
back: * Appendicular artery. * Branch of the ileocolic artery (or its posterior cecal branch). * It is a functional end artery; occlusion leads to gangrenous appendicitis.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: The thick, longitudinal mucosal folds that increase surface area and allow the stomach to expand are known as [___].
back: ● Rugae. ● Flatten out when the stomach is distended with food. ● Prominent in the body and antrum.

category: Mark the abdominal incisions on simulated patient/ subject and explain their anatomical basis
front: Explain the anatomical sequence of muscular and fascial layers encountered during a McBurney's incision before entering the peritoneal cavity.
back: * Skin and superficial fascia. * External oblique aponeurosis. * Internal oblique and Transversus abdominis. * Transversalis fascia and Extraperitoneal fat. * Parietal peritoneum.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: The [___] nodes are located along the inferior aspect of the greater curvature and receive lymph from the lower part of the gastric body.
back:
* Right gastro-omental nodes.
* Also known as right gastroepiploic nodes.
* Lymph follows the right gastro-omental artery.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
coreConcept: Anatomy of Hiatus Hernia in GERD
front: Describe how a hiatus hernia serves as an anatomical basis for the development of severe GERD symptoms.
back:
• Protrusion of stomach through the esophageal hiatus
• Loss of the diaphragmatic 'pinch-cock' extrinsic sphincter mechanism
• Disruption of the normal acute Angle of His between esophagus and stomach

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Contrast the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) dynamics in achalasia versus gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
back:
- Achalasia: Failure of the LES to relax due to myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus degeneration.
- GERD: Hypotonic or incompetent LES allowing retrograde acid flow into the esophagus.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Identify the primary artery supplying the gallbladder and specify the vessel from which it most commonly originates.
back:
• Cystic artery.
• Usually arises from the right hepatic artery.
• Located within the cystohepatic triangle (of Calot).

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Visceral afferent fibers concerned with peritoneal pain sensation from abdominal organs typically travel alongside [___] nerves to reach the spinal cord.
back:
- Sympathetic nerves.
- Enter the cord via posterior roots.
- Overdistension of the organ triggers pain through these pathways.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: The somatic pain associated with parietal peritonitis is precisely localized to the site of irritation because the peritoneum is innervated by the [___] nerves.
back:
• Lower six thoracic nerves (T7–T11)
• Subcostal nerve (T12)
• First lumbar nerve (L1)
These somatic nerves provide high-fidelity sensory input compared to visceral afferents.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Describe the anatomical path taken by bile from the liver to the duodenum when the gallbladder is absent or removed.
back:
• Bile flows through right/left hepatic ducts to the common hepatic duct
  • Passes directly into the common bile duct
  • Enters the second part of the duodenum via the major duodenal papilla

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
front: The inguinal ligament is formed by the thickened, lower border of the [___] aponeurosis, which is folded backward on itself between two bony points.
back: - Derived from the external oblique muscle aponeurosis - Functions as a biological retinaculum for the groin - Spans the gap from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
front: A patient with rapid weight loss presents with postprandial vomiting and epigastric pain. Imaging reveals the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the aorta and the [___] artery.
back: * Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) * Causes 'SMA Syndrome' by reducing the aortomesenteric angle * Specifically affects the transverse (third) part of the duodenum

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient requires an extraction of the upper central incisors. To anesthetize the palatal mucosa behind these teeth, the dentist must target the [___] nerve as it emerges from the incisive foramen.
back:
• Nasopalatine nerve.
• Branch of the maxillary nerve (V2).
• Supplies the mucosa of the anterior hard palate.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Identify the two specific segments of the gastrointestinal tract that form the posterior relations of the gallbladder's body.
back: * Transverse colon. * First and second parts of the duodenum. * Clinical note: Sites for gallstone ulceration or fistulae.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: A 65-year-old male presents with obstructive jaundice and a palpable gallbladder. Imaging reveals a tumor in the head of the pancreas. Identify the specific segment of the biliary tree most likely compressed.
back:
• Distal (Infraduodenal) bile duct
• Location: Situated in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head
• Clinical: Causes backup of bile and jaundice

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Contrast the motor innervation of the tongue muscles with the palatoglossus muscle regarding their cranial nerve origins.
back:
• Tongue Muscles: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
• Palatoglossus: Pharyngeal plexus (Vagus nerve, CN X)
• This is the only tongue muscle not supplied by CN XII.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Biliary Tree
front: In cases of acute cholecystitis, the fundus of the gallbladder is found at the intersection of the [___] and the ninth right costal cartilage.
back: • Linea semilunaris (lateral edge of rectus abdominis) • Corresponds to the clinical site for Murphy's sign • Anatomical landmark for the gallbladder fundus

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Describe the physiological role of the hormone Gastrin in the management of the gastroesophageal junction's tone.
back:
Increases LES pressure.
* Action: Stimulates contraction of the esophageal circular muscle.
* Benefit: Helps maintain the barrier against gastric acid reflux.
* Contrast: Secretin and CCK generally decrease LES tone.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
front: Explain how the 'folded-back' extent of the inguinal ligament facilitates the creation of the retro-inguinal space for neurovascular structures.
back: - Creates a bridge between the ilium and the pubis - Forms the superior boundary of the space - Allows the femoral nerve, artery, and vein to exit the abdomen

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Identify the parent vessel of the sigmoid arteries, which supply the descending and sigmoid colon via the mesocolon.
back:
Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA).
• Primary artery of the hindgut.
• Also gives rise to the left colic and superior rectal arteries.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Specify the termination site of the common bile duct and the anatomical structure it forms upon joining the main pancreatic duct.
back:
• Termination: Medial wall of the second part of the duodenum
  • Structure: Hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
  • Surface landmark: Major duodenal papilla

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: The anatomic and physiologic sphincter situated on the transpyloric plane that controls the outflow of gastric contents into the duodenum is the [___].
back:
Pyloric sphincter:
- Formed by a thickened circular muscle coat.
- Situated at the level of the transpyloric plane (L1).
- Acts as a valve controlling the rate of chyme delivery into the second part of the duodenum.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the thoracic esophagus with that of the abdominal esophagus.
back: • Thoracic: Drains into posterior mediastinal lymph nodes. • Abdominal: Drains into left gastric and celiac lymph nodes. • Critical for determining the spread of esophageal malignancies.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: An elderly male presents with ischemic colitis of the sigmoid colon. On a cadaver, the arterial trunk supplying this region arises from the aorta at the [___] level.
back: * L3 vertebra level. * Identified as the Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA). * Supplies the hindgut, including the descending colon, sigmoid, and upper rectum.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: Explain the anatomical basis for the sacculated appearance (haustrations) of the colon compared to the smooth surface of the small intestine.
back: * Caused by the teniae coli being shorter than the actual length of the colon. * This discrepancy causes the circular muscle to bunch up into saccules. * Haustra are absent in the rectum.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Explain the role of the soft palate and Passavant’s ridge in preventing food from entering the nasopharynx during swallowing.
back: The levator veli palatini elevates the palate while the tensor veli palatini tenses it. This approximates the posterior pharyngeal wall (Passavant’s ridge), sealing the pharyngeal isthmus and directing the bolus downward.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
