front: A surgeon performing a cholecystectomy identifies a structure in the right free margin of the lesser omentum, anterior to the epiploic foramen. Identify this duct and its immediate posterior relation.
back:
• Bile duct (Common bile duct)
  • Immediate posterior relation: Portal vein
  • Medial relation: Hepatic artery
  • Forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow)

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: The [___] tonsil is situated in the midline of the roof and the upper part of the posterior wall of the nasopharynx.
back: * Pharyngeal (or Nasopharyngeal) tonsil. * Commonly referred to as adenoids when pathologically enlarged.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
coreConcept: Nerve supply and action of Rectus Abdominis
front: The rectus abdominis muscle, which is characterized by three transverse tendinous intersections and forms the 'six-pack' appearance, is innervated by the [___].
back: • Anterior rami of lower six thoracic nerves (T7 to T12). • Action: Flexes the trunk and stabilizes the pelvis. • Compresses abdominal viscera to assist in forced expiration, defecation, and micturition.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Explain the surface anatomical boundaries used to identify the base of the appendix at McBurney's point.
back:
• Located at the junction of the lateral and middle thirds
• Along a line drawn from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Explain the role of Cholecystokinin (CCK) in the biological mechanism of gallbladder emptying after a fatty meal.
back: Fatty acids in the duodenum trigger CCK release from the mucosa. CCK enters the bloodstream, causing the gallbladder's muscular wall to contract while simultaneously relaxing the hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi) to release bile.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Explain the role of the Sphincter of Oddi (hepatopancreatic sphincter) during the inter-digestive state.
back:
• Maintains tonic contraction during fasting
  • Prevents bile entry into the duodenum
  • Causes bile to back up into the cystic duct for storage and concentration in the gallbladder

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids and regurgitation of undigested food. Barium swallow demonstrates a 'bird-beak' tapering at the lower esophagus. Identify the primary neuroanatomical defect.
back:
• Achalasia of the cardia
• Degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus
• Leads to failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Explain the role of the obturator nerve in the sensory supply of the peritoneum.
back:
- Provides sensory innervation to the parietal peritoneum in the pelvis.
- Irritation of pelvic peritoneum (e.g., pelvic appendix) is detected via rectal or vaginal exam.
- Originates from L2-L4 lumbar plexus.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Explain the anatomical pathway of venous blood from the small intestine until it enters the systemic circulation via the inferior vena cava.
back: - Drains into the Superior Mesenteric Vein. - Joins Splenic Vein behind pancreatic neck to form Portal Vein. - Enters liver sinusoids. - Hepatic Veins empty into the Inferior Vena Cava.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Contrast the anatomical drainage sites of the Major Duodenal Papilla and the Minor Duodenal Papilla.
back:
* Major Papilla: Receives Bile duct and Main Pancreatic duct (Ampulla of Vater) in the 2nd part.
* Minor Papilla: Receives Accessory Pancreatic duct (Santorini), located 2cm superior to the major papilla.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: Explain the role of the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems in regulating the pyloric sphincter.
back: ● Sympathetic: Motor (causes contraction). ● Parasympathetic (Vagus): Inhibitory (causes relaxation). ● Regulates gastric emptying into the duodenum.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: The fundus of the gallbladder typically makes contact with the anterior abdominal wall at the level of the [___] costal cartilage, where the lateral border of the rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.
back:
9th costal cartilage.

*   Identified as the intersection of the linea semilunaris and the costal margin.
*   Standard clinical landmark for gallbladder palpation.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: A surgeon is performing a midline laparotomy. List the specific fascial and tissue layers traversed between the skin and the parietal peritoneum in the exact midline.
back:
• Skin and superficial fascia (Camper’s and Scarpa’s).
• Thin deep fascia.
• Fibrous Linea alba.
• Transversalis fascia.
• Extraperitoneal fat.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: The surface projection of the base of the appendix is known as [___] point, located one-third of the way along a line from the ASIS to the umbilicus.
back:
* McBurney's Point.
* Corresponds to the attachment of the appendix to the cecum.
* Primary site of tenderness in classic appendicitis.
* Found in the right lower quadrant.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Anatomic Site of Portal Vein Formation
front: The hepatic portal vein is anatomically formed by the union of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein behind the [___] of the pancreas.
back:
• Neck of the pancreas
• Occurs at the level of the L2 vertebra
• Forms the primary channel of the portal venous system

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Explain the anatomical mechanism by which the gastroesophageal junction prevents the regurgitation of gastric contents.
back: • Physiological gastroesophageal sphincter. • Tonic contraction of circular smooth muscle. • Vagal control (augmented by gastrin). • External support from the right crus of the diaphragm.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Inguinal Ligament and Fascia Lata Relationship
front: The [___] of the thigh is firmly attached to the inferior rounded border of the inguinal ligament, influencing its characteristic anatomical curve.
back: - Fascia lata (deep fascia of the thigh) - Tension in this fascia maintains the ligament's downward convex shape - Defines the anatomical transition between the abdomen and lower limb

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: Distinguish the attachments and contents of the Mesentery of the Small Intestine from the Transverse Mesocolon.
back:
• Mesentery: Connects jejunum/ileum to posterior wall; carries superior mesenteric vessels
• Transverse Mesocolon: Connects transverse colon to pancreas; carries middle colic vessels
• Both are double-layered peritoneal folds

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Posterior Relations and Vascular Complications of the Stomach
front: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic gastric ulcers presents with sudden onset of severe back pain. Erosion of a posterior gastric ulcer into the lesser sac is suspected. Which major artery running along the superior border of the pancreas is most likely involved?
back:
Splenic artery.
- Runs horizontally along the upper pancreatic border.
- Forms part of the stomach bed.
- Erosion leads to massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage into the lesser sac.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: The arterial supply of the head of the pancreas is derived from the [___] and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, representing a high-yield anastomosis between the celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery.
back:
Superior pancreaticoduodenal.

* Branch of the gastroduodenal artery (from celiac trunk).
* Inferior branch originates from the superior mesenteric artery.
* Together they supply the head and the second part of the duodenum.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of injury to hypoglossal nerve
front: Specify the anatomical landmark where the hypoglossal nerve turns forward to enter the carotid triangle, looping around a specific vessel.
back:
• Occipital artery
• The nerve hooks around the artery's origin
• It then crosses the internal and external carotid arteries superficially.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The blind-ended pouch of the large intestine situated in the right iliac fossa, which typically lacks a mesentery but remains mobile, is the [___].
back:
Cecum
- Located below the ileocecal junction.
- Completely covered by peritoneum.
- Often distended with gas, making it palpable in the right iliac fossa.

category: Describe the structure of tongue with attachments of muscles, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A patient with a history of a deep submandibular abscess presents with a tongue that deviates to the left side when protruded. This indicates an injury to the [___] [___] nerve.
back:
* Left Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
* Pathophysiology: Unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus muscle.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A 45-year-old male presents with deviation of the tongue to the right side upon protrusion. Identify the nerve injured and the muscle primarily responsible for this action.
back:
* Right Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
* Genioglossus muscle
* Tongue deviates toward the side of the paralyzed muscle

category: Differentiate between direct and indirect inguinal hernias
front: Explain the role of the conjoint tendon in reinforcing the inguinal canal against the formation of direct inguinal hernias.
back:
• Formed by internal oblique and transversus abdominis
• Strengthens the posterior wall of the canal
• Lies directly behind the superficial inguinal ring
• Resists protrusion through Hesselbach’s triangle

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
front: The entire length of the anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the [___].
back:
* External oblique aponeurosis
* Supported laterally by origin of internal oblique
* Strongest opposite the deep inguinal ring

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Contrast the right and left anterior subphrenic spaces in terms of their anatomical boundaries relative to the falciform ligament.
back: * Right Anterior: Between diaphragm and right lobe of liver. * Left Anterior: Between diaphragm and left lobe of liver. * Separated by the falciform ligament attachment to the diaphragm.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish between the sensory distribution of the nasopalatine and greater palatine nerves on the hard palate.
back:
• Nasopalatine: Supplies the anterior portion (premaxilla area) behind the incisors.
• Greater Palatine: Supplies the posterior majority of the hard palate mucosa up to the gingiva.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The continuous arterial channel formed by anastomoses between the SMA and IMA along the mesenteric border of the colon is the [___].
back:
• Marginal Artery (of Drummond)
• Formed by ileocolic, right, middle, and left colic arteries
• Vital for collateral circulation in bowel ischemia

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Detail the primary arterial supply and the significant venous relation encountered during the surgical removal of the palatine tonsils.
back: * Artery: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (primary). * Vein: External palatine vein (descends from the soft palate lateral to the tonsillar capsule).

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Contrast the lymphatic drainage of the lesser curvature with that of the pyloric region of the stomach.
back: • Lesser Curvature: Drains via left and right gastric nodes to celiac nodes. • Pyloric Region: Drains to subpyloric and hepatic nodes, then to celiac nodes. • Both follow their respective arterial supplies.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
front: A 30-year-old male presents with a ruptured penile urethra and scrotal swelling. Urine is tracking up the anterior abdominal wall but is notably absent from his thighs. This anatomical restriction occurs because [___] is firmly attached to the fascia lata.
back:
• Scarpa's fascia (Membranous layer)
• Attachment to fascia lata prevents fluid from entering the thigh compartment
• Creates a potential space continuous with the superficial perineal pouch
• Results in extravasation of urine between the fascia and muscle layers

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: Distinguish between the anatomical characteristics of a 'steer-horn' stomach and a 'J-shaped' stomach.
back: * Steer-horn: High and transverse; common in short, obese individuals. * J-shaped: Vertical and elongated; common in tall, thin individuals.

category: Discuss the skeletal framework of hard palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The lymphatic drainage from the hard palate primarily terminates in the [___] lymph nodes.
back: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: A patient with cirrhosis presents with a patent Paraumbilical vein. Identify the specific branch of the portal vein from which this vessel originates and its drainage destination.
back:
• Origin: Left branch of the portal vein
• Destination: Superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall
• Clinical Sign: Caput medusae

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Explain the role of the coronary ligaments in creating the vertical 'bare area' of the liver.
back:
* Peritoneum reflects vertically from the diaphragm to the liver
* Superior and inferior layers are widely separated
* This area lacks a visceral peritoneal covering
* It is in direct contact with the diaphragm.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: A patient with a perforated gastric ulcer on the posterior wall presents with fluid accumulation in a space behind the stomach. Identify this space and its anterior boundary.
back:
• Lesser sac (Omental bursa)
• Anterior boundary: Stomach and lesser omentum
• Posterior boundary: Pancreas and left kidney
• Allows for unhindered stomach expansion during digestion

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: In the clinical diagnosis of appendicitis, the anatomical landmark situated one-third of the way up the line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus is [___].
back:
* McBurney's Point
* Corresponds to the base of the appendix
* Site of maximal tenderness in acute inflammation
* Convergence point for the teniae coli on the cecum.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: List the three anatomical constrictions of the esophagus and their respective distances from the upper incisor teeth.
back:
• Pharyngoesophageal (Cricopharyngeal): 15 cm
• Aortobronchial (Arch of aorta/Left bronchus): 25 cm
• Diaphragmatic (Hiatal): 40 cm.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: The large, apron-like fold of peritoneum that reflects from the greater curvature of the stomach and covers the loops of the small intestine is the [___].
back: * Greater omentum. * It reflects back to attach to the transverse colon. * Known as the "abdominal policeman" for its role in localizing infections.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Explain the role of the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) in gastrointestinal stability.
back:
*   Function: Maintains the position of the duodenojejunal flexure
*   Attachment: Connects the fourth part of the duodenum to the right crus of the diaphragm
*   Composition: Contains both skeletal and smooth muscle fibers

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: Specify the clinical significance of the "bare area" of the liver regarding the spread of infection.
back: * Area devoid of peritoneum in direct contact with the diaphragm. * Situated between the layers of the coronary ligament. * Potential route for infection to spread from the abdomen to the thorax.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Describe the portosystemic communication that occurs at the 'bare area' of the liver.
back:
Hepatic/portal tributaries and Phrenic veins.
* Occurs where liver lacks peritoneum.
* Systemic component: Diaphragmatic/Phrenic veins.
* Phrenic veins drain into the IVC.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Specify the three anatomical divisions of the gallbladder and the extent of their peritoneal covering.
back:
• Fundus: Completely surrounded by peritoneum.
• Body and Neck: Bound to the visceral surface of the liver by peritoneum.
• The neck is continuous with the cystic duct.

category: Identify the blood vessels supplying GIT on anatomical model and cadaver
front: A 60-year-old patient presents with acute ischemia of the foregut. On a vascular model, which major celiac branch—noted for its tortuous course along the superior pancreatic border—is most likely impacted?
back:
Splenic Artery.
• Largest branch of the celiac trunk.
• Provides short gastric and left gastro-omental branches.
• Runs in the splenorenal ligament to reach the splenic hilum.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of oral cavity with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Differentiate the primary lymphatic drainage sites for the tip of the tongue versus the posterior third.
back:
• Tip: Submental lymph nodes
• Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes
• Lateral sides drain to submandibular nodes first
• Vital for staging oral malignancies

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: In surgical oncology, the [___] omentum must be removed during radical gastrectomy because it contains the nodes draining the inferior portion of the stomach.
back: Greater omentum. • Houses the right gastro-omental lymph nodes. • Essential for oncological clearance of the inferior stomach territory. • Prevents recurrence by removing primary metastatic pathways.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Inguinal Ligament
front: A mass is palpated halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. This location corresponds to the [___].
back: - Midpoint of the inguinal ligament - Located superior to the femoral artery - Anatomical landmark for identifying the internal (deep) inguinal ring position

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
front: Identify the anatomical landmarks used to define the levels for the T7, T10, and L1 dermatomes.
back:
- T7: Epigastrium at the xiphoid process level.
- T10: Level of the umbilicus.
- L1: Just superior to the inguinal ligament and symphysis pubis.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Describe the lymphatic pathway from the gallbladder to the celiac nodes.
back:
● Cystic lymph node (near gallbladder neck)
● Hepatic nodes (along hepatic artery)
● Celiac lymph nodes (final pre-aortic destination)

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: A surgeon identifies a segment of the large intestine. Contrast the peritoneal attachment of the transverse colon with that of the ascending colon.
back:
• Transverse colon: Intraperitoneal; suspended by the transverse mesocolon
• Ascending colon: Secondarily retroperitoneal; fixed to the posterior wall
• Only anterior and lateral surfaces of the ascending colon are covered.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Describe the mechanism of lymphatic spread to the liver in advanced gastric carcinoma.
back:
- Follows retrograde flow if celiac nodes are obstructed.
- Communication exists between gastric lymphatics and hepatic nodes in the porta hepatis.
- Spread travels via the hepatic artery's lymphatic plexus.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: A child presents with a translucent, bluish, fluctuant swelling in the floor of the mouth. What is the most likely diagnosis associated with sublingual gland duct blockage?
back:
Ranula.
- A mucus extravasation cyst in the floor of mouth.
- Caused by trauma or obstruction of sublingual ducts (Bartholin or Rivinus).
- May plunge below mylohyoid (Plunging Ranula).

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Analyze why the common hepatic duct is at significant risk of accidental ligation or injury during a cholecystectomy.
back:
* Anatomical variations in the cystic artery and duct are extremely common.
* A congenitally short or absent cystic duct may cause confusion.
* The common hepatic duct may be mistaken for the cystic duct.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: How does the subcecal position of the appendix differ from the pelvic position in terms of its relation to the pelvic brim?
back:
Subcecal vs. Pelvic.
- Subcecal: Tip stays in the Right Iliac Fossa, below the cecum.
- Pelvic: Tip crosses the pelvic brim to enter the true pelvis.
- Subcecal is often extraperitoneal.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: The deep peritoneal recess located between the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney is the [___].
back:
• Hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch).
• Lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in a supine patient.
• Frequent site for collection of infected fluid/abscesses.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: A 22-year-old male presents with fever, bilateral pre-auricular swelling, and subsequent testicular tenderness. Identify the diagnosis and its primary reproductive complication.
back:
- Mumps (Viral Parotiditis).
- Caused by Paramyxovirus.
- Complication: Orchitis.
- Risk: Permanent infertility/sterility due to germ cell destruction.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Name the venous structures that typically drain blood from the gallbladder into the portal system.
back:
• Cystic veins
• May drain directly into the liver or the portal vein

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Distinguish between the second and third anatomical constrictions of the esophagus by the structures causing them.
back: 1. Second Constriction: Crossing of the Arch of Aorta and Left Main Bronchus (T4/T5). 2. Third Constriction: Esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm (T10).

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
front: Distinguish between the pre-ileal and post-ileal positions of the vermiform appendix based on their relation to the small intestine.
back:
* Pre-ileal: Appendix situated anterior to the terminal ileum
* Post-ileal: Appendix situated posterior to the terminal ileum
* Both represent rare variations compared to the retrocecal variant

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
coreConcept: Origin of the Inferior Mesenteric Artery
front: The inferior mesenteric artery, supplying the hindgut derivatives, typically originates from the abdominal aorta at the level of the [___] lumbar vertebra.
back:
Third (L3). 
- Arises about 1.5 inches above the aortic bifurcation. 
- Supplies the distal transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Describe the mechanical process and primary anatomical risk associated with ileocolic intussusception in children.
back:
• Process: Telescoping of the ileum (intussusceptum) into the cecum (intussuscipiens)
• Mechanism: Triggered by violent peristalsis, often involving enlarged Peyer patches
• Risk: Compression of mesenteric vessels leading to ischemia and gangrene.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A 55-year-old male with a history of dyspepsia presents with sudden, severe back pain. Imaging reveals fluid collection in the lesser sac. Which posterior structure is most likely affected by this penetrating gastric ulcer?
back:
• Pancreas
• Stomach posterior wall forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac
• Erosion into the pancreas produces pain referred to the back
• Risk of splenic artery hemorrhage.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: Explain the mechanical role of the diaphragm in the movement of infected peritoneal fluid toward the subphrenic spaces.
back:
• Diaphragmatic contractions create negative pressure in the upper abdomen.
• Respiratory excursions act as a 'pump' for peritoneal fluid.
• Fluid and particulate matter are directed toward the subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries for absorption.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: During a radical gastrectomy for pyloric antrum cancer, the surgeon identifies nodes along the right gastro-omental artery. These are classified as [___] nodes.
back:
Right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) nodes.
- They drain the lower part of the greater curvature.
- They relay lymph to the subpyloric nodes.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
front: The dome-shaped portion of the stomach that projects superiorly and to the left of the cardiac orifice is the [___].
back: ● Fundus. ● Usually contains the gas bubble on radiographs. ● Lacks acid-producing cells in some species, but in humans contains gastric glands.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Identify the specific structures related posteriorly to the second part (descending) of the duodenum.
back:
* Hilum of the right kidney.
* Right ureter.
* Right psoas major muscle.
* Bile duct and main pancreatic duct (medially).

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Detail the anatomical rationale for performing a 'Surgical Portacaval Shunt' in a patient with intractable portal hypertension.
back:
• Reduces portal pressure by bypassing the liver
• Anastomoses the portal vein with the inferior vena cava (IVC)
• Diverts blood into the systemic circulation

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: The fundus of the gallbladder is situated at the point where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis muscle crosses the costal margin, specifically at the level of the [___] costal cartilage.
back:
* Ninth (9th) costal cartilage
* Corresponds to the transpyloric plane level
* Located at the tip of the 9th rib
* Landmark for the Murphy’s sign examination

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of anterior abdominal wall
front: Name the specific nerve that innervates the pyramidalis muscle and describe its anatomical role.
back: - Nerve: 12th thoracic (subcostal) nerve. - Role: Tenses the linea alba during muscle contraction. - Location: Small triangular muscle in the lower rectus sheath anterior to the rectus abdominis.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: To perform an effective field block of the nerves supplying the rectus sheath, identify the anatomical level where anesthetic should be infiltrated.
back:
• Lower border of the costal margin
• Targets nerves T7 through T11 as they emerge toward the sheath.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
front: Describe how the internal oblique aponeurosis contributes to the rectus sheath between the costal margin and the arcuate line.
back:
• It splits into anterior and posterior laminae
• Anterior lamina fuses with the external oblique aponeurosis
• Posterior lamina fuses with the transversus abdominis aponeurosis

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Identify the distinct gross anatomical features used to differentiate the large intestine from the small intestine during abdominal surgery.
back:
* Teniae coli (three longitudinal muscle bands)
* Appendices epiploicae (fatty tags)
* Haustra (sacculations of the wall)
* Relative fixity (ascending and descending parts are retroperitoneal).

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A 5-year-old presents with nasal regurgitation of fluids and hypernasal speech. Examination reveals the soft palate fails to elevate on the right. This indicates a lesion in the [___].
back:
• Pharyngeal plexus (Vagus nerve/CN X).
• Specifically the cranial root of the Accessory nerve via Vagus.
• Leads to failure of the pharyngeal isthmus to close during swallowing.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Contrast the Tensor Veli Palatini and Levator Veli Palatini regarding their anatomical relationship with the auditory (Eustachian) tube.
back: Tensor veli palatini: Originates from the scaphoid fossa and auditory tube; its contraction opens the tube. Levator veli palatini: Originates from the petrous temporal bone and auditory tube; it primarily elevates the palate.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the diaphragmatic opening and the specific vertebral level where the esophagus enters the abdominal cavity.
back:
• Esophageal hiatus.
• Located in the right crus of the diaphragm.
• Occurs at the T10 vertebral level.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Identify the specific arteries providing the segmental blood supply to the cervical, thoracic, and abdominal esophagus.
back: 1. Cervical: Inferior thyroid artery. 2. Thoracic: Esophageal branches of aorta. 3. Abdominal: Left gastric and left inferior phrenic arteries.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
front: Detail the sequence of lymphatic drainage from the pancreatic body to the thoracic duct.
back:
* Drainage into pancreaticosplenic nodes along the splenic artery.
* Efferent vessels pass to the celiac and superior mesenteric lymph nodes.
* Lymph enters the cisterna chyli via the intestinal trunk.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
front: A 55-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with a severely distended abdomen and positive shifting dullness. Explain the anatomical basis for this clinical finding.
back:
• Portal hypertension increases capillary hydrostatic pressure.
• Excessive serous fluid (ascites) leaks into the peritoneal cavity.
• Fluid accumulates in dependent areas like the pelvic cavity or Morison's pouch.

category: Describe the fascia of anterior abdominal wall with its clinical significance
coreConcept: Extravasation of Urine and Fascial Attachments
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a ruptured penile urethra. Examination shows urine collection in the scrotum and lower abdomen, but not the thighs. This limitation is due to the attachment of Scarpa's fascia to [___].
back:
• Fascia lata of the thigh.
• Attachment occurs one fingerbreadth below the inguinal ligament.
• This fusion prevents extravasated urine from descending into the lower limbs.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: Distinctive aggregations of lymphoid follicles located predominantly on the antimesenteric border of the ileum are known as [___].
back:
• Peyer’s patches
• Found in the lamina propria and submucosa
• Most numerous in the distal ileum
• Important for gut mucosal immunity

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Identify the most likely artery eroded in this scenario.
back:
* Gastroduodenal artery.
* It descends directly behind the first part of the duodenum.
* Erosion causes life-threatening hemorrhage due to its proximity and size.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Name the three specific anatomical structures that the esophagus is related to posteriorly as it descends through the neck.
back:
• Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
• Longus colli muscles.
• Vertebral column (C6 to T1).

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A 35-year-old female complains of retrosternal burning and acid regurgitation, especially after heavy meals. Which anatomical landmark separates the esophagus from the stomach and serves as the primary barrier in this condition?
back:
Gastroesophageal junction (Z-line).
* Primary barrier: Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES).
* Pathogenesis: Transient LES relaxations or low resting pressure.
* Condition: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
front: During a cholecystectomy, fluid is found in the right subhepatic space. Name this space and identify its clinical significance regarding fluid accumulation in the supine position.
back:
• Morison’s pouch (Hepatorenal recess)
• Lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in supine patients
• Common site for abscess or blood collection post-trauma.

category: List the structures and coverings of spermatic cord
front: Identify the anatomical point where the spermatic cord officially begins and state its relationship to the inguinal ligament.
back:
• Deep Inguinal Ring
• Location: Halfway between the ASIS and symphysis pubis, ~0.5 inch above the inguinal ligament.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: A patient with a subphrenic abscess complains of sharp pain referred to the right shoulder. Explain the neuroanatomical basis for this presentation.
back: * Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the central diaphragmatic peritoneum. * Supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) supply the shoulder skin. * Both share common spinal cord segments.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Distinguish the drainage points of the left and right gastric veins from those of the short gastric veins.
back:
• Left/Right Gastric: Drain directly into the portal vein
• Short Gastric: Drain into the splenic vein

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Early appendicitis pain is felt in the umbilical region, but late appendicitis is felt in the right iliac fossa. Apply your knowledge of peritoneal innervation to explain this shift.
back:
• Early: Visceral afferents (T10) detect stretch in appendix/visceral peritoneum.
• Late: Somatic nerves detect inflammation of the parietal peritoneum.
• Somatic pain is precise and localized to McBurney’s point.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: Identify the two major vessels typically anastomosed in a surgical 'Portacaval shunt' to decompress the portal system.
back:
• Portal vein (at the epiploic foramen)
• Inferior vena cava
• Goal: Direct diversion of high-pressure portal blood to systemic circulation.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Describe how respiratory movements of the diaphragm facilitate the flow and absorption of peritoneal fluid toward the lymphatic system.
back:
• Diaphragmatic movements create pressure gradients moving fluid toward subphrenic spaces.
• Fluid is rapidly absorbed by subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries.
• Absorption is most efficient in the diaphragmatic region.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
front: Explain the role of the 'shutter mechanism' involving the internal oblique and transversus abdominis during increased intra-abdominal pressure.
back: * Arched lower fibers contract and flatten. * This compresses the canal contents against the floor. * Effectively closes the inguinal canal to prevent herniation during straining.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe the anatomical relationships of the esophagus within the neck (cervical portion).
back: • Anterior: Trachea and recurrent laryngeal nerves. • Posterior: Prevertebral fascia and longus colli muscle. • Lateral: Lobes of the thyroid gland and carotid sheath.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Distinguish the lingual tonsil from the palatine tonsil based on their distinct anatomical locations within the oral cavity and pharynx.
back: ● Lingual: Embedded in the posterior one-third of the tongue, posterior to the sulcus terminalis ● Palatine: Suspended on the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
front: The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the [___] and the [___].
back:
• Superior mesenteric vein
• Splenic vein
• Occurs at the level of L2 vertebra
• Lacks valves, allowing retrograde flow.

category: Discuss the clinical correlates of parotid gland: parotiditis, Mumps, Frey’s syndrome, parotid duct injury and parotid tumor surgery with its complications
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of facial nerve function in benign versus malignant parotid gland tumors.
back:
• Benign: Slowly growing, facial nerve function usually remains intact
• Malignant: Rapidly invasive, early facial nerve palsy (unilateral paralysis)
• Malignancy directly destroys nerve branches within the gland substance

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
front: Describe the physiological mechanism that ensures peritoneal fluid always flows toward the subphrenic spaces.
back:
Diaphragmatic Sucking Action

*   Respiratory movements create pressure gradients
*   Pulls fluid toward the extensive diaphragmatic peritoneum
*   Allows rapid absorption into subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: Describe how the innervation of the upper one-third of the esophagus differs from the lower two-thirds regarding muscle type.
back: 1. Upper 1/3: Striated muscle supplied by Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve. 2. Lower 2/3: Smooth muscle supplied by Vagus (Autonomic esophageal plexus).

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: Identify the four anatomical boundaries encountered during a horizontal trace of the epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow).
back:
* Anterior: Free edge of lesser omentum (portal triad)
* Posterior: Inferior Vena Cava (IVC)
* Superior: Caudate lobe of the liver
* Inferior: First part of the duodenum.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: List the primary anatomical factors that maintain the competency of the gastroesophageal junction against reflux.
back:
- Tone of the physiological lower esophageal sphincter.
- Right crus of the diaphragm (pinch-cock effect).
- Acute Angle of His.
- Phrenoesophageal ligament.

category: Describe the Waldeyer’s ring
front: Contrast the clinical consequences of hypertrophy in the superior component of Waldeyer's ring versus the tubal components in a pediatric patient.
back:
Superior (Pharyngeal): Leads to nasal obstruction, snoring, and mouth breathing. 
- Tubal: Causes blockage of the auditory tube, leading to middle ear effusion and hearing loss.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
front: Analyze the anatomical reason why the gallbladder is significantly less prone to gangrene compared to the vermiform appendix during acute inflammation.
back:
* The appendix has a single end-arterial supply (appendicular artery).
* The gallbladder has a dual supply: the cystic artery and small vessels from the liver bed.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: The sublingual salivary gland is situated immediately superior to the [___] muscle and lateral to the genioglossus muscle.
back:
Mylohyoid muscle.
- It sits in the sublingual fossa of the mandible.
- Creates the visible sublingual fold in the floor of the mouth.
- Primarily secretes mucous saliva.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Explain why the sigmoid colon is significantly more prone to volvulus than the ascending or descending colon.
back:
* Sigmoid colon is intraperitoneal with a long, mobile mesentery (sigmoid mesocolon).
* Ascending/descending colons are retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior abdominal wall.
* This mobility allows for axial rotation and torsion.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
front: Contrast the anatomical basis of pain felt in the right shoulder versus pain felt in the epigastrium during acute cholecystitis.
back:
• Shoulder: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) via irritation of diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum
• Epigastrium: Visceral afferents (T7-T9) via celiac plexus and splanchnic nerves.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
front: Contrast the direction of venous blood flow around the umbilicus in Caput Medusae versus Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) obstruction.
back:
*   Caput Medusae: Blood flows away from umbilicus (radiating)
*   IVC Obstruction: Blood flows upward from lower abdomen to axilla
*   IVC shunts via thoracoepigastric veins

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: A patient with a known peptic ulcer presents with severe, sudden-onset epigastric pain and board-like abdominal rigidity. Radiography shows air under the right dome of the diaphragm. Identify the anatomical site of rupture.
back:
• Anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
• Opens into the greater sac of the peritoneal cavity
• Causes rapid chemical peritonitis

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Describe the role of Peyer patches in the pathophysiology of pediatric ileocolic intussusception.
back:
* Patches: Lymphoid aggregations in the ileum
* Mechanism: Viral infection causes lymphoid hypertrophy/swelling
* Result: Enlarged patch acts as a 'lead point' for peristalsis to telescope ileum into cecum

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
front: The peritoneal fold that reflects horizontally between the liver's porta hepatis and the lesser curvature of the stomach is the [___].
back:
* Lesser omentum
* Composed of hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments
* Formed from the embryological ventral mesentery
* Contains the portal triad in its right free margin.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
front: The sickle-shaped free margin of the falciform ligament contains the [___], which is the fibrous remnant of the left umbilical vein.
back: * Ligamentum teres. * Connects the umbilicus to the liver. * Joins the left branch of the portal vein in the porta hepatis.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
coreConcept: Tributaries of the Inferior Mesenteric Vein
front: Identify the venous tributaries that form the Inferior Mesenteric Vein (IMV) and specify its role in the portal-systemic anastomosis.
back:
- Tributaries: Superior rectal, sigmoid, and left colic veins. 
- Role: Connects the portal system to systemic veins via the superior rectal vein anastomosing with middle/inferior rectal veins.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with dysphagia to both solids and liquids and chronic regurgitation. Imaging reveals a dilated proximal esophagus with a 'bird-beak' distal narrowing. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back: * Achalasia cardia. * Failure of the gastroesophageal sphincter to relax. * Caused by degeneration of the parasympathetic myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
front: Specify the anatomical location and general surface characteristics of the lingual tonsil.
back: ● Posterior Tongue Root ● Situated on the dorsal surface of the posterior third of the tongue ● Lacks a distinct capsule compared to palatine tonsils ● Features single crypts and lymphoid nodules beneath the epithelium.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Formation of the Common Hepatic Duct
front: The common hepatic duct is formed at the porta hepatis by the union of the [___] and [___] hepatic ducts.
back: Right and left hepatic ducts. They emerge from the liver lobes and represent the first extrahepatic component of the biliary tree.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
front: Identify the specific group of lymph nodes that receives drainage from the distal lesser curvature and the pyloric region before emptying into the celiac nodes.
back:
Right gastric lymph nodes.
- Located along the right gastric artery.
- Accompanied by pyloric nodes.
- Drain the distal third of the lesser curvature.
- Efferents pass to the celiac axis.

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
front: Contrast the tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini in terms of their anatomical pathways and primary effect on the palatine aponeurosis.
back:
• Tensor: Hooks around the pterygoid hamulus; tenses the palate horizontally
  • Levator: Enters the palate directly; elevates and retracts the palate posteriorly
  • Innervation: Tensor (V3) vs. Levator (CN X)

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The venous blood from the lower third of the esophagus primarily drains into the [___] vein, a key tributary of the portal system.
back:
• Left gastric vein.
• It anastomoses with the azygos system.
• Portal hypertension here leads to the development of esophageal varices.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Describe the dual mechanism by which Cholecystokinin (CCK) facilitates bile delivery from the biliary tree into the duodenum.
back:
• Stimulates contraction of the gallbladder smooth muscle
• Causes relaxation of the Sphincter of Oddi.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
front: In the internal view of a cadaveric stomach, the characteristic longitudinal folds of the mucosa that flatten out during distension are called [___].
back: Rugae (Gastric folds)

category: Describe the attachments, nerve supply and actions of muscles of soft palate
coreConcept: Vagus Nerve Lesion and Uvula Deviation
front: A patient presents with a sagging soft palate and the uvula deviates to the right when saying 'Ah.' Which cranial nerve is likely lesioned and on which side?
back:
• Left Vagus Nerve (CN X)
  • The uvula deviates away from the side of the lesion
  • Caused by paralysis of the levator veli palatini on the affected side

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
front: The [___] acts as a physiological sphincter at the junction of the small and large intestines, preventing the reflux of fecal matter into the terminal ileum.
back:
### Ileocecal Valve
* Formed by two horizontal mucosal folds.
* Controlled by the ileocecal sphincter (smooth muscle).
* Tone increases with cecal distension; relaxes with gastrin.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
front: Identify the specialized circular muscle that regulates the common exit of the biliary and pancreatic systems at the duodenal wall.
back:
• Sphincter of Oddi (Sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla)
  • Relaxes in response to cholecystokinin (CCK)
  • Contracts when fat is absent in the duodenum

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: The abdominal portion of the esophagus is primarily supplied by branches of the [___] artery.
back: • Left gastric artery. • A branch of the celiac trunk. • It also receives supply from the left inferior phrenic artery.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
front: Describe the neuroanatomical mechanism differentiating pain referral from central diaphragmatic irritation versus peripheral diaphragmatic irritation.
back:
• Central: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) refers pain to the shoulder tip.
• Peripheral: Lower intercostal nerves (T7-T11) refer pain to the overlying skin of the abdominal wall.
• Distinction helps differentiate subphrenic from lower thoracic pathology.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
front: A 45-year-old male undergoes an emergency appendectomy. The surgeon makes an oblique incision in the right iliac region, about 2 inches above and medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, splitting the abdominal muscles along their fiber direction. Identify this incision.
back:
* McBurney’s incision.
* Primarily used for appendectomy or cecostomy.
* Involves splitting the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles.
* Results in minimal postoperative weakness due to muscle-splitting rather than cutting.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Massive hematemesis in portal hypertension results from the rupture of varices at the gastroesophageal anastomosis, specifically involving the [___] gastric vein.
back:
• Left gastric (coronary) vein
• Anastomoses with systemic esophageal veins (azygos system)

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
front: Distinguish the clinical consequences of an anterior versus a posterior duodenal ulcer perforation.
back:
* Anterior: Perforates into the greater sac; causes generalized peritonitis
* Posterior: Erodes gastroduodenal artery; causes massive hemorrhage or enters the lesser sac

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Formation and Extent of Inguinal Ligament
front: The inguinal ligament is created by the thickened, folded-back lower border of the [___] aponeurosis, which extends between two specific bony landmarks.
back: - External oblique aponeurosis. - Extent: From anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to pubic tubercle. - Clinical role: Forms the floor of the inguinal canal.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
front: Name the final regional lymph node group that drains the entire stomach and must be evaluated in cases of gastric carcinoma.
back:
• Celiac lymph nodes
• Located around the root of the celiac artery
• Receives lymph from gastric, gastroepiploic, and short gastric nodes
• Ultimate destination for all stomach lymphatic drainage.

category: Identify the muscles of anterolateral abdominal wall on anatomical model and/or cadaver
front: The [___] is a triangular opening in the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle, situated superior and medial to the pubic tubercle, through which the spermatic cord or round ligament exits the inguinal canal.
back:
Superficial inguinal ring.
- Exit of the inguinal canal.
- Located in the external oblique aponeurosis.
- Transmits the spermatic cord (male) or round ligament (female).
- Boundaries are the medial and lateral crura.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of soft palate with its neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
front: A 25-year-old patient exhibits uvular deviation to the right when asked to say 'Ah'. Identify the specific cranial nerve and side affected.
back:
• Left Vagus Nerve (CN X).
• The uvula deviates toward the functional side.
• Indicates paralysis of the left levator veli palatini muscle.

category: Describe anatomical features, relations and neurovascular supply of submandibular and sublingual glands with their ducts
front: Describe the parasympathetic secretomotor pathway for the sublingual gland starting from the brainstem.
back:
* Superior salivatory nucleus → CN VII → Chorda tympani → Lingual nerve → Submandibular ganglion (synapse)
* Postganglionic fibers reach the sublingual gland directly

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
front: Describe the physiological significance of the portal vein's lack of valves in the context of retrograde blood flow.
back:
• Permits bidirectional flow
• High pressure in the liver (cirrhosis) forces blood backward
• Facilitates shunting into systemic circuits via various anastomoses

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Formation of the Common Bile Duct
front: Identify the location where the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct unite to form the bile duct.
back: The right free margin of the lesser omentum. This union typically occurs anterior to the portal vein and to the right of the hepatic artery.
